learningObjective: Recognize the clinical and genetic features of Miller-Dieker syndrome.
vignette: A 6-month-old infant presents with profound developmental delay, hypotonia, and intractable seizures. On examination, the infant exhibits severe microcephaly and distinct facial dysmorphisms, including micrognathia, low-set ears, a thin upper lip, a short nose with upturned nares, a prominent forehead, and bitemporal hollowing. MRI of the brain reveals classical lissencephaly (agyria).
leadIn: This presentation is most classically associated with a microdeletion involving which of the following?

options.rationale: The constellation of microcephaly, distinct facies (micrognathia, low-set ears, thin upper lip, short nose with upturned nares, prominent forehead, bitemporal hollowing), and lissencephaly defines Miller-Dieker syndrome. It is caused by microdeletions on chromosome 17 in the LIS1 gene, which encodes for a protein regulating microtubules and dynein function.
This option describes the deletion seen in Prader-Willi or Angelman syndromes.

options.text: Chromosome X in the DCX gene
options.rationale: This option describes X-linked lissencephaly, which primarily affects males but lacks the classic Miller-Dieker facial features.

options.text: Chromosome Xq28 in the FLNA gene
options.rationale: This option describes the mutation responsible for Periventricular Nodular Heterotopia.

learningObjective: Identify the primary biochemical defect in Nonketotic Hyperglycinemia.
leadIn: An infant presents with severe encephalopathy, hypotonia, myoclonic seizures, and respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. The cerebrospinal fluid to serum glycine ratio is 0.8 (normal <0.4). This catastrophic disorder is driven by a defect in 1 of 3 proteins that make up a specific enzymatic system. This defect leads to which of the following pathophysiologic consequences?

options.text: Accumulation of galactocerebrosides in macrophages of the white matter
options.rationale: This option describes Krabbe disease.

options.text: Defective copper transport across the intestinal membrane and the blood-brain barrier
options.rationale: This option describes Menkes disease.

options.text: Complete absence of mitochondrial glycine cleavage system function and accumulation of glycine in all body tissues
options.rationale: Nonketotic hyperglycinemia (glycine encephalopathy) is caused by a defect in 1 of 3 proteins that make up the mitochondrial glycine cleavage system. This leads to the complete absence of function and accumulation of glycine in all body tissues, including the CNS, driving the severe encephalopathy and seizures.

options.text: Impaired ability to oxidize very long chain fatty acids leading to peroxisomal accumulation
options.rationale: This option describes X-linked Adrenoleukodystrophy.

learningObjective: Diagnose Menkes disease based on its unique neurovascular presentation.
vignette: A 10-month-old male infant presents with severe developmental delay, hypotonia, and epilepsy. MRI and MRA of the brain reveal progressive cerebral atrophy, bilateral subdural hygromas, and a distinct cerebral vasculopathy characterized by tortuous and kinked intra- and extracranial vessels. Laboratory studies reveal low serum ceruloplasmin levels.
leadIn: The underlying pathophysiology of this disease involves a defect in the transport of which of the following elements?

options.rationale: This option describes molybdenum cofactor deficiency (sulfite oxidase deficiency).

options.text: Very long-chain fatty acids into the peroxisome
options.rationale: This option is the mechanism for X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

options.text: Copper across the intestinal membrane and blood-brain barrier
options.rationale: The triad of epilepsy, severe developmental delay, and cerebral vasculopathy with tortuous and kinked intra- and extracranial vessels (plus subdural hemorrhages/hygromas) is highly characteristic of Menkes disease. This X-linked recessive disorder is caused by defective copper transport across the intestinal membrane and across the blood-brain barrier, leading to low levels of copper in plasma, liver, and brain.
This option describes neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (PKAN).

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical and histologic hallmarks of Krabbe disease.
leadIn: A 6-month-old infant presents with extreme irritability, hypersensitivity to stimuli, and increasing hypertonicity with eventual opisthotonos. The infant is also noted to have unexplained low-grade fevers and optic atrophy resulting in blindness. A brain biopsy would classically demonstrate which of the following specific pathologic findings?

options.text: Accumulation of galactocerebrosides in macrophages leading to the formation of globoid cells, with sparing of U fibers
options.rationale: The clinical picture of extreme irritability, hypersensitivity, opisthotonos, and optic atrophy with blindness is the classic presentation of Krabbe disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy). The underlying mechanism leads to the accumulation of galactocerebrosides in macrophages, forming PAS+ multinucleated "globoid cells". A key radiologic/pathologic feature is progressive demyelination with sparing of the U fibers.

options.text: Metachromatic material accumulating in macrophages giving a "tigroid" appearance
options.rationale: This option describes Metachromatic Leukodystrophy.

options.text: Diffuse accumulation of Rosenthal fibers in the subpial and perivascular areas
options.rationale: This option describes Alexander disease.

options.text: Symmetric demyelination of cerebral white matter with predominant involvement of subcortical U fibers
options.rationale: This option describes Canavan disease, which involves U fibers.

learningObjective: Differentiate Sialidosis Type 1 from other cherry-red spot syndromes.
vignette: A 16-year-old adolescent presents with progressive action myoclonus, ataxia, and visual deterioration (loss of visual acuity and night blindness). Her intellect and cognitive functions are entirely normal, and she has no coarse facial features or skeletal abnormalities. Fundoscopic examination reveals bilateral cherry-red spots in the maculae.
leadIn: This presentation is caused by a deficiency of which of the following lysosomal enzymes?

options.rationale: The presentation of myoclonic epilepsy, visual deterioration, and cherry-red spots without dysmorphisms or cognitive decline in an adolescent is the classic description of Sialidosis Type 1. It is caused by a deficiency of lysosomal-alpha-N-acetyl neuraminidase (sialidase), leading to increased urinary excretion of sialic-acid containing oligosaccharides.
This option causes Tay-Sachs disease (infantile onset, severe regression).
This option causes Fabry disease.
This option deficiency (along with N-acetyl neuraminidase) causes Sialidosis Type 2, which features severe neurological features, coarse facial features, and severe dysostosis.

learningObjective: Correlate Infantile Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis with its electron microscopy findings.
leadIn: The neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCL) are a group of autosomal recessive disorders characterized by progressive psychomotor slowing, seizures, blindness, and myoclonic jerks. In the infantile form (CLN1 mutation), which of the following is the characteristic ultrastructural finding seen on electron microscopy of accumulated storage material?

options.rationale: Infantile NCL (CLN1 mutation) is characterized by neurons accumulating membrane-bound granular osmiophilic deposits on EM, which leads to neuronal loss and cortical atrophy.
This option is characteristic of Late Infantile NCL (CLN2).
This option is the hallmark of Alexander disease, a leukodystrophy.
This option is characteristic of Juvenile NCL (Batten's disease, CLN3).

learningObjective: Recognize the sequential cutaneous manifestations of Incontinentia Pigmenti.
vignette: A female neonate is evaluated in the nursery for the presence of widespread vesiculobullous skin lesions. The mother states she had multiple miscarriages of male fetuses. The infant is brought back to the clinic at 6 weeks of age, at which point the vesicular lesions have resolved but new verrucous (wart-like) lesions have appeared. The dermatologist predicts that as she grows, she will develop hyperpigmented lesions that follow the lines of Blaschko.
leadIn: This clinical progression is the hallmark of an X-linked dominant disorder known as:

options.rationale: Incontinentia pigmenti is an X-linked dominant disorder (lethal in males) defined by a highly specific, staged cutaneous progression: vesiculobullous lesions present at birth, verrucous lesions appearing around 6 weeks, and then hyperpigmented lesions following Blaschko lines (which may later fade to hypopigmentation or atresia).
This option features giant hairy nevi and leptomeningeal melanosis.
This option features slightly raised patches of hyperpigmentation present at birth (epidermal nevi) and is not staged in this classic vesiculobullous-to-verrucous manner.
This option features ash-leaf spots and shagreen patches.

learningObjective: Diagnose alobar holoprosencephaly based on core radiologic and gross anatomic features.
vignette: A stillborn fetus is autopsied following termination of a pregnancy complicated by severe midline facial defects. Examination of the brain reveals that the cerebral hemispheres are completely fused with an absence of the interhemispheric fissure and corpus callosum. The ventricular system consists of a single midline ventricle. Furthermore, there is complete absence of the olfactory bulb and tracts.
leadIn: The absence of the olfactory bulb and tracts in this specific disorder is termed:

options.rationale: This option is a neuronal migration disorder characterized by cerebrospinal fluid-filled clefts lined by gray matter extending from the ventricle to the pial surface.

The autopsy describes the most severe type of holoprosencephaly (alobar), defined by fused hemispheres, a single midline ventricle, and absent corpus callosum. The associated absence of the olfactory bulb and tracts (which typically develop when the prosencephalon divides) is specifically termed arrhinencephaly.
This option is enlargement of the central canal of the spinal cord.
This option refers to lissencephaly (smooth brain).

learningObjective: Correlate Epidermal Nevus Syndrome with hemi-megalencephaly.
vignette: A 3-year-old child presents with intellectual disability and poorly controlled seizures. Physical examination is notable for a slightly raised patch of hyperpigmentation on the left side of his face and scalp that has been present since birth and has slowly enlarged. MRI of the brain reveals severe asymmetric enlargement of the entire left cerebral hemisphere.
leadIn: This presentation is highly characteristic of which of the following neurocutaneous conditions?

options.rationale: This option presents with a facial port-wine stain and leptomeningeal angioma, leading to cerebral atrophy, not hemi-megalencephaly.
This option presents with progressive loss of facial tissue and cartilage leading to hemifacial atrophy.
This option does not classically feature large unilateral epidermal nevi or hemi-megalencephaly.

Epidermal nevus syndrome is defined by epidermal nevi (raised hyperpigmented patches present at birth/childhood) combined with neurological manifestations. The classic neurological triad includes intellectual disability, seizures, and ipsilateral brain malformations—most classically hemi-megalencephaly or lissencephaly.

learningObjective: Identify the genetic mutation and mechanism for Periventricular Nodular Heterotopia.
vignette: A 16-year-old female presents for evaluation of new-onset epilepsy. She has normal intelligence and a normal physical examination. Brain MRI demonstrates multiple nodules of tissue that are isointense to gray matter lining the walls of the lateral ventricles bilaterally. Family history reveals her mother also has epilepsy and has suffered multiple miscarriages of male fetuses.
leadIn: This condition is most commonly caused by a mutation in which of the following genes?

options.rationale: This option causes Alexander disease.
This option causes classic lissencephaly (Miller-Dieker).
This option causes X-linked lissencephaly in males and subcortical band heterotopia in females.

The patient has Periventricular Nodular Heterotopia (PVNH), which most commonly presents with seizures and learning disabilities. It is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by a mutation in the FLNA (Filamin A) gene on chromosome Xq28. This gene encodes a protein involved in cytoskeleton stabilization; its mutation impedes the attachment of neurons to the radial glia during migration. It is typically lethal in males.

learningObjective: Identify the expected clinical course of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS).
leadIn: A 40-year-old patient presents with a severe, recurrent "thunderclap" headache. Angiography reveals multifocal, segmental vasoconstriction of the cerebral arteries. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis is completely normal, ruling out primary CNS angiitis. By definition, to definitively confirm the diagnosis of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS), these angiographic changes must spontaneously resolve within what timeframe?

options.rationale: RCVS is by definition a self-limited vasculopathy whose angiographic changes resolve within 12 weeks. Persistence of vasoconstriction at 1 year would exclude RCVS and prompt evaluation for primary CNS angiitis or another persistent arteriopathy.
, and D provide incorrect diagnostic timeframes for the resolution of the vasospasm.
, and D provide incorrect diagnostic timeframes for the resolution of the vasospasm.
RCVS is characterized by severe headaches (with or without other neurological symptoms) and angiographic evidence of vasoconstriction of cerebral arteries that spontaneously resolves in 12 weeks.

learningObjective: Localize the Betz cells within the layers of the cerebral cortex.
leadIn: The neocortex is histologically divided into six distinct layers. The principal efferent projections for all motor-related subcortical structures, which include the giant Betz cells, are primarily located in which of the following cortical layers?

options.rationale: This option are incorrect cortical localizations for the giant pyramidal motor efferent cells.
This option are incorrect cortical localizations for the giant pyramidal motor efferent cells.
Layer 5 is the internal pyramidal cell layer. It contains the Betz cells and serves as the principal efferent pathway for all motor-related subcortical structures.
This option is the internal granular layer, which primarily receives afferent input from the thalamus.

learningObjective: Recognize the neurovascular and neuropathic manifestations of Fabry disease.
vignette: A 25-year-old male presents to the clinic with severe, episodic burning pain in his hands and feet (acroparesthesias) that is prominently induced by exposure to cold temperatures. Physical examination reveals punctate, non-blanching blue-black lesions (angiokeratomas) on his lower abdomen. The patient recently suffered an ischemic stroke, and neuroimaging revealed a dolichoectatic enlargement of the basilar artery.
leadIn: The underlying enzymatic deficiency in this disorder results in the toxic accumulation of which of the following substances in epithelial, mesenchymal, and neural cells?

options.rationale: The clinical triad of acroparesthesias (small fiber neuropathy induced by cold), angiokeratomas, and cerebrovascular disease (ischemic stroke due to vascular ectasia/dolichoectatic basilar artery) is diagnostic of Fabry disease. It is caused by an alpha-galactosidase deficiency, which results in the accumulation of ceramide trihexoside.
This option accumulates in Krabbe disease.
This option accumulates in Molybdenum cofactor deficiency.
This option accumulates in Adrenoleukodystrophy.

learningObjective: Identify the prevention and biomarker for Neural Tube Defects (NTDs).
leadIn: A pregnant woman at 16 weeks gestation undergoes prenatal screening, which reveals an elevated level of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). A subsequent fetal ultrasound demonstrates a failure of the posterior neuropore to fuse. According to established guidelines, maternal supplementation with which of the following is recommended prior to and during early pregnancy to prevent this specific class of anomalies?

options.rationale: This option are incorrect vitamins for the primary prevention of NTDs.
This option is a known teratogen that significantly increases the risk of NTDs.

Failure of the neural tube to close (open neuropore) allows fetal CSF components like AFP to leak, and the level of elevated AFP correlates directly with the degree of the neural tube defect (NTD). Maternal folate deficiency is a major risk factor, as folate is involved in nucleic acid synthesis and DNA methylation; supplementation with 0.4 mg of folic acid is universally recommended to prevent NTDs.
This option are incorrect vitamins for the primary prevention of NTDs.

learningObjective: Identify the target antibody in Rasmussen's encephalitis.
leadIn: A 6-year-old child presents with epilepsia partialis continua (EPC) and progressive unilateral neurologic dysfunction. Over time, the child develops a progressive hemiparesis and cognitive decline. MRI reveals progressive unilateral cortical atrophy. The pathophysiology of this inflammatory brain disease involves autoantibodies directed against which of the following targets?

options.rationale: This option is the target in Neuromyelitis Optica (NMO). -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Pediatric Neurology Clerkship Blueprint and Clinical Applications
This option is the target in LGI1 or CASPR2 encephalitis.

options.text: The GluR3 subunit of the AMPA receptor
options.rationale: Rasmussen's encephalitis is an inflammatory brain disease characterized by progressive unilateral cortical atrophy, progressive neurologic dysfunction (hemiparesis, cognitive decline), and epilepsia partialis continua (EPC). The pathophysiology is driven by autoantibodies targeting the GluR3 subunit of the AMPA receptor.

options.text: The NR1 subunit of the NMDA receptor
options.rationale: This option is the target in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

learningObjective: Distinguish developmental regression from developmental delay as a critical warning sign.
vignette: A 20-month-old girl is evaluated in the pediatric neurology clinic. Her parents report that she successfully learned to walk independently at 13 months and had a vocabulary of about 10 words. However, over the past three months, she has stopped speaking entirely and now prefers to crawl rather than walk.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate conceptual framework for the medical student to use when presenting this patient's history?

options.text: The patient is exhibiting developmental regression, which is a major red flag for a neurodegenerative or metabolic disorder.
options.rationale: During the clerkship, a core skill is differentiating delay from regression; regression is a critical warning sign that points toward a neurodegenerative or metabolic condition and requires urgent evaluation. This patient is losing previously acquired milestones, which defines regression.

options.text: The patient is exhibiting signs of an acute ischemic stroke.
options.rationale: This option is incorrect because an acute stroke presents with sudden, focal deficits rather than a subacute, global loss of milestones over months.

options.text: The patient is exhibiting isolated gross motor and language delay.
options.rationale: This option incorrectly minimize the loss of milestones as mere "delay" or "plateauing," which misses the clinical urgency of regression.

options.text: The patient is exhibiting a normal variant of developmental plateauing.
options.rationale: This option incorrectly minimize the loss of milestones as mere "delay" or "plateauing," which misses the clinical urgency of regression.

learningObjective: Differentiate central from peripheral hypotonia based on the physical examination.
vignette: A 4-month-old infant is consulted on for "floppiness." On examination, the medical student notes profound head lag and a "slip-through" sensation when the infant is held under the axillae. However, the infant is highly alert, tracks faces beautifully, and has brisk (3+) deep tendon reflexes in all extremities.
leadIn: This specific pattern of reflexes and consciousness most strongly suggests which of the following localizations?

options.rationale: , and D represent peripheral causes of hypotonia, which typically present with absent or depressed deep tendon reflexes and severe weakness, rather than hyperreflexia.

Skeletal muscle pathology (congenital myopathies, muscular dystrophies) is a peripheral cause of hypotonia and characteristically produces depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes. The brisk reflexes and preserved alertness here point to a central, not peripheral, localization.

A key clerkship skill is distinguishing central vs. peripheral hypotonia based on the pattern of reflexes, strength, and consciousness. Hypotonia accompanied by brisk reflexes and preserved alertness (normal consciousness) strongly localizes to the central nervous system (e.g., upper motor neuron lesions or cerebral palsy).
, and D represent peripheral causes of hypotonia, which typically present with absent or depressed deep tendon reflexes and severe weakness, rather than hyperreflexia.

learningObjective: Recognize the "red flags" for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy and select the appropriate initial screening test.
vignette: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because he falls frequently and has difficulty climbing stairs. The medical student observes the child rising from the floor by placing his hands on his knees and pushing himself upright. The student also notes bilateral enlargement of the calf muscles.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line screening laboratory test to order?

options.rationale: This option evaluates for Myasthenia Gravis.
This option screens for Guillain-Barré Syndrome (acute flaccid paralysis), not chronic progressive myopathy.

The child exhibits classic "red flags" for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), specifically the Gowers sign and calf pseudohypertrophy. The medical student must recognize these clues and understand that a serum creatine kinase (CK) level is the essential and most immediate screening test, as it will be massively elevated.
This option evaluates for Strep pharyngitis, relevant for Sydenham chorea, not a myopathy.

learningObjective: Recognize the semiology of infantile spasms and understand the urgency of treatment.
vignette: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department. The parents show the medical student a video of the baby abruptly flexing his head, trunk, and arms forward in a "jackknife" motion. These movements occur in clusters of 10 to 15, primarily just after the baby wakes up.
leadIn: The medical student should recognize this presentation as an emergency because delayed treatment is heavily associated with which of the following?

options.text: Progression to recurrent febrile status epilepticus
options.rationale: , and D are incorrect consequences. The primary medical emergency of infantile spasms is the profound, permanent cognitive and developmental devastation.
, and D are incorrect consequences. The primary medical emergency of infantile spasms is the profound, permanent cognitive and developmental devastation.

options.text: Severe developmental impact and epileptic encephalopathy
options.rationale: The clinical description is classic for infantile spasms, a critical topic for medical students on a child neurology rotation. Students must recognize the classic age, semiology, and the urgency of treatment due to the risk of severe developmental impact if the underlying epileptic encephalopathy (hypsarrhythmia) is not rapidly arrested.

Infantile spasms do not carry an increased risk of sudden cardiac arrest. The urgency of treatment relates to preventing the catastrophic cognitive and developmental impact of ongoing hypsarrhythmia and untreated epileptic encephalopathy.

learningObjective: Differentiate childhood absence seizures from behavioral daydreaming.
vignette: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because her teacher reports she frequently "zones out" during class. The episodes last 5 to 10 seconds, during which she stares blankly and exhibits subtle eye fluttering. She does not respond to her name during the events and resumes her schoolwork immediately afterward without confusion.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely electroencephalogram (EEG) correlate for these episodes?

options.rationale: This option suggests a focal structural lesion rather than a primary generalized absence seizure.
This option is the EEG pattern for infantile spasms.

Distinguishing absence seizures vs daydreaming and knowing the basic EEG correlation is a high-yield clerkship topic. The brief staring spells with eye fluttering, lack of responsiveness, and immediate recovery define absence seizures, which classically correlate with 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges on EEG.

options.text: Normal waking background with no epileptiform abnormalities
options.rationale: This option would be expected if the child were simply daydreaming or inattentive, which does not fit the classic clinical seizure description.

learningObjective: Identify red-flag secondary causes of headache in children.
vignette: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for headaches that have been occurring daily for the past month. The medical student takes the history and notes that the headaches are most severe right after waking up in the morning and are frequently accompanied by forceful vomiting. On physical examination, the student visualizes blurred optic disc margins bilaterally.
leadIn: The medical student should urgently propose which of the following as the next step in management?

options.text: Initiate a trial of sumatriptan for pediatric migraine
options.rationale: This option are treatments for primary headaches, which is inappropriate when dangerous red flags are present.

options.text: Obtain an urgent neuroimaging study (e.g., MRI or CT of the brain)
options.rationale: Medical students must differentiate primary headaches (migraine vs. tension) from red-flag secondary causes (e.g., tumor, increased intracranial pressure). The pattern of morning headache, morning vomiting, and papilledema check abnormalities are absolute indications for urgent neuroimaging to rule out a space-occupying lesion.

options.text: Prescribe ibuprofen and schedule a follow-up in one month
options.rationale: This option are treatments for primary headaches, which is inappropriate when dangerous red flags are present.

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is a classic presentation of tension headache
options.rationale: This option is incorrect as tension headaches do not cause papilledema or daily morning vomiting.

learningObjective: Recognize sickle cell disease as a primary risk factor for pediatric stroke.
vignette: An 8-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with the sudden onset of right-sided facial droop, slurred speech, and weakness in his right arm. During the neurologic history, the medical student explores potential risk factors for this acute focal deficit.
leadIn: A past medical history of which of the following conditions is the most highly relevant risk factor for this patient's acute presentation?

options.rationale: In the pediatric population, recognizing unilateral weakness or speech change as an emergency requires an understanding of pediatric stroke risk factors. Sickle cell disease is a major, high-yield cause of pediatric stroke and arteriopathies.
This option causes seizures, not classic acute focal ischemic strokes.
This option is associated with tumors (optic gliomas) and cognitive issues, but sickle cell is the classic textbook risk factor for pediatric ischemic stroke.
This option causes chronic progressive weakness, not acute stroke.

learningObjective: Identify post-varicella arteriopathy as a cause of childhood stroke.
leadIn: While taking a focused neurologic history for a 5-year-old child presenting with an acute ischemic stroke of the basal ganglia, the medical student asks the caregivers about recent infections. A history of an active infection with which of the following viruses 6 months prior is a well-recognized cause of pediatric focal cerebral arteriopathy?

options.rationale: Rotavirus causes acute gastroenteritis and does not have an established association with cerebral arteriopathy or pediatric arterial ischemic stroke.

A high-yield clerkship topic in pediatric stroke is identifying infectious risk factors. Post-varicella arteriopathy is a classic, testable cause of unilateral weakness and ischemic stroke in children.
, and D are common childhood viruses but are not the classic, highly tested infectious trigger for large vessel cerebral arteriopathy in children.
, and D are common childhood viruses but are not the classic, highly tested infectious trigger for large vessel cerebral arteriopathy in children.

learningObjective: Formulate a management plan for a simple febrile seizure.
vignette: A 14-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after experiencing a 2-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. In the ED, she has a temperature of 102.5°F (39.2°C) and is diagnosed with acute otitis media. She is now fully awake, playful, and back to her baseline neurologic status. This is her first seizure.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management for the medical student to propose to the attending?

options.text: Reassure the parents, treat the otitis media, and provide education on simple febrile seizures
options.rationale: The patient had a classic simple febrile seizure (generalized, <15 minutes, solitary event in 24 hours, returning to baseline). Clerkship students must understand febrile seizures (simple vs complex, workup, counseling). Simple febrile seizures do not require EEG, MRI, or daily anti-seizure prophylaxis; reassurance and counseling are the standard of care.

options.text: Order an urgent MRI of the brain
options.rationale: , and C represent unnecessary, over-aggressive testing and treatment for a simple febrile seizure.

options.text: Prescribe a daily prophylactic anti-seizure medication
options.rationale: Daily prophylactic anti-seizure medication is explicitly not recommended for simple febrile seizures. The risks of chronic AED therapy outweigh both the modest recurrence risk and the very small (~1%) excess lifetime epilepsy risk.
, and C represent unnecessary, over-aggressive testing and treatment for a simple febrile seizure.

learningObjective: Understand the indications and risks of ordering an MRI with sedation in a young child.
leadIn: A medical student suggests ordering a brain MRI for a 2-year-old patient with new-onset developmental regression. The attending agrees but asks the student to explain the logistical plan to the parents. To safely obtain a high-quality, motion-free MRI in a patient of this age, the student must counsel the family about the risks and necessity of which of the following?

options.text: Lumbar puncture prior to the scan
options.rationale: This option is not a prerequisite for an MRI.

options.text: Placement of a central venous catheter
options.rationale: This option is unnecessary; standard peripheral IV access is sufficient for contrast or sedation.
This option applies to nuclear medicine scans (e.g., PET/SPECT), not standard MRI.

A practical clerkship competency is understanding the indications, basics of how to consent, and major risks for... MRI with sedation in kids. Children under age 6 typically cannot remain perfectly still for the duration of an MRI, making procedural sedation or general anesthesia a practical necessity and a primary point of informed consent.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation of acute chorea (Sydenham chorea).
vignette: A 10-year-old girl is evaluated for new, involuntary, "dance-like" movements of her arms and face that started three days ago. Her parents also note she has become extremely emotionally lable. A review of her chart reveals she was treated for a severe sore throat and fever one month ago.
leadIn: The medical student should recognize this presentation as an acute movement disorder heavily associated with which of the following underlying etiologies?

options.text: Acute ischemic stroke of the cerebellum
options.rationale: This option causes ataxia, not chorea.
This option causes rigidity and bradykinesia, not chorea.

The presentation of chorea and emotional lability following a recent pharyngitis is classic for Sydenham chorea. Recognizing acute chorea (Sydenham, autoimmune) is a core, high-yield movement disorder topic for pediatric neurology clerkships.
This option describes Parkinson's disease, not an acute pediatric chorea.

learningObjective: Differentiate motor tics from focal motor seizures.
vignette: A 9-year-old boy presents with repetitive, rapid blinking and frequent shoulder shrugging. The parents are worried he is having seizures. The medical student observes the child and asks him if he can stop the movements. The boy replies, "I can stop them for a little while if I try really hard, but then I get a weird feeling in my shoulder and I just have to do it."
leadIn: This clinical description best supports which of the following localizations/diagnoses?

options.rationale: Differentiating tics vs. seizures is a fundamental clerkship skill in pediatric movement disorders. Tics are characterized by premonitory urges ("a weird feeling") and are temporarily suppressible by voluntary effort, whereas focal motor seizures are entirely unsuppressible and lack a premonitory sensory urge.
This option features staring spells with loss of awareness, not suppressible shoulder shrugging.
This option features hypertonia and upper motor neuron signs, not suppressible rapid movements.
This option is incorrect because seizures cannot be voluntarily suppressed.

learningObjective: Identify the basic skin findings associated with Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1).
leadIn: A medical student is performing a physical examination on a 6-year-old child referred for developmental delay. During the skin exam, the student notes six large, flat, hyperpigmented oval patches on the child's trunk and freckling in the axillae. The student should immediately suspect which of the following neurocutaneous syndromes?

options.rationale: Recognizing "must recognize" neurocutaneous syndromes like NF1, TSC, and Sturge-Weber, including basic skin findings and associated CNS issues is explicitly required for students. Café-au-lait spots and axillary freckling are the hallmark cutaneous findings of NF1.
This option is characterized by a facial port-wine stain.
This option is characterized by hypopigmented (ash-leaf) spots, not hyperpigmented café-au-lait macules.
This option is characterized by ocular and cutaneous telangiectasias.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical clues for Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA).
leadIn: A 5-month-old infant is evaluated for failure to meet motor milestones. The medical student performs a neurologic exam and notes severe, symmetric, flaccid weakness, diffuse areflexia, and a bell-shaped chest. Which of the following diagnoses should be at the top of the differential as a "must-recognize" pediatric neuromuscular emergency?

options.rationale: This option is a seizure disorder of adolescence.
This option presents with spasticity (hypertonia) and hyperreflexia, not flaccid areflexia.
This option typically presents in older toddlers/preschoolers with calf pseudohypertrophy and proximal weakness, rather than profound infantile areflexia.

Recognizing SMA clues and indications to refer quickly is a core objective. The combination of severe flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and normal cognition in an infant is the classic presentation of Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a disease of the anterior horn cells. Early recognition is vital due to the availability of time-sensitive gene therapies.

learningObjective: Identify signs of increased intracranial pressure and shunt malfunction.
blueprintTopic: Brain and Spinal Trauma / Critical Care
vignette: A 4-year-old boy with a history of congenital hydrocephalus treated with a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is brought to the emergency department. He has been complaining of a severe headache, has vomited three times this morning, and now appears extraordinarily lethargic.
leadIn: The medical student should recognize this presentation as an emergency and advocate for immediate evaluation for which of the following?

options.rationale: This option involves a fever and a brief seizure, which does not fit this history.

options.text: Shunt malfunction and increased intracranial pressure (ICP)
options.rationale: A key pediatric neuro emergency is recognizing shunt malfunction and increased ICP signs. Headache, vomiting, and lethargy in a child with a VP shunt are the classic triad of shunt failure leading to life-threatening hydrocephalus.
This option presents with acute spinal cord signs (paraplegia, sensory level), not classic increased ICP.
This option manifests as continuous clinical or electrographic seizures, not isolated headache/vomiting/lethargy.

learningObjective: Differentiate seizure, syncope, and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES).
vignette: A 15-year-old boy collapses while standing in the hot sun during a lengthy choir assembly. Witnesses report he appeared pale and sweaty just before falling. While on the ground, he had three brief, asynchronous jerks of his arms. He woke up less than a minute later, knew where he was, and did not experience any tongue biting or loss of bowel control.
leadIn: Based on the medical student's knowledge of episodic disorders, what is the most likely etiology of this event?

options.rationale: This option typically features prolonged, variable, emotionally triggered thrashing with forced eye closure, not a classic orthostatic collapse.
This option typically lack the orthostatic/heat prodrome and are followed by a significant post-ictal period of confusion and lethargy.
This option typically lack the orthostatic/heat prodrome and are followed by a significant post-ictal period of confusion and lethargy.

Differentiating seizure vs. syncope vs. PNES is a core clerkship skill. The prodrome of pallor/diaphoresis in a provocative setting (prolonged standing/heat), followed by a brief loss of consciousness with minor myoclonic jerks (convulsive syncope) and an immediate, clear-headed recovery is the textbook presentation of vasovagal syncope.

learningObjective: Recognize acute flaccid paralysis and the need to rule out spinal cord compression.
vignette: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the ED with acute onset of severe back pain and rapidly progressive weakness in both legs. During the neurologic exam, the medical student notes that she has 1/5 strength in her lower extremities, absent reflexes at the knees and ankles, and a distinct loss of pinprick sensation below her umbilicus.
leadIn: This presentation requires emergent neuroimaging (MRI) to rule out which of the following conditions?

options.rationale: This option causes fatigable weakness (ptosis, bulbar signs) without a distinct sensory level.

options.text: Spinal cord compression or transverse myelitis
options.rationale: Evaluating "Back pain with neuro signs" (cauda equina, cord compression, transverse myelitis) is a "must-master" emergency skill. The presence of a sensory level (umbilicus) with acute paraparesis and back pain points directly to a spinal cord localization, necessitating urgent MRI to rule out a compressive lesion.

options.text: Stroke of the middle cerebral artery
options.rationale: This option causes unilateral face and arm weakness, not paraparesis with a thoracic sensory level.
This option is an epilepsy syndrome.

learningObjective: Associate hypomelanotic macules and infantile spasms with Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.
leadIn: A medical student is evaluating a 7-month-old infant who presents with developmental delay and clusters of epileptic spasms. Using a Wood's lamp, the student identifies three ash-leaf shaped hypopigmented macules on the infant's trunk. This combination of findings strongly supports a diagnosis of which of the following?

options.rationale: This option features a facial port-wine stain.
This option is a muscular dystrophy, not a neurocutaneous disorder causing infantile spasms.

The clerkship student must possess a pattern-recognition level understanding of neurocutaneous syndromes. The triad of infantile spasms, developmental delay, and hypomelanotic (ash-leaf) macules is highly characteristic of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC).
This option features café-au-lait spots, not ash-leaf spots.

learningObjective: Identify the pattern of spastic diplegic cerebral palsy and its association with prematurity.
vignette: An 18-month-old boy is evaluated in the clinic for motor delays. He was born prematurely at 28 weeks gestation. The medical student examines the child and notes significant spasticity and hyperreflexia in both legs, while the arms have relatively normal tone and strength.
leadIn: The medical student correctly hypothesizes that this child's movement disorder represents which of the following patterns of cerebral palsy?

options.rationale: A key clerkship topic is understanding hypotonia vs. spasticity and cerebral palsy patterns. A history of extreme prematurity coupled with spasticity that affects the lower extremities significantly more than the upper extremities is the classic description of spastic diplegic cerebral palsy.
This option affects one entire side of the body (arm and leg), typically due to a focal perinatal stroke.
This option features involuntary twisting movements, often due to basal ganglia injury (kernicterus).
This option features primary incoordination and balance issues, localizing to the cerebellum.

learningObjective: Recognize the basic algorithm concept for treating pediatric status epilepticus.
blueprintTopic: Epilepsy and Episodic Disorders / Critical Care
vignette: The pediatric neurology team is called to the emergency department for a 5-year-old child who has been having a continuous, generalized convulsive seizure for the past 15 minutes despite an initial dose of rectal diazepam given by parents at home.
leadIn: When the medical student is asked to propose the next step in the treatment algorithm, they should emphasize which of the following core concepts?

options.text: Awaiting a stat MRI before administering further medications
options.rationale: This option are incorrect because diagnostic tests (MRI, LP) should never delay the emergent administration of life-saving abortive anti-seizure medications.

options.text: Performing an immediate lumbar puncture to rule out meningitis
options.rationale: This option are incorrect because diagnostic tests (MRI, LP) should never delay the emergent administration of life-saving abortive anti-seizure medications.

options.text: Administering a rapidly acting intravenous benzodiazepine using weight-based dosing
options.rationale: A "must master" emergency for students is the status epilepticus algorithm basics and weight-based dosing concept. The immediate priority in a patient with ongoing status epilepticus is terminating the seizure with a weight-based dose of a first-line IV/IM benzodiazepine (e.g., lorazepam or midazolam).

options.text: Discharging the patient with reassurance if the seizure stops within the next 10 minutes
options.rationale: This option is inappropriate because a 15-minute seizure constitutes impending/established status epilepticus, requiring medical intervention and admission/observation, not immediate discharge.

learningObjective: Identify venous sinus thrombosis as a pediatric stroke etiology.
vignette: A 4-year-old girl is admitted with acute dehydration secondary to severe gastroenteritis. On hospital day 2, she develops a severe headache, papilledema, and new-onset focal motor seizures of her right arm.
leadIn: The medical student should recognize that this clinical picture (dehydration, increased ICP, focal seizures) strongly suggests which of the following pediatric vascular emergencies?

options.rationale: This option cause arterial ischemic strokes, which present with focal deficits but typically lack the diffuse increased ICP signs (papilledema) driven by impaired venous drainage seen in venous thrombosis.

In the pediatric stroke curriculum, students must recognize specific causes like sickle cell, arteriopathies, and venous sinus thrombosis. The classic presentation of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis in a child involves a hypercoagulable state (e.g., severe dehydration or infection), leading to signs of increased ICP (headache, papilledema) and focal neurological deficits or seizures.

This option cause arterial ischemic strokes, which present with focal deficits but typically lack the diffuse increased ICP signs (papilledema) driven by impaired venous drainage seen in venous thrombosis.
This option is a diagnosis of exclusion in a patient with acute focal seizures and papilledema.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical phenotype of Rett syndrome.
leadIn: A medical student is reviewing the chart of a 3-year-old girl coming into the clinic. The chart notes that she developed normally until 18 months of age, at which point she began to lose her expressive language and purposeful hand use. She concurrently developed repetitive hand-wringing stereotypies and an abnormal gait. This specific pattern of regression is highly characteristic of which of the following syndromes?

options.rationale: This option are neurocutaneous syndromes defined by specific skin lesions and tumors.

The clerkship guide emphasizes knowing high-yield syndromes like Fragile X, Rett, and leukodystrophies at a pattern-recognition level. The classic phenotype of normal early development followed by severe regression (loss of speech and purposeful hand use) and the emergence of midline hand-wringing stereotypies almost exclusively in females defines Rett syndrome.
This option are neurocutaneous syndromes defined by specific skin lesions and tumors.
This option is a common cause of inherited intellectual disability and autism, particularly in males, but does not feature this specific pattern of profound loss of hand skills and hand-wringing.

learningObjective: Demonstrate appropriate professional communication skills when presenting a clinical plan to a family.
vignette: A 10-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a first-time, unprovoked generalized tonic-clonic seizure. The medical student performs a thorough neurologic history and examination, which are completely normal. The attending neurologist asks the student to practice explaining the assessment and plan to the parents.
leadIn: Based on core clerkship competencies, which of the following is the best approach for the student to take?

options.text: Explain the localization and diagnostic uncertainty in simple, accessible language, and offer a clear, simple plan (e.g., ordering an outpatient EEG).
options.rationale: A core clerkship behavior is practicing explaining localization and uncertainty in simple language and learning how your team delivers new diagnoses... and long-term prognostic discussions. A first-time seizure often involves diagnostic uncertainty, and offering a clear, simple plan (like an EEG) in layman's terms is the expected professional standard.

options.text: Avoid mentioning any uncertainty to ensure the parents do not become anxious.
options.rationale: This option are unprofessional and unethical, as guaranteeing outcomes or hiding uncertainty violates truth-telling and informed consent principles.

options.text: Guarantee the parents that the child will never have another seizure.
options.rationale: This option are unprofessional and unethical, as guaranteeing outcomes or hiding uncertainty violates truth-telling and informed consent principles.

options.text: Use complex neuroanatomical terminology to demonstrate competence to the parents.
options.rationale: This option violates the principle of using simple, accessible language.

learningObjective: Formulate a basic localization hypothesis for a patient with altered mental status.
vignette: The neurology consult team is called to see a 16-year-old patient in the ICU. The patient has been "unresponsive" for 24 hours. The medical student performs a neurologic exam. When the student applies a sternal rub, the patient grimaces and purposefully pushes the student's hand away with both his right and left arms. His brainstem reflexes (pupillary, corneal) are entirely intact.
leadIn: When presenting this patient to the attending, the student should propose which of the following localizations as the least likely cause of the patient's altered mental status?

options.text: Massive structural lesion destroying the brainstem
options.rationale: A key clerkship skill is formulating a localized hypothesis: "Always come with a localized hypothesis when presenting" and understanding the differential for "Altered mental status" (delirium vs metabolic vs nonconvulsive status). Because the patient has intact brainstem reflexes and symmetric purposeful motor responses, the brainstem is functioning. Therefore, a massive brainstem-destroying lesion is the least likely localization.
, and D are all highly likely causes of diffuse altered mental status (coma/delirium) that leave brainstem pathways intact.

Diffuse cortical dysfunction (post-anoxic injury, severe metabolic encephalopathy) can cause profound unresponsiveness while sparing brainstem reflexes, and remains a real consideration in this presentation. It is not the *least* likely cause.
, and D are all highly likely causes of diffuse altered mental status (coma/delirium) that leave brainstem pathways intact.

learningObjective: Adapt the neurologic examination for pediatric patients.
leadIn: A medical student is beginning their child neurology rotation and is preparing to examine a 2-month-old infant. According to clerkship guidelines for adapting the neurologic exam by age, which of the following specific examination components is uniquely essential for this infant compared to an adult patient?

options.text: Detailed assessment of tandem gait and Romberg sign
options.rationale: , and D represent components of the adult neurological exam that require the patient to follow complex commands or walk, which is impossible in a 2-month-old infant. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- NM & Neurodevelopmental Board Review (25)

options.text: Formal visual field testing by confrontation
options.rationale: , and D represent components of the adult neurological exam that require the patient to follow complex commands or walk, which is impossible in a 2-month-old infant. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- NM & Neurodevelopmental Board Review (25)

options.text: Two-point discrimination testing of the lower extremities
options.rationale: Two-point discrimination requires verbal report and cooperation that a 2-month-old cannot provide. It is not part of the infant neurologic examination.

options.text: Assessment of primitive reflexes, tone, and head control
options.rationale: A "must master" skill on the neuro rotation is adapting the exam by age—infant primitive reflexes, tone, head control, visual tracking. Infants cannot follow commands, so the exam relies heavily on observational tone, primitive reflexes (e.g., Moro, rooting), and developmental posture (head control).

learningObjective: Recognize the unique clinical presentation and genetic defect of Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy.
vignette: A 6-month-old infant is evaluated for delayed motor milestones and generalized weakness. Physical examination reveals severe proximal joint contractures at the elbows and knees, but striking hyperlaxity of the distal joints, including the wrists and ankles. The infant also has prominent protrusion of the calcanei.
leadIn: A genetic mutation affecting which of the following proteins is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

options.rationale: This option mutations cause Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy, which feature calf pseudohypertrophy and Gowers sign, not the classic proximal contracture/distal hyperlaxity combination.

Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy classically presents with neonatal weakness, proximal joint contractures, striking distal joint hyperlaxity, and protrusion of the calcanei. It is caused by a mutation in the collagen type VI gene.
This option mutations cause Spinal Muscular Atrophy, which presents with profound flaccid paralysis and areflexia, without the specific distal hyperlaxity and prominent calcanei.
This option mutations cause Central Core Myopathy, which presents with proximal weakness and malignant hyperthermia risk, but lacks the distinct contracture/hyperlaxity presentation.

learningObjective: Identify the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) age guidelines for routine autism spectrum disorder screening.
leadIn: The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends utilizing standardized, validated tools such as the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT) to screen for autism spectrum disorders. At which of the following well-child visits is routine, specific autism screening explicitly recommended?

options.rationale: The AAP Bright Futures guidelines recommend specific screening for autism spectrum disorder at the 18-month and 24-month well-child visits.
This option and
This option is incorrect, as the first screening should happen earlier at 18 months to facilitate early intervention.
This option are incorrect; while general developmental surveillance happens at every visit, autism-specific screening occurs later.

learningObjective: Differentiate Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) Type 1 from other hypotonic infant presentations based on exam and EMG findings.
vignette: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the clinic for profound hypotonia and weak cry. The mother notes decreased fetal movements during the third trimester. On examination, the infant lies in a "frog-leg" posture, demonstrates diffuse areflexia, and has prominent tongue fasciculations. The infant is completely unable to achieve antigravity movements in the arms or legs.
leadIn: Which of the following electromyography (EMG) findings is most consistent with this infant's diagnosis?

options.text: Electrodecremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation
options.rationale: This option describes a neuromuscular junction transmission defect, such as myasthenia gravis.

options.text: Acute and chronic denervation/reinnervation with large polyphasic motor units
options.rationale: The clinical picture of profound infantile hypotonia, frog-leg posture, diffuse areflexia, and bulbar involvement (tongue fasciculations) represents Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) Type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffman disease). Because this is an anterior horn cell (motor neuron) disease, EMG shows acute and chronic denervation and reinnervation with large polyphasic motor units.

options.text: Severe slowing of conduction velocities with conduction block
options.rationale: This option describes a demyelinating peripheral neuropathy, such as Guillain-Barré syndrome or Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1.

options.text: Myopathic process with positive sharp waves and small, polyphasic motor units
options.rationale: This option describes a primary myopathy (e.g., congenital myopathy or muscular dystrophy).

learningObjective: Recognize the risk factors and clinical presentation of spastic diplegic cerebral palsy.
vignette: An 18-month-old boy with a history of extreme prematurity and bilateral intraventricular hemorrhages is evaluated for motor delays. He is currently not walking. On examination, he has significantly increased tone in his lower extremities compared to his upper extremities. When he is lifted vertically by his axillae, his legs demonstrate prominent "scissoring."
leadIn: This clinical presentation is most strongly associated with ischemic injury to which of the following brain regions?

options.rationale: This option injury or malformation causes ataxic cerebral palsy or Dandy-Walker malformation symptoms.
This option injury in term infants typically causes watershed infarcts, which can cause proximal limb weakness, but PVL is the hallmark of preterm spastic diplegia.

Spastic diplegia is the most common form of cerebral palsy seen in preterm infants. It typically affects the legs more than the arms and presents with scissoring of the legs when held vertically and hyperreflexia. It is classically caused by periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), which is ischemic damage to the periventricular white matter where the descending corticospinal tracts for the lower extremities run.
This option injury, often from kernicterus or profound asphyxia, results in dyskinetic/choreoathetoid cerebral palsy.

learningObjective: Diagnose Walker-Warburg syndrome based on the triad of muscular dystrophy, brain malformations, and ocular anomalies.
vignette: A neonate is evaluated in the NICU for profound generalized hypotonia and an elevated creatine kinase (CK) level. Ophthalmologic examination reveals bilateral microphthalmia, congenital cataracts, and retinal dysplasia. Brain MRI demonstrates severe hydrocephalus, cerebellar hypoplasia, and a completely unlayered cortex consistent with cobblestone lissencephaly.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option also features cobblestone lissencephaly but typically lacks the severe structural anterior eye defects (like microphthalmia and cataracts) seen in Walker-Warburg.
This option can present with neonatal hypotonia and cataracts, but it does not cause cobblestone lissencephaly or microphthalmia.
This option shares a similar triad but is clinically milder; cortical changes are less severe, and the eyes are not as profoundly affected as in Walker-Warburg syndrome.

The classic triad of congenital muscular dystrophy (hypotonia, elevated CK), severe brain malformations (hydrocephalus, cobblestone lissencephaly, cerebellar hypoplasia), and severe ocular anomalies (microphthalmia, retinal dysplasia, cataracts) characterizes Walker-Warburg syndrome. It is an autosomal recessive disorder.

learningObjective: Identify normal developmental variants in reading skills to avoid overdiagnosing learning disorders.
leadIn: Parents of a 6-year-old first-grader express concern to their pediatrician because the child occasionally reverses the letters "b" and "d" when reading and writing. The child's vision and hearing screens are normal, and he is otherwise meeting all developmental milestones. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice regarding this finding?

options.text: The child should undergo a comprehensive ophthalmologic evaluation for visual tracking deficits.
options.rationale: This option is incorrect because a reading disorder is a neurocognitive deficit in phonological processing, not a primary visual deficit.

options.text: The child requires an immediate psychoeducational evaluation for a specific learning disorder (dyslexia).
options.rationale: This option is incorrect as this is a normal variant at age 6; a full psychoeducational evaluation is premature.

options.text: Letter reversal at this age is a normal developmental finding and is not diagnostic of a reading disorder.
options.rationale: Letter reversals are a common finding in typically developing children up to 7 years old and are not, by themselves, diagnostic of a reading disorder. Education of the family is critical to avoid unnecessary anxiety and over-testing.

options.text: The child should be initiated on a trial of stimulant medication for suspected inattention.
options.rationale: This option is inappropriate, as there is no evidence of ADHD in the vignette.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation and specific autonomic features of infant botulism.
vignette: An 8-month-old previously healthy infant is brought to the emergency department for progressive weakness over the past 4 days. The parents report the infant has not had a bowel movement in 5 days and has been feeding poorly. On examination, the infant has severe generalized hypotonia, a weak cry, and absent deep tendon reflexes. Pupillary examination reveals sluggish, poorly reactive pupils.
leadIn: The parents' dietary history is most likely to reveal recent ingestion of which of the following?

options.rationale: Infant botulism presents with constipation (often the first sign), poor feeding, descending flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, and distinct autonomic signs such as sluggish pupillary reflexes. In infants, it is classically caused by the ingestion of Clostridium botulinum spores found in raw honey or soil, which germinate in the infant's immature intestinal tract.
This option carries risks for Listeria, Campylobacter, and Brucella, but is not the classic vehicle for infant botulism.
This option is the classic vehicle for foodborne botulism (ingestion of preformed toxin), which typically affects adults, whereas infants ingest spores from honey.
This option is a classic cause of folate-deficiency macrocytic anemia in infants, not botulism.

learningObjective: Identify early handedness as a red flag for hemiplegic cerebral palsy.
vignette: A 9-month-old infant is brought to the clinic for a routine well-child check. The mother proudly reports that the infant is already showing a strong preference for using his right hand to reach for objects and feed himself. The infant was born at term but required a brief NICU stay for presumed neonatal seizures.
leadIn: The pediatrician should recognize this "early handedness" as a potential red flag for which of the following conditions?

options.rationale: , and D are neurodevelopmental and neuromuscular disorders, but they do not characteristically present with early asymmetric hand preference.

ADHD is a behavioral diagnosis made in school-aged children based on inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. It does not present in infancy with motor asymmetry and is unrelated to early hand preference.
, and D are neurodevelopmental and neuromuscular disorders, but they do not characteristically present with early asymmetric hand preference.

Hand preference typically does not develop until after 1 year of age. The development of hand preference before age one is a significant red flag for possible hemiplegia (spastic hemiplegic cerebral palsy) affecting the contralateral limb. This infant's history of neonatal seizures further raises the suspicion for a perinatal stroke, the most common cause of hemiplegic cerebral palsy.

learningObjective: Identify the genetic mutation and associated anesthetic risk in Central Core Myopathy.
leadIn: A 2-year-old child with delayed motor development and proximal muscle weakness undergoes a muscle biopsy, which demonstrates central areas within muscle fibers that lack oxidative enzyme activity. Genetic testing confirms Central Core Myopathy. This disorder is autosomal dominant and is caused by a mutation in the ryanodine receptor (RYR1) gene. Because of this specific mutation, the patient is at extremely high risk for which of the following complications during surgical procedures?

options.rationale: This option are not the classic, direct, highly-tested surgical risks associated with RYR1 mutations.

Central core myopathy is an autosomal dominant congenital myopathy caused by a mutation in the ryanodine receptor gene (RYR1) on chromosome 19q13.1. The RYR1 receptor regulates calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Mutations in this gene strongly predispose individuals to malignant hyperthermia when exposed to volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine.

options.text: Prolonged apnea due to pseudocholinesterase deficiency
options.rationale: This option is a distinct pharmacogenetic condition that causes prolonged paralysis after succinylcholine administration, but it is not linked to the RYR1 gene or central core disease.
This option are not the classic, direct, highly-tested surgical risks associated with RYR1 mutations.

learningObjective: Correlate dyskinetic cerebral palsy with extreme hyperbilirubinemia (kernicterus) and basal ganglia injury.
vignette: A 4-year-old child is followed in the neurology clinic for severe motor impairment. The child exhibits constant, large-amplitude, involuntary, purposeless movements of the distal limbs and face. The child also has significant dysarthria and upward gaze paresis. A review of the birth records reveals the child was born at 36 weeks gestation and suffered from profound neonatal jaundice requiring exchange transfusion.
leadIn: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of this patient's brain is most likely to show scarring and volume loss in which of the following structures?

options.rationale: This option are affected in spinal muscular atrophy or polio, presenting with flaccid paralysis.

The child has dyskinetic (choreoathetoid) cerebral palsy resulting from kernicterus (bilirubin toxicity). Extreme unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia leads to bilirubin deposition and selective damage to the basal ganglia (globus pallidus) and brainstem oculomotor nuclei. This manifests as prominent extrapyramidal signs (chorea, athetosis, dystonia) and gaze abnormalities.
This option damage results in ataxic cerebral palsy.
This option damage results in spastic diplegia, typical of prematurity without kernicterus.

learningObjective: Distinguish Klumpke palsy from Erb's palsy based on clinical exam.
vignette: A newborn infant is evaluated after a difficult vaginal delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia. The infant's right arm is held closely to the body. On examination, the infant has active shoulder abduction and elbow flexion, but the right hand is held in a claw-like posture with paralyzed wrist and finger flexors. The grasp reflex is absent on the right. Additionally, the infant has right-sided ptosis and miosis.
leadIn: This clinical presentation indicates an injury to which of the following nerve roots?

options.rationale: This option is the middle trunk; isolated injuries here are rare and would primarily affect elbow/wrist extension.

The infant has Klumpke palsy, a lower trunk brachial plexus injury involving the C8 and T1 nerve roots. It presents with paralysis of the intrinsic muscles of the hand (claw hand) and an absent grasp reflex. Because the sympathetic fibers to the eye travel through the T1 root, an associated ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) is common and indicates a severe avulsion injury.
This option involves the lumbosacral plexus, which would affect the lower extremities.
This option describes Erb's palsy, which presents with the "waiter's tip" posture (adducted shoulder, extended elbow, pronated forearm) and an intact grasp reflex.

learningObjective: Recognize the classic dysmorphic features of Cornelia de Lange syndrome.
leadIn: A newborn female is evaluated for intrauterine growth restriction and a weak cry. Physical examination reveals striking facial features: the eyebrows are thick and meet in the midline (synophrys), the eyelashes are very long, the nose is small and upturned, and the upper lip is very thin with downward-turned corners. The infant also has severe micromelia (shortening of the limbs) and syndactyly. This constellation of dysmorphic features is highly diagnostic of which of the following genetic syndromes?

options.rationale: This option features a "Greek helmet" appearance with severe ocular hypertelorism and a prominent glabella.
This option features a long face, large prominent ears, and large testicles in males.

The highly distinctive phenotype of synophrys (fused eyebrows), long eyelashes, low hairline, downward-turned mouth, thin upper lip, intrauterine growth restriction, and severe limb reduction defects (micromelia, syndactyly) is classic for Cornelia de Lange syndrome.
This option features a smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures, and microcephaly, but lacks the striking synophrys and micromelia.

learningObjective: Differentiate congenital acetylcholinesterase deficiency from autoimmune myasthenia gravis based on diagnostic testing.
vignette: A 4-month-old male infant presents with progressive axial and respiratory weakness. The parents report he has had generalized hypotonia since birth. On examination, the infant has bilateral ptosis. His pupillary response to direct light is noted to be significantly delayed. An edrophonium (Tensilon) test is administered, but it results in absolutely no improvement in his clinical weakness.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option would lack the long-standing congenital hypotonia from birth and would present acutely with constipation.
This option is an autoimmune disorder typically presenting after 10 years of age and shows robust improvement with edrophonium.

Congenital myasthenic syndromes are a genetically heterogeneous group of non-autoimmune NMJ disorders. The specific subtype of acetylcholinesterase deficiency presents in early infancy with axial/respiratory weakness, a characteristic delayed pupillary response to light, and crucially, no response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors like edrophonium or pyridostigmine (because the enzyme is already deficient).
This option is caused by transplacental maternal antibodies and typically resolves within the first 3-5 weeks of life.

learningObjective: Identify the comorbidities frequently associated with Tourette syndrome.
vignette: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the neurology clinic by his parents due to frequent, repetitive throat clearing and facial grimacing that has been present daily for the last 14 months. The child describes an "uncomfortable urge" in his neck that is relieved only after he performs the movements.
leadIn: In addition to treating his primary movement disorder, the physician should explicitly screen this child for which of the following frequently co-occurring psychiatric conditions?

options.rationale: Tourette syndrome is a tic disorder characterized by multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic persisting for >1 year. It is highly comorbid with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and screening for these conditions is mandatory as they frequently cause more functional impairment than the tics themselves.

options.text: Bipolar disorder and generalized anxiety disorder
options.rationale: , and D represent other psychiatric and behavioral disorders that are not the defining, classically highly-tested primary comorbidities of Tourette syndrome.

options.text: Oppositional defiant disorder and specific learning disorder
options.rationale: ODD and learning disorders can co-occur in children with Tourette syndrome, but the two highest-yield comorbidities — present in roughly half of patients and central to management — are OCD and ADHD.
, and D represent other psychiatric and behavioral disorders that are not the defining, classically highly-tested primary comorbidities of Tourette syndrome.

learningObjective: Identify the histologic hallmark of Nemaline Myopathy.
leadIn: A term neonate is intubated in the delivery room for profound respiratory distress and generalized hypotonia. The infant has severe facial weakness, an open mouth, and a high-arched palate, but normal extraocular movements. A muscle biopsy is performed to confirm the suspected diagnosis of a congenital myopathy. Which of the following histopathological findings is the hallmark of Nemaline Myopathy?

options.text: Elongated, rod-like structures localized beneath the sarcolemma
options.rationale: Nemaline myopathy is a congenital myopathy that often presents with severe neonatal hypotonia, respiratory failure, and pronounced facial weakness. The diagnostic histopathological finding is the presence of nemaline bodies (rod-like structures) typically located beneath the sarcolemma.

options.text: Ragged red fibers with prominent cytochrome c oxidase negativity
options.rationale: This option describes the findings seen in mitochondrial myopathies (e.g., MERRF or MELAS).

options.text: Central areas of muscle fibers lacking oxidative enzyme activity
options.rationale: This option describes Central Core Myopathy.

options.text: Extensive replacement of muscle tissue with fat and connective tissue
options.rationale: This option describes the late-stage dystrophic changes seen in Duchenne or Becker Muscular Dystrophy.

learningObjective: Diagnose Fetal Alcohol Syndrome based on facial dysmorphology and neurodevelopmental status.
vignette: A 6-year-old boy, recently placed in foster care, is evaluated for extreme hyperactivity, poor impulse control, and learning difficulties in the first grade. His physical examination is notable for microcephaly and growth restriction (height and weight < 5th percentile). Facial examination reveals a thin upper lip, a completely smooth philtrum, and short palpebral fissures.
leadIn: The patient's clinical presentation is most strongly associated with maternal consumption of which of the following substances during pregnancy?

options.rationale: This option causes prematurity, placental abruption, and jitteriness, but not this classic pattern of facial dysmorphology.

The classic facial triad of short palpebral fissures, a thin upper lip, and a smooth philtrum, combined with growth restriction, microcephaly, and neurobehavioral deficits (ADHD, learning disabilities) defines Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (ethanol teratogenicity).
This option causes neural tube defects (spina bifida).
This option causes Fetal Hydantoin Syndrome (cleft lip/palate, hypoplastic nails, and cardiac defects).

learningObjective: Differentiate Spinal Muscular Atrophy Type 2 based on age of onset and maximum motor milestones achieved.
vignette: An 18-month-old child is referred to the pediatric neurology clinic for delayed motor milestones. The parents note that he learned to sit independently at 8 months of age, but he has never been able to pull to a stand or walk. On examination, he is alert and interactive. He has prominent flaccid weakness of the proximal legs and absent deep tendon reflexes. A fine tremor of the hands is also noted.
leadIn: Which of the following describes the most likely clinical trajectory for this patient's disease subtype?

options.text: The patient will eventually learn to walk but will require a wheelchair by late adolescence.
options.rationale: This option describes SMA Type 3 (Kugelberg-Welander), where patients learn to walk independently but develop weakness later in childhood.

options.text: The patient will likely never ambulate independently but can survive into adulthood with respiratory and nutritional support.
options.rationale: The clinical picture of proximal weakness, areflexia, hand tremors, and the ability to sit but not walk, presenting between 6 and 18 months, is classic for Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) Type 2. These patients never achieve independent ambulation but generally survive into adulthood with appropriate care.

options.text: The patient will likely lose the ability to sit independently and will succumb to respiratory failure by age 2.
options.rationale: This option describes SMA Type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffman), which presents before 6 months, and patients never achieve independent sitting.

options.text: The patient will have a normal lifespan and achieve all motor milestones, albeit significantly delayed.
options.rationale: This option is incorrect for SMA, which is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder of anterior horn cells.

learningObjective: Recognize the biphasic clinical presentation of Prader-Willi syndrome.
vignette: A 5-year-old boy presents to the clinic for rapid weight gain and obesity. His parents state that he has an insatiable appetite (hyperphagia) and will frequently hoard food. A review of his medical records reveals that as a neonate, he suffered from profound hypotonia, a weak cry, and failure to thrive requiring nasogastric tube feedings for the first three months of life. He also has mild intellectual disability.
leadIn: Genetic testing will most likely reveal an abnormality involving which of the following chromosomes?

options.rationale: This option causes DiGeorge/Velo-Cardio-Facial syndrome.

Prader-Willi syndrome presents with a classic biphasic course: profound neonatal hypotonia and failure to thrive, followed in early childhood by hyperphagia leading to severe obesity. It is also associated with hypogonadism and mild intellectual disability. It is caused by the loss of imprinted genes on the paternally inherited chromosome 15q11-q13.
This option causes Angelman syndrome, which presents with severe intellectual disability, ataxia, seizures, and a "happy puppet" demeanor.

options.text: Expansion of CGG repeats on the X chromosome
options.rationale: This option causes Fragile X syndrome.

learningObjective: Diagnose Juvenile Myasthenia Gravis based on clinical symptoms and diagnostic tests.
vignette: A 13-year-old girl complains of intermittent double vision and drooping of her eyelids that is significantly worse in the evening and after reading for long periods. Her physical examination is normal in the morning, but by the late afternoon, she demonstrates prominent bilateral ptosis and weakness of her proximal arm muscles. Deep tendon reflexes are completely normal and preserved.
leadIn: Intravenous administration of which of the following agents is most likely to produce rapid, temporary improvement in her symptoms?

options.rationale: The presentation of fluctuating, fatigable weakness involving the extraocular muscles (ptosis, diplopia) and proximal limbs that worsens at the end of the day with preserved reflexes is classic for Juvenile Myasthenia Gravis. Diagnosis can be supported by the edrophonium (Tensilon) test, an ultra-short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that rapidly and transiently restores strength by increasing acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft.
This option is a GABA agonist used for spasticity.
This option is used to treat spasticity in cerebral palsy; it would worsen NMJ weakness.
This option is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker.

learningObjective: Differentiate congenital Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection from other TORCH infections based on neuroimaging.
vignette: A neonate born at 38 weeks gestation is noted to have a head circumference below the 3rd percentile (microcephaly). Physical examination reveals petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, and jaundice. Brain computed tomography (CT) demonstrates extensive calcifications outlining the walls of the lateral ventricles. An auditory brainstem response (ABR) test indicates profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely infectious etiology?
