options.rationale: This option presents with cataracts, sensorineural hearing loss, and congenital heart defects (e.g., patent ductus arteriosus).
This option typically presents with diffuse scattered intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis, and hydrocephalus.

Congenital Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common congenital viral infection. It classically presents with microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss (the most common cause of non-genetic hearing loss in children), and periventricular calcifications on head CT.
This option presents with snuffles, periostitis, and a maculopapular rash.

learningObjective: Recognize Muscle-Eye-Brain disease and distinguish it from Walker-Warburg Syndrome.
vignette: A 2-year-old child presents with global developmental delay and generalized hypotonia. Serum creatine kinase (CK) is elevated. Ophthalmologic exam reveals high myopia and mild congenital glaucoma. Brain MRI reveals a form of cobblestone lissencephaly, but the cortical and white matter changes are notably focal and milder than the total disorganization seen in severe congenital muscular dystrophies.
leadIn: This clinical presentation is most consistent with which of the following disorders?

options.rationale: This option is a motor neuron disease with normal CK and normal brain MRI/eyes.

Muscle-eye-brain disease is an autosomal recessive congenital muscular dystrophy. Like Walker-Warburg syndrome, it features muscular dystrophy, brain malformations (cobblestone lissencephaly), and ocular defects. However, it is explicitly distinguished by being a milder phenotype; the cortical changes are less severe/more focal, and the eyes are not as devastated (lacking the severe microphthalmia/retinal dysplasia of Walker-Warburg).
This option features profound, severe structural disruption of the brain and eyes, often leading to death in infancy.
This option lacks the classic combination of lissencephaly and congenital eye malformations.

learningObjective: Diagnose Landau-Kleffner syndrome (Acquired Epileptic Aphasia).
vignette: A 4-year-old boy, who previously had entirely normal motor and language development, begins to gradually stop speaking. Initially, his parents thought he was ignoring them, as he stopped responding to his name, but audiometry confirms his hearing is normal. Over the next six months, he develops a complete expressive and receptive aphasia. He also suffers from occasional focal motor seizures.
leadIn: An overnight electroencephalogram (EEG) is most likely to demonstrate which of the following patterns?

options.text: Chaotic, high-voltage slowing with multifocal spikes (hypsarrhythmia)
options.rationale: This option describes West syndrome (infantile spasms), which presents in the first year of life.

options.text: Continuous spike-and-wave discharges during slow-wave sleep (CSWS)
options.rationale: The clinical presentation of a previously normal preschooler who experiences profound language regression (auditory agnosia leading to aphasia) accompanied by clinical seizures is the hallmark of Landau-Kleffner Syndrome (Acquired Epileptic Aphasia). The diagnostic EEG finding is continuous or near-continuous spike-and-wave discharges during slow-wave sleep (CSWS).

options.text: Occipital spikes that attenuate with eye opening
options.rationale: This option describes Childhood Occipital Epilepsy (Gastaut or Panayiotopoulos types).
This option describes Childhood Absence Epilepsy, which presents with brief staring spells, not progressive language regression.

learningObjective: Identify the inheritance pattern and protein defect of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.
vignette: A 4-year-old boy is evaluated for frequent falls and difficulty climbing stairs. When asked to rise from the floor, he places his hands on his knees and pushes himself up (Gowers sign). Examination reveals notably enlarged, firm calf muscles. Laboratory testing shows a serum creatine kinase (CK) level of 15,000 U/L (normal < 200 U/L).
leadIn: This condition is caused by a genetic mutation resulting in the complete absence of a protein located in which of the following cellular structures?

options.rationale: This option describes the pathology of mitochondrial myopathies (e.g., MELAS, MERRF).
This option describes the pathology of presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorders, like botulism or Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

options.text: The sarcolemma of skeletal muscle fibers
options.rationale: The patient has Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), characterized by Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, and massively elevated CK. DMD is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the DMD gene, resulting in the absence of dystrophin. Dystrophin is a critical structural protein located on the cytoplasmic face of the sarcolemma (muscle cell membrane), linking the cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix.

options.text: The anterior horn of the spinal cord
options.rationale: This option describes the pathology of Spinal Muscular Atrophy.

learningObjective: Recognize the diagnostic criteria for Neurofibromatosis Type 1.
vignette: A 6-year-old girl is referred to the clinic due to learning disabilities and hyperactivity in school. During a full physical examination, the physician notes the presence of severe axillary freckling and nine distinct, flat, hyperpigmented macules on her trunk and extremities, ranging from 10 to 20 mm in diameter.
leadIn: To fully evaluate the diagnostic criteria for her suspected underlying genetic condition, the patient requires a slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist to look for which of the following?

options.rationale: This option is seen in Tay-Sachs, Niemann-Pick, and other lipid storage diseases.

The patient meets criteria for Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1), characterized by ≥6 café-au-lait macules (>5 mm prepubertal), axillary/inguinal freckling, learning disabilities, and optic gliomas. A key diagnostic criterion for NF1 is the presence of two or more Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), which are best identified via slit-lamp examination.
This option are a classic finding in Tuberous Sclerosis Complex, not NF1.
This option are pathognomonic for Aicardi syndrome (associated with infantile spasms and agenesis of the corpus callosum).

learningObjective: Identify the clinical characteristics of spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy.
vignette: A 3-year-old child with a history of severe perinatal asphyxia is completely wheelchair-bound. Examination demonstrates profound spasticity involving all four extremities, though the legs are slightly more rigid than the arms. The child frequently chokes when swallowing liquids, requires a gastrostomy tube for primary nutrition, and suffers from intractable generalized seizures.
leadIn: Which of the following classifications best describes this patient's cerebral palsy?

options.rationale: This option affects only one side of the body, usually due to a focal perinatal stroke. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Vascualr, Headache, and Neuroinflammatroy Board Review Questions (25)
This option primarily affects the legs, with relative sparing of the arms and bulbar musculature, typically seen in premature infants.
This option features involuntary extrapyramidal movements (chorea, athetosis, dystonia), not primary profound spasticity.

Spastic quadriplegia involves severe upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia) affecting all four limbs (legs often > arms). It is typically caused by severe diffuse insults like severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy/asphyxia, multicystic encephalomalacia, or severe CNS infections. It is heavily associated with severe comorbidities including pseudobulbar palsy (swallowing difficulties predisposing to aspiration), severe intellectual disability, and intractable seizures.

learningObjective: Identify the mechanism of action of natalizumab and its major complication.
vignette: A 28-year-old woman with highly active relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis is started on a monthly intravenous infusion therapy after failing interferon beta. Ten months later, she presents with progressive cognitive decline, aphasia, and hemiparesis. Brain MRI reveals new, expanding, non-enhancing white matter lesions in the parieto-occipital regions. A lumbar puncture confirms the presence of John Cunningham (JC) virus DNA.
leadIn: The disease-modifying therapy this patient is receiving exerts its therapeutic effect via which of the following mechanisms?

options.rationale: This option describes the mechanism of ocrelizumab or rituximab.

options.text: Activation of the glatiramer acetate polypeptide sequence
options.rationale: This option describes the mechanism of glatiramer acetate (Copaxone), which modulates T cells in the periphery.

The patient has developed Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML), a classic complication of Natalizumab (Tysabri). Natalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to integrin alpha4, a cell adhesion molecule on the surface of lymphocytes, thereby preventing them from crossing the blood-brain barrier.
This option describes the mechanism of fingolimod.

learningObjective: Localize the target of the pathogenic antibody in Neuromyelitis Optica (NMO).
leadIn: Neuromyelitis Optica (Devic's disease) is a severe inflammatory demyelinating disease that classically targets the optic nerves and spinal cord, typically presenting with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis spanning three or more vertebral segments. The highly specific NMO-IgG antibody targets Aquaporin-4 (AQP4). Where is this target protein primarily located in the central nervous system?

options.rationale: This option are incorrect anatomical locations for the Aquaporin-4 water channel.

options.text: Astrocytic foot processes at the blood-brain barrier
options.rationale: Aquaporin-4 (AQP4) is a water channel predominantly located in the astrocytic foot processes that surround cerebral microvessels at the blood-brain barrier.

options.text: Neuronal axonal membranes at the nodes of Ranvier
options.rationale: This option are incorrect anatomical locations for the Aquaporin-4 water channel.
This option describes the primary target in multiple sclerosis and anti-MOG antibody disease (Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein).

learningObjective: Associate the Anti-Yo antibody with paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration and ovarian cancer.
vignette: A 62-year-old woman is evaluated for a subacute, progressive gait disturbance, severe truncal ataxia, and dysarthria evolving over the last four weeks. Brain MRI is initially normal, but a repeat scan two months later demonstrates diffuse cerebellar atrophy. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis. A paraneoplastic antibody panel returns positive for anti-Yo antibodies.
leadIn: Based on this immunologic finding, the patient should be urgently screened for which of the following occult malignancies?

options.rationale: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration presenting with anti-Yo antibodies is classically associated with gynecologic malignancies, particularly ovarian and breast cancers. The pathology involves immune-mediated loss of cerebellar Purkinje cells.
This option is not classically associated with the anti-Yo antibody.
This option is associated with opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome in children (typically without a specific identifiable antibody).
This option is classically associated with anti-Hu (sensory neuronopathy/encephalomyelitis), anti-CRMP-5, or anti-VGCC (Lambert-Eaton).

learningObjective: Localize Alexia without Agraphia to the left PCA territory and the splenium of the corpus callosum.
vignette: A 68-year-old right-handed man with a history of atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden-onset visual difficulties. Neurologic examination reveals a right homonymous hemianopsia. Interestingly, when asked to write a sentence on a piece of paper, he does so perfectly. However, when asked to read the exact sentence he just wrote, he is completely unable to read the words. He has no other language deficits and can name objects placed in his hands.
leadIn: This classic clinical syndrome localizes to an infarction in the territory of the left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) that specifically encompasses the left occipital lobe and which of the following structures?

options.rationale: This option is the location of Wernicke's area; lesions here cause fluent (receptive) aphasia.

The patient presents with Alexia without Agraphia (the ability to write, but the inability to read). This occurs due to an infarction in the left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) territory that destroys the left visual cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum. Visual information from the intact right occipital lobe cannot cross the damaged splenium to reach the language comprehension centers in the left hemisphere.
This option connects the anterior frontal lobes and is not involved in visual-language pathways.
This option lesions cause Gerstmann's syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, right-left confusion, finger agnosia) or Alexia with Agraphia.

learningObjective: Identify the required autonomic features for SUNCT syndrome.
leadIn: Short-lasting Unilateral Neuralgiform headache attacks with Conjunctival injection and Tearing (SUNCT) is a rare Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgia (TAC) most common in men. It involves numerous daily attacks of severe orbital/temporal pain lasting 1 to 600 seconds. By definition, a diagnosis of SUNCT explicitly requires the presence of which of the following autonomic symptoms?

options.rationale: This option are autonomic features common in Cluster Headaches, but they are not the defining, required pair for diagnosing SUNCT.
SUNCT requires the presence of both conjunctival injection and lacrimation during the headache attacks.
This option are autonomic features common in Cluster Headaches, but they are not the defining, required pair for diagnosing SUNCT.

options.text: Either conjunctival injection or lacrimation, but not necessarily both
options.rationale: This option describes the criteria for SUNA (Short-lasting Unilateral Neuralgiform headache attacks with cranial autonomic symptoms), which requires only one or neither of conjunctival injection and lacrimation.

learningObjective: Diagnose a Medial Medullary Syndrome (Dejerine syndrome).
vignette: A 72-year-old man presents with acute onset of weakness. Neurologic examination reveals spastic hemiparesis of the right arm and right leg, accompanied by a loss of vibratory and position sense on the right side of his body. Pain and temperature sensation are preserved bilaterally. When asked to protrude his tongue, it deviates distinctly to the left side, and fasciculations are noted on the left half of the tongue.
leadIn: This constellation of findings is most likely caused by an occlusion of which of the following vessels?

options.rationale: This option causes Lateral Pontine Syndrome, featuring ipsilateral facial paralysis and deafness/tinnitus.

options.text: Left vertebral artery or anterior spinal artery
options.rationale: The clinical triad of contralateral arm/leg weakness (pyramidal tract), contralateral loss of vibration/proprioception (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral tongue weakness/deviation (hypoglossal nerve, CN XII) defines Medial Medullary Syndrome. This is caused by occlusion of the vertebral artery or its medial branches, such as the anterior spinal artery.

options.text: Right middle cerebral artery (MCA) lenticulostriate branches
options.rationale: This option causes a pure motor stroke without crossed cranial nerve XII palsy.

This option causes Lateral Medullary Syndrome (Wallenberg), which presents with crossed pain/temp loss, ataxia, Horner's syndrome, and bulbar symptoms (dysphagia/hoarseness), but typically spares motor strength and the hypoglossal nerve.

learningObjective: Differentiate Paroxysmal Hemicrania based on its absolute responsiveness to Indomethacin.
leadIn: A 35-year-old woman complains of excruciating, severe, unilateral orbital pain that occurs approximately 10 to 15 times a day. Each attack lasts between 10 and 25 minutes and is accompanied by ipsilateral eye watering and nasal congestion. She has tried multiple triptans without relief. Which of the following medications is both diagnostic and completely abortive/preventative for her specific headache syndrome?

options.rationale: This option is the first-line preventative for Cluster Headaches.
This option is the first-line acute abortive therapy for Cluster Headaches, which last longer (15-180 minutes) and occur less frequently per day.
This option is a preventative for migraines.

The patient has Paroxysmal Hemicrania, a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia characterized by severe, short-lived unilateral headaches (2-30 minutes) occurring multiple times a day (>5 times), mostly in women. It is classically and absolutely an "Indomethacin-responsive headache".

learningObjective: Diagnose Neurosarcoidosis based on neuroimaging and classic cranial nerve involvement.
vignette: A 35-year-old African American woman presents with subacute onset of left-sided facial weakness, blurred vision, and excessive thirst (polydipsia). Examination reveals a left lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy. Brain MRI with gadolinium shows striking, diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement that is most prominent at the base of the brain, wrapping around the optic chiasm and pituitary stalk. CSF shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein.
leadIn: A biopsy of the meninges or affected nervous tissue is most likely to reveal which of the following?

options.text: Multinucleated giant cells and microglial nodules
options.rationale: This option describes the pathology of HIV-associated dementia.

options.text: Perivascular cuffs of lymphocytes and florid plaques with amyloid
options.rationale: This option describes the pathology of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (florid plaques).

The clinical picture of cranial neuropathy (most commonly CN VII), hypothalamic/pituitary dysfunction (diabetes insipidus), and basilar leptomeningeal enhancement is the classic presentation of Neurosarcoidosis. The defining histologic feature is the presence of noncaseating granulomas.
This option describes Krabbe disease (globoid cells).

learningObjective: Recognize the Artery of Percheron and its associated bilateral thalamic stroke syndrome.
vignette: A 50-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found abruptly comatose at home. Upon evaluation, he is deeply obtunded. Oculomotor examination reveals restricted vertical gaze. An emergency MRI of the brain reveals acute, restricted diffusion symmetrically involving the bilateral medial thalami and the rostral midbrain.
leadIn: This symmetric, bilateral infarction is most commonly due to the occlusion of a single anatomic vascular variant known as the Artery of Percheron. This artery typically arises from which of the following parent vessels?

options.rationale: This option occlusion (Top of the basilar syndrome) also causes thalamic and midbrain infarcts, but involves the temporal and occipital lobes heavily. The Artery of Percheron is specifically a branch off the P1 PCA.
This option supplies the lateral convexity and deep basal ganglia, causing aphasia/neglect and hemiparesis.

The Artery of Percheron is a well-known anatomic variant where a single arterial trunk arises from the P1 segment of one of the Posterior Cerebral Arteries (PCA) to supply the bilateral medial thalami and often the rostral midbrain. Occlusion leads to bilateral thalamic infarcts, presenting with altered mental status/coma and vertical gaze palsies.
This option supplies the anterior medial frontal lobes.

learningObjective: Identify the pathophysiology of the migraine aura.
leadIn: Migraine with aura affects 15-20% of migraineurs. The visual, sensory, or dysphasic symptoms of a typical aura usually develop gradually over 5 to 20 minutes and last less than an hour. Which of the following pathophysiological phenomena is widely considered the primary driver of the migraine aura?

options.rationale: This option is associated with Subarachnoid Hemorrhage complications or RCVS, not the primary mechanism of a classic spreading aura.
This option causes a subdural hematoma.

The migraine aura is driven by Cortical Spreading Depression (CSD). CSD is a slow, self-propagating wave of neuronal and glial depolarization across the cerebral cortex, followed by prolonged inhibition and transient vascular changes. It disrupts ion homeostasis and releases neurochemicals that subsequently activate the trigeminovascular system.
This option is a mechanism of allergic reactions/anaphylaxis, not the central driver of migraine aura.

learningObjective: Distinguish Primary CNS Lymphoma in an immunocompromised host.
vignette: A 42-year-old man with untreated HIV (CD4 count = 45 cells/mcL) presents with a 3-week history of worsening right-sided weakness, lethargy, and confusion. Brain MRI with contrast reveals a single, large, homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass in the left frontal lobe. A lumbar puncture is performed, and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is positive for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option is a primary astrocytic tumor featuring necrosis and irregular ring enhancement, not directly driven by EBV in AIDS patients.
This option is caused by the JC virus and presents as non-enhancing, asymmetric white matter lesions without significant mass effect.

In an immunocompromised patient (AIDS), a homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass strongly suggests Primary CNS Lymphoma. These tumors are almost exclusively diffuse large B-cell lymphomas and are heavily driven by Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) co-infection; an EBV-positive CSF PCR is highly sensitive and specific in this context.
This option typically presents with multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia, and relies on Toxoplasma IgG/PCR, not EBV.

learningObjective: Diagnose Moyamoya disease based on clinical presentation and angiographic appearance.
vignette: A 6-year-old girl of East Asian descent is brought to the emergency department after experiencing sudden, transient weakness of her right arm and difficulty speaking while hyperventilating crying. She had a similar episode two months ago. MRI of the brain shows small, acute ischemic infarcts in the watershed regions of the left hemisphere. A cerebral angiogram demonstrates severe stenosis of the distal internal carotid arteries bilaterally, surrounded by a prominent network of hazy, fragile collateral vessels at the base of the brain.
leadIn: Which of the following describes the most common clinical presentation of this disorder when it occurs in adult patients (4th decade of life)?

options.rationale: The child has Moyamoya disease, characterized by non-inflammatory progressive occlusion of the intracranial internal carotid arteries and the formation of a "puff of smoke" collateral network. While children classically present with ischemic strokes and TIAs (often provoked by hyperventilation/crying), adults in their 3rd to 4th decade typically present with intracerebral hemorrhage due to the rupture of these fragile, high-pressure collateral vessels.
This option is typical of CADASIL or neurodegenerative dementias.
This option is typical of progressive myoclonic epilepsies (e.g., Lafora, Unverricht-Lundborg).
This option are typically driven by vertebrobasilar atherosclerosis or dissection, rather than the classic anterior circulation targets of Moyamoya.

learningObjective: Identify the typical profile and management of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS).
leadIn: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a sudden, explosive "thunderclap" headache that reached maximum intensity within seconds, occurring during sexual intercourse. She has no focal neurologic deficits. A non-contrast head CT and a subsequent lumbar puncture are entirely normal, ruling out a subarachnoid hemorrhage. Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) demonstrates multifocal, segmental narrowing and dilatation ("beading") of the cerebral arteries.

options.text: The condition requires lifelong anticoagulation to prevent stroke.
options.rationale: This option are incorrect; the prognosis for RCVS is generally good once the vasospasm resolves.

options.text: The condition requires immediate administration of high-dose intravenous corticosteroids.
options.rationale: This option is the treatment for Primary Angiitis of the CNS (PACNS), which RCVS mimics radiographically, but PACNS features insidious headaches, abnormal CSF, and does not spontaneously resolve.

options.text: The condition is universally fatal due to progression to massive cerebral edema.
options.rationale: This option are incorrect; the prognosis for RCVS is generally good once the vasospasm resolves.

options.text: The condition is typically self-limiting and resolves spontaneously within 12 weeks.
options.rationale: Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS) classically presents with recurrent thunderclap headaches (often provoked by exertion, Valsalva, or sexual intercourse) and a "string of beads" appearance on angiography due to multifocal vasospasm. Unlike primary CNS vasculitis, the CSF is typically normal, and the condition spontaneously resolves within 12 weeks. Treatment is supportive (e.g., calcium channel blockers).

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical and histopathological features of Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy.
vignette: A 75-year-old man with a history of mild cognitive impairment presents with acute onset of confusion, left homonymous hemianopsia, and left-sided weakness. A non-contrast CT of the head reveals a large, acute lobar hemorrhage in the right parieto-occipital region. The patient has a history of a similar, smaller lobar hemorrhage in the left frontal lobe two years ago. His blood pressure has historically been well-controlled.
leadIn: A pathological specimen of this patient's cerebral vasculature is most likely to demonstrate which of the following?

options.text: Deposition of Congo red-positive material in the media and adventitia of small cortical arteries
options.rationale: Recurrent, spontaneous lobar hemorrhages in an elderly patient without severe hypertension are the hallmark of Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy (CAA). CAA is characterized by the deposition of beta-amyloid (Congo red-positive, congophilic material) in the media and adventitia of small and medium-sized cortical and leptomeningeal vessels, making them fragile and prone to rupture.

options.text: Basophilic granular material in the vascular walls associated with a NOTCH3 mutation
options.rationale: This option describes the pathology of CADASIL, which causes subcortical ischemic strokes and dementia, not typically large lobar hemorrhages.

options.text: Granulomatous inflammation and giant cells in the media of the temporal artery
options.rationale: This option describes Temporal Arteritis (Giant Cell Arteritis).

options.text: Severe lipohyalinosis of the deep penetrating lenticulostriate arteries
options.rationale: This option describes the pathology of hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage, which typically involves deep structures (putamen, thalamus, pons) rather than lobar cortical regions.

learningObjective: Recall the effect of oral versus intravenous corticosteroids in the treatment of Optic Neuritis.
leadIn: A 25-year-old woman presents with acute, painful vision loss in her right eye, and is diagnosed with optic neuritis. The classic Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) established critical guidelines for the management of this condition and its relationship to the development of multiple sclerosis. According to the ONTT, what was the clinical effect of administering isolated oral prednisone compared to intravenous methylprednisolone or placebo?

options.text: Oral prednisone increased the risk of recurrent optic neuritis attacks.
options.rationale: The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) showed that intravenous steroids followed by an oral taper sped up visual recovery, but neither IV nor oral steroids changed long-term visual acuity outcomes at 1 year compared to placebo. Crucially, the trial found that treating with oral prednisone alone actually increased the risk of recurrent optic neuritis attacks compared to placebo or IV steroids.

options.text: Oral prednisone prevented the eventual development of multiple sclerosis.
options.rationale: , and D are factually incorrect based on the ONTT results.

options.text: Oral prednisone caused a higher rate of permanent blindness compared to placebo.
options.rationale: The ONTT did not demonstrate a higher rate of permanent blindness with oral prednisone. The actual finding was an increased rate of recurrent optic neuritis attacks in the oral-prednisone arm, which is why isolated oral prednisone is no longer recommended.

options.text: Oral prednisone significantly improved long-term visual acuity at 1 year compared to placebo.
options.rationale: , and D are factually incorrect based on the ONTT results.

learningObjective: Apply contraindications for IV tPA in acute ischemic stroke.
vignette: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with acute onset of right-sided hemiparesis and aphasia. He was last known well 2 hours ago. His NIH Stroke Scale score is 14. A non-contrast head CT shows no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage and an ASPECTS score of 9. His point-of-care blood glucose is 110 mg/dL, and his platelet count is 250,000/μL. His blood pressure is persistently measuring 195/115 mmHg despite initial medical interventions.
leadIn: According to standard guidelines, which of the following is an absolute contraindication to the administration of intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) in this patient?

options.rationale: This option is not a contraindication (though age >80 is an exclusion criterion for the extended 3-4.5 hour window, this patient is within the 3-hour window and under 80).

This option indicates a small infarct core and is actually an indication that the patient is a good candidate for tPA or thrombectomy; an ASPECTS <7 (indicating a large completed stroke >1/3 of the MCA territory) is a contraindication.

options.text: Blood pressure strictly greater than 185/110 mmHg
options.rationale: Severe, uncontrolled hypertension (BP >185/110 mmHg) is an absolute contraindication for IV tPA administration due to the prohibitively high risk of hemorrhagic transformation of the ischemic infarct. BP must be carefully lowered and stabilized below this threshold before thrombolytics can be given.

options.text: An NIH Stroke Scale score greater than 10
options.rationale: This option represents a moderate-to-severe stroke, which is exactly what tPA is intended to treat. A very low NIHSS (minor/rapidly improving symptoms) is a relative contraindication.

learningObjective: Identify the age-dependent diagnostic criteria for pediatric migraines.
leadIn: The International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD) diagnostic criteria for migraines differ slightly between adults and children. In pediatric patients, migraines often lack the classic adult presentation. Which of the following duration criteria explicitly distinguishes a pediatric migraine from an adult migraine?

options.text: Pediatric migraines must last at least 24 hours, whereas adult migraines can last 2 hours.
options.rationale: , and D are incorrect representations of the migraine duration criteria. (Tension-type headaches can be 30 minutes to 7 days).

options.text: Pediatric migraines typically last less than 30 minutes.
options.rationale: , and D are incorrect representations of the migraine duration criteria. (Tension-type headaches can be 30 minutes to 7 days).

options.text: Pediatric migraines can be as short as 2 hours, whereas adult migraines must last at least 4 hours.
options.rationale: According to diagnostic criteria, an untreated migraine attack in children and adolescents can be much shorter, lasting from 2 to 72 hours, whereas in adults, the attack must last 4 to 72 hours. Furthermore, pediatric migraines are often bilateral rather than strictly unilateral.

options.text: Pediatric migraines must be continuous and unremitting for 7 days.
options.rationale: Pediatric migraines are episodic, lasting 2–72 hours per attack. Continuous unremitting headache for 7 days does not meet ICHD migraine criteria and would suggest status migrainosus or a different headache disorder.

learningObjective: Localize a brainstem stroke causing Benedikt syndrome.
vignette: A 55-year-old woman with chronic, poorly controlled hypertension experiences a sudden neurologic deficit. Examination reveals a complete paralysis of her left oculomotor nerve (CN III), characterized by a dilated left pupil, severe left ptosis, and an inability to look up, down, or medially with the left eye. Additionally, she exhibits prominent, involuntary, choreoathetoid movements and a rest tremor of her right arm and leg. She has no significant hemiparesis.
leadIn: This stroke syndrome localizes to an infarction in which of the following specific regions of the brainstem?

options.text: Midbrain tegmentum involving the red nucleus
options.rationale: The combination of an ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral choreoathetosis and tremor (without dense hemiparesis) defines Benedikt's syndrome. It is caused by an infarction in the mesencephalic (midbrain) tegmentum that damages the oculomotor nerve fascicle and the red nucleus (which causes the contralateral extrapyramidal hyperkinetic movements).

options.text: Lateral medulla involving the nucleus ambiguus
options.rationale: This option causes Wallenberg syndrome.

options.text: Ventral pons involving the corticospinal tracts
options.rationale: This option causes Millard-Gubler or Foville syndrome (ipsilateral CN VI/VII, contralateral hemiparesis).

This option causes Weber syndrome, which features an ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral dense hemiparesis (due to corticospinal tract damage), but lacks the prominent choreoathetosis/tremor of red nucleus involvement.

learningObjective: Diagnose Anti-Hu syndrome.
vignette: A 68-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with a 3-month progressive history of severe, burning pain, numbness, and tingling in his feet and hands that has now spread proximally. Neurologic examination reveals profound asymmetric sensory loss to all modalities, completely absent deep tendon reflexes, and severe sensory ataxia. Motor strength is remarkably well-preserved. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies confirm a severe sensory neuronopathy (ganglionopathy) with absent sensory nerve action potentials and normal motor studies.
leadIn: Which of the following paraneoplastic autoantibodies is most highly associated with this specific neurologic presentation and underlying malignancy?

options.rationale: This option causes Neuromyelitis Optica.
This option causes opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome.

A severe, rapidly progressive, asymmetric sensory neuronopathy (ganglionopathy) in a heavy smoker is the classic presentation of a paraneoplastic syndrome driven by Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) antibodies, almost exclusively associated with small cell lung cancer.
This option causes subacute cerebellar degeneration (breast/ovarian cancer).

learningObjective: Identify the classic MRI finding of a Cavernous Malformation.
leadIn: Intracranial vascular malformations frequently present with headaches, seizures, or focal hemorrhage. One specific subtype is characterized histologically by clusters of thin-walled, dilated vascular channels with absolutely no intervening brain parenchyma. What is the classic appearance of this specific malformation on a T2-weighted brain MRI?

options.text: A "caput medusae" pattern of venous drainage
options.rationale: This option describes a Developmental Venous Anomaly (Venous Angioma).

options.text: A "popcorn-like" core with a complete, dark rim of hemosiderin
options.rationale: Cavernous malformations (cavernous angiomas) are composed of clustered, thin-walled capillaries without intervening brain tissue. Because they are low-pressure systems, they ooze slowly, creating a distinct "popcorn-like" appearance on MRI with a dark, low-signal hemosiderin rim on T2/gradient-echo sequences.

options.text: An enhancing nodule within a large cystic cavity
options.rationale: This option describes a Hemangioblastoma or Pilocytic Astrocytoma.

options.text: A tangled "bag of worms" appearance with prominent flow voids
options.rationale: This option describes an Arteriovenous Malformation (AVM), which contains high-flow arteries shunting directly to veins, appearing as flow voids.

learningObjective: Diagnose Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri).
vignette: A 16-year-old girl with obesity presents with daily, diffuse, pounding headaches over the past month. She reports occasional horizontal double vision and episodes where her vision completely "grays out" for a few seconds when she stands up quickly. Her neurologic examination is normal except for bilateral papilledema and a subtle right abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy. MRI of the brain is normal.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis and provide immediate therapeutic relief?

options.rationale: This option is unnecessary as the MRI is normal and the clinical picture points solidly to IIH. (MR Venogram is often done to rule out CSVT, but a standard angiogram is not the immediate next step).
This option are indicated for Temporal Arteritis, which typically affects patients >50 years old and features jaw claudication, not papilledema and obesity.

options.text: Lumbar puncture with measurement of opening pressure
options.rationale: The clinical presentation of headaches, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, papilledema, and a false-localizing CN VI palsy in an overweight adolescent female with a normal brain MRI is classic for Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri). The definitive diagnostic and acutely therapeutic step is a lumbar puncture to document an opening pressure >250 mm H2O and drain CSF to relieve symptoms.
This option are indicated for Temporal Arteritis, which typically affects patients >50 years old and features jaw claudication, not papilledema and obesity.

learningObjective: Diagnose Dejerine-Roussy syndrome (Thalamic Pain Syndrome).
vignette: A 60-year-old woman is admitted for an acute ischemic stroke that presents purely as complete loss of touch, pain, temperature, and proprioception on the entire right side of her face and body. Over the next month, her sensory deficits partially improve, but she develops severe, agonizing, burning pain over the right side of her body. Even the light touch of her clothing against her skin provokes an excruciating pain response (allodynia).
leadIn: The initial ischemic infarct most likely involved which of the following anatomic structures?

options.rationale: This option lesions can cause sensory loss, but pure hemisensory strokes without cortical signs (aphasia, neglect, agnosia) classically localize to the deep thalamic nuclei.

options.text: Left ventral posterolateral (VPL) and ventral posteromedial (VPM) thalamic nuclei
options.rationale: The patient experienced a "pure sensory" lacunar stroke, which typically localizes to the contralateral thalamus (specifically the VPL and VPM sensory relay nuclei). Weeks to months later, she developed Dejerine-Roussy syndrome (thalamic pain syndrome), characterized by severe neuropathic pain, hyperesthesia, and allodynia on the previously affected side.
This option strokes typically cause pure motor hemiparesis.
This option causes crossed sensory signs (ipsilateral face, contralateral body), not complete hemisensory loss.

learningObjective: Institute immediate therapy for suspected Temporal Arteritis (Giant Cell Arteritis).
vignette: A 75-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 2-week history of severe, new-onset right temporal headaches, scalp tenderness when brushing his hair, and fatigue. He also notes significant pain in his jaw muscles when chewing meat. Blood work demonstrates a remarkably elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).
leadIn: What is the most critical immediate next step in the management of this patient?

options.rationale: The patient presents with classic signs of Giant Cell Arteritis (Temporal Arteritis): age >50, new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and a high ESR. Because GCA can lead to acute, irreversible ischemic optic neuropathy (blindness) due to ophthalmic artery occlusion, high-dose corticosteroids must be initiated immediately upon clinical suspicion. Treatment must never be delayed while waiting for a temporal artery biopsy.
This option treats migraines, not a dangerous systemic vasculitis.

options.text: Schedule an urgent temporal artery biopsy before starting any medication
options.rationale: This option is incorrect; while a biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis, steroids must be given first to prevent permanent blindness.

options.text: Order a brain MRI to rule out an intracranial mass
options.rationale: This option delays critical sight-saving therapy.

learningObjective: Diagnose Primary Angiitis of the Central Nervous System (PACNS).
vignette: A 45-year-old man presents with a 6-month insidious history of unremitting headache, progressive encephalopathy, and two separate episodes of small ischemic strokes in different vascular territories. Extensive systemic rheumatologic and infectious workups are completely negative. CSF analysis reveals a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein. A conventional cerebral angiogram demonstrates multiple, alternating areas of stenosis and dilatation ("beading") across several small and medium-sized cerebral arteries.
leadIn: What is the gold standard method to achieve a definitive diagnosis of this patient's condition?

options.text: Identification of anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) in the serum
options.rationale: This option is utilized to diagnose secondary systemic vasculitides (like GPA/Wegener's or Microscopic Polyangiitis), but PACNS is ANCA-negative and isolated to the CNS.

options.text: Resolution of symptoms following a trial of calcium channel blockers
options.rationale: This option is the clinical confirmation for RCVS, which resolves spontaneously, whereas true PACNS requires aggressive immunosuppression (steroids + cyclophosphamide).

The clinical picture of insidious headache, encephalopathy, and multifocal strokes with an abnormal CSF and a "beaded" angiogram without systemic disease points to Primary Angiitis of the Central Nervous System (PACNS). Because angiography can be mimicked by RCVS (which has normal CSF and no encephalopathy) or atherosclerosis, a definitive diagnosis of PACNS strictly requires a brain and leptomeningeal biopsy showing granulomatous or lymphocytic inflammation of the vessel walls.

options.text: High-resolution MRI of the brain with gadolinium
options.rationale: This option shows nonspecific ischemic/inflammatory changes but cannot definitively confirm vasculitis over other etiologies.

learningObjective: Identify the optimal surgical versus medical management for symptomatic carotid stenosis based on the NASCET trial.
vignette: A 68-year-old man experiences a 10-minute episode of right-hand weakness and expressive aphasia that completely resolves. Carotid duplex ultrasound and subsequent CT angiography confirm an atherosclerotic plaque causing 80% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. The right internal carotid artery has 30% stenosis. The patient is medically stable and has no major surgical contraindications.
leadIn: Based on the results of the North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial (NASCET), what is the most appropriate management for this patient?

options.text: Maximum medical therapy with dual antiplatelets and high-dose statin alone
options.rationale: This option is the preferred treatment for asymptomatic mild-to-moderate stenosis or intracranial stenosis (SAMMPRIS trial).

options.text: Carotid endarterectomy of the left internal carotid artery
options.rationale: The NASCET trial established that for patients with symptomatic severe (70-99%) internal carotid artery stenosis, Carotid Endarterectomy (CEA) is significantly superior to medical management alone in reducing the risk of a subsequent ipsilateral stroke. (Note: Currently, symptomatic patients with 50-99% stenosis generally benefit from revascularization).

options.text: Endovascular stenting of the right internal carotid artery
options.rationale: This option targets the wrong side (the right side is asymptomatic and mild).

This option was proven ineffective for preventing strokes compared to medical therapy in the EC/IC Bypass Study. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Neurogenetics Board Review Comprehensive Question Set (25) Here is a brand new, highly targeted set of 25 neurogenetics questions specifically tailored to your requested difficulty distribution (3 Very Easy, 7 Relatively Straightforward, 7 Medium, 5 Hard, and 3 Very Hard). These questions draw heavily on the chromosomal, metabolic, and inherited neurological disorder concepts from the provided "Board Review" and "Pediatric Board Study Guide" resources, ensuring zero redundancy with your previous question sets. VERY EASY (3 Questions)

learningObjective: Identify the proper cytogenetic notation for Down syndrome mosaicism.
leadIn: Down syndrome is most commonly caused by meiotic nondisjunction resulting in a full trisomy 21. However, a small percentage of patients possess a mixture of normal euploid cells and trisomy 21 cells due to a post-zygotic mitotic nondisjunction event. Which of the following is the proper cytogenetic notation for a female patient with Down syndrome mosaicism?

options.rationale: Mosaicism is denoted by listing the abnormal karyotype followed by a slash and the normal karyotype. A female with Down syndrome mosaicism has a mixture of trisomy 21 cells (47,XX,+21) and normal cells (46,XX).
This option denotes triploidy (a completely extra set of all chromosomes), which is typically incompatible with life.
This option denotes a chromosomal inversion on chromosome 21, not mosaicism.
This option is the karyotype for Klinefelter syndrome (a male with an extra X chromosome).

learningObjective: Identify the genetic mechanism of Huntington disease.
leadIn: A 42-year-old man presents with progressive chorea, psychiatric disturbances, and cognitive decline. His father died of a similar condition in his late 50s. This patient’s neurodegenerative condition is caused by which of the following genetic mechanisms?

options.text: Expansion of a GAA trinucleotide repeat on chromosome 9
options.rationale: This option is the mechanism for Friedreich ataxia (frataxin gene).

options.text: Expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat on chromosome 4
options.rationale: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by the expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT (huntingtin) gene on chromosome 4.

options.text: Expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat on the X chromosome
options.rationale: This option is the mechanism for Fragile X syndrome.

options.text: Deletion of the 15q11-q13 region on the paternal chromosome
options.rationale: This option is the mechanism for Prader-Willi syndrome.

learningObjective: Identify the chromosomal location and gene product associated with Neurofibromatosis Type 1.
leadIn: Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) is a common neurocutaneous syndrome characterized by café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, and Lisch nodules. Which of the following pairs correctly identifies the affected chromosome and its corresponding gene product in NF1?

options.rationale: This option describes the genetics of Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2).
NF1 is caused by a mutation on chromosome 17q11.2, which encodes the tumor suppressor protein neurofibromin.

This option describes the genetics of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex Type 2 (TSC2). -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- RELATIVELY STRAIGHTFORWARD (7 Questions)
This option describes the genetics of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex Type 1 (TSC1).

learningObjective: Diagnose Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome based on characteristic facial dysmorphisms and neurological features.
vignette: A newborn female is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for profound hypotonia and early-onset seizures. Physical examination reveals microcephaly, ocular hypertelorism, a prominent glabella, and frontal bossing, giving the face a distinct "Greek helmet" appearance.
leadIn: Which of the following chromosomal abnormalities is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?

options.text: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-)
options.rationale: This option causes Cri-du-chat syndrome, which features a moon face, cat-like cry, and down-slanting palpebral fissures.

options.text: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4 (4p-)
options.rationale: The clinical presentation of severe hypotonia, seizures, microcephaly, and the classic "Greek helmet" facies (prominent glabella, wide-spaced eyes) is highly specific for Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome, which is caused by a deletion on the short arm of chromosome 4 (4p-).
This option causes DiGeorge syndrome, featuring cardiac defects, immune deficiency, and cleft palate.
This option causes midline defects like holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, and polydactyly.

learningObjective: Diagnose Cri-du-chat syndrome based on characteristic clinical findings.
vignette: A 2-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for poor weight gain and developmental delay. On examination, the infant has microcephaly, a distinct "moon face," widely spaced eyes (hypertelorism), and down-slanting palpebral fissures. When the infant becomes agitated during the exam, the pediatrician notes a very distinct, high-pitched, mewing cry.
leadIn: This infant's syndrome is most commonly caused by which of the following cytogenetic abnormalities?

options.text: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-)
options.rationale: The triad of microcephaly, a round "moon face" with down-slanting palpebral fissures, and a high-pitched, cat-like cry defines Cri-du-chat syndrome. It is caused by a deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-).
This option is Edwards syndrome (prominent occiput, rocker-bottom feet, overlapping fingers).
This option is Williams syndrome (elfin facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcemia).

options.text: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4 (4p-)
options.rationale: This option is Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome ("Greek helmet" face).

learningObjective: Identify the intracellular signaling pathway dysregulated in Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.
leadIn: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in either the TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin) genes. In healthy individuals, the hamartin-tuberin protein complex acts as a critical tumor suppressor. Which of the following intracellular signaling pathways is directly inhibited by this complex, leading to uncontrolled cellular growth when the complex is defective?

options.rationale: Notch signaling regulates cell-fate decisions and is implicated in T-cell leukemias and other malignancies, but it is not the pathway disrupted in TSC. The hamartin-tuberin complex acts as a GAP for Rheb, directly inhibiting mTORC1.
, and D are critical neurodevelopmental and oncologic pathways, but they are not the primary target of the TSC1/TSC2 complex. (Notch signaling is heavily implicated in CADASIL).

The hamartin-tuberin complex primarily functions to inhibit the mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) pathway. Mutations in TSC1 or TSC2 result in mTOR overactivation, leading to the widespread formation of hamartomas (e.g., cortical tubers, SEGAs). This forms the basis for treating TSC tumors with mTOR inhibitors like everolimus or rapamycin.
, and D are critical neurodevelopmental and oncologic pathways, but they are not the primary target of the TSC1/TSC2 complex. (Notch signaling is heavily implicated in CADASIL).

learningObjective: Correlate the "molar tooth sign" on MRI with Joubert syndrome.
vignette: A 2-year-old child presents to the neurogenetics clinic with profound hypotonia, ataxia, and global developmental delay. The parents report that during the newborn period, the child had bizarre, episodic breathing patterns characterized by alternating tachypnea and apnea. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain reveals hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis accompanied by thickened and elongated superior cerebellar peduncles.
leadIn: The characteristic neuroimaging finding in this patient is classically referred to as which of the following?

options.rationale: The clinical combination of neonatal episodic hyperpnea/apnea, ataxia, hypotonia, and cerebellar vermis hypoplasia with elongated superior cerebellar peduncles is diagnostic of Joubert syndrome (a ciliopathy). The classic axial MRI appearance of the midbrain/hindbrain in this disorder is the "molar tooth sign."
This option is pathognomonic for Pantothenate Kinase-Associated Neurodegeneration (PKAN).
This option is seen in Glutaric Aciduria Type 1.

options.text: Face of the giant panda sign
options.rationale: This option is characteristic of neurological Wilson disease.

learningObjective: Diagnose Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) based on family history and clinical presentation.
vignette: A 68-year-old man presents with a progressive intention tremor, an unsteady, wide-based gait, and recent memory decline. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain demonstrates distinct T2 hyperintensities in the bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles. While taking the family history, the neurologist learns that the patient’s daughter is healthy, but his 6-year-old grandson was recently diagnosed with severe intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder.
leadIn: Which of the following genetic mechanisms is the most likely cause of this 68-year-old patient's neurological symptoms?

options.text: Expansion of CAG repeats in the HTT gene
options.rationale: This option causes Huntington disease (chorea, psychiatric decline).

options.text: Full mutation of the FMR1 gene (>200 CGG repeats)
options.rationale: This option causes classic Fragile X syndrome in childhood (intellectual disability, macroorchidism), not FXTAS in late adulthood.

options.text: Expansion of GAA repeats in the FXN gene
options.rationale: This option causes Friedreich ataxia (early-onset ataxia, areflexia, cardiomyopathy).

options.text: Premutation of the FMR1 gene (55 to 200 CGG repeats)
options.rationale: The patient has Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS), which occurs in older adult male carriers of the FMR1 premutation (55 to 200 CGG repeats). It presents with ataxia, intention tremor, cognitive decline, and the classic MRI finding of middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP) hyperintensities. His grandson has the full mutation (>200 repeats) causing classic Fragile X syndrome.

learningObjective: Identify the defective gene in X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMTX).
leadIn: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT) represents a genetically heterogeneous group of inherited polyneuropathies. The second most common variant, CMTX, presents similarly to CMT1 with slowly progressive distal weakness, pes cavus, and demyelination, but is inherited in an X-linked pattern and affects males more severely. This specific variant is caused by a mutation in the gene encoding which of the following proteins?

options.rationale: This option is the cause of CMT1A, the most common autosomal dominant form.
CMTX is an X-linked demyelinating neuropathy caused by a mutation in the GJB1 gene, which encodes the gap junction protein Connexin 32.
This option is the cause of CMT1B.
This option is the defective protein in Friedreich Ataxia.

learningObjective: Identify the genetic defect associated with Familial Hemiplegic Migraine type 1 (FHM1).
leadIn: Familial hemiplegic migraine (FHM) is an autosomal dominant subtype of migraine with aura that includes fully reversible motor weakness. Type 1 (FHM1) is the most common form and is frequently associated with concurrent progressive cerebellar ataxia. FHM1 is caused by a primary channelopathy affecting which of the following?

options.rationale: This option mutations cause FHM2 and Alternating Hemiplegia of Childhood, which do not typically feature progressive cerebellar ataxia.

FHM1 is caused by mutations in the CACNA1A gene on chromosome 19, which encodes the alpha-1A subunit of the P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel. Because this channel is highly expressed in the cerebellum, mutations often cause concurrent cerebellar ataxia.
This option mutations cause Myotonia Congenita (Thomsen/Becker types). -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- MEDIUM (7 Questions)
This option mutations cause FHM3, as well as Dravet syndrome and GEFS+.

learningObjective: Identify the primary cellular function of the NF2 gene product, Merlin.
leadIn: Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by the development of multiple central nervous system tumors, particularly bilateral vestibular schwannomas. It is caused by a mutation in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22. The product of this gene, Merlin (also known as schwannomin), functions primarily as which of the following?

options.text: A lysosomal enzyme involved in the degradation of sphingolipids
options.rationale: This option describes lysosomal enzymes mutated in storage disorders (e.g., Hexosaminidase A, Arylsulfatase A).

options.text: A transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor for nerve growth factor
options.rationale: This option describes receptor tyrosine kinases like TrkA (mutated in CIPA/HSAN IV).

options.text: A nuclear transcription factor regulating neural crest cell migration
options.rationale: This option describes transcription factors involved in developmental syndromes, not specifically the mechanism of Merlin in NF2.

options.text: A cytoskeletal protein involved in cell growth control and tumor suppression
options.rationale: Merlin is a structural cytoskeletal protein (related to the ezrin-radixin-moesin family) that links actin filaments to cell membrane proteins. It acts as a tumor suppressor by regulating contact-dependent inhibition of cell growth; loss of its function leads to the unchecked proliferation of Schwann cells and meningeal cells.

learningObjective: Recognize the somatic/sporadic inheritance pattern of Sturge-Weber syndrome.
vignette: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department for new-onset focal motor seizures involving the left arm. Physical examination is notable for a large, deep-red vascular malformation (port-wine stain) covering the right forehead and upper eyelid. A brain MRI with contrast demonstrates prominent leptomeningeal enhancement over the right cerebral hemisphere. The parents are highly distressed and ask for genetic counseling regarding the risk of this condition occurring in their future children.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate genetic counseling advice for this family?

options.text: The condition is autosomal dominant, carrying a 50% chance of transmission to future offspring.
options.rationale: This option is the inheritance pattern for Tuberous Sclerosis and Neurofibromatosis.

options.text: The condition arises from a spontaneous, somatic mutation, and the recurrence risk for future pregnancies is negligible.
options.rationale: The patient has Sturge-Weber Syndrome (SWS), characterized by a facial port-wine stain (V1/V2 distribution), seizures, and ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis. Unlike NF1 or TSC, SWS is not an inherited disorder. It is caused by a spontaneous somatic mosaic mutation in the GNAQ gene that occurs after conception. Therefore, the recurrence risk for siblings is effectively zero.

options.text: The condition requires carrier screening for both parents because it is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
options.rationale: This option is the inheritance pattern for most metabolic storage diseases.

options.text: The condition is X-linked recessive, meaning future male offspring have a 50% chance of being affected.
options.rationale: This option is the inheritance pattern for disorders like Menkes disease or Adrenoleukodystrophy.

learningObjective: Differentiate megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC) from other infantile macrocephalic leukodystrophies.
vignette: A 14-month-old boy is evaluated in the neurogenetics clinic for a rapidly enlarging head size. The parents report his development has been generally normal, though he recently became slightly unsteady when walking. His head circumference is >99th percentile. Brain MRI reveals diffuse, confluent T2 hyperintensity of the cerebral white matter with relative sparing of the deep gray matter. Notably, there are prominent, bilateral fluid-filled cysts in the subcortical white matter of the anterior temporal and frontoparietal lobes.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option presents with macrocephaly but classically features an anterior-to-posterior gradient of white matter involvement and enhancement of the periventricular rim, without massive temporal cysts.
This option causes microcephaly and severe early irritability/rigidity, not macrocephaly with cysts.

The differential for macrocephaly with leukodystrophy includes Alexander disease, Canavan disease, and Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC/van der Knaap disease). The hallmark MRI finding of MLC is diffuse white matter swelling accompanied by large subcortical cysts, particularly in the anterior temporal and frontoparietal regions, usually presenting with macrocephaly and relatively mild/delayed motor impairment initially.
This option presents in older boys (4-8 years) with normal head size, behavioral changes, and posterior-predominant white matter demyelination.

learningObjective: Correlate SURF1 gene mutations with Leigh syndrome and complex IV deficiency.
vignette: A 2-year-old child who previously met all developmental milestones is admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with acute respiratory failure, hypotonia, and severe ataxia following a viral upper respiratory infection. MRI of the brain reveals bilateral, symmetric areas of restricted diffusion and T2 hyperintensity in the periaqueductal gray matter, midbrain tegmentum, and subthalamic nuclei. Genetic testing confirms a homozygous mutation in the SURF1 gene.
leadIn: This specific genetic mutation results in a severe deficiency of which of the following mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes?

options.rationale: This option deficiencies can also cause Leigh syndrome (e.g., NDUFV1 mutations), but SURF1 specifically targets Complex IV.
This option are incorrect specific complex targets for the SURF1 mutation.
This option are incorrect specific complex targets for the SURF1 mutation.

The clinical presentation of acute developmental regression, brainstem/basal ganglia symmetric lesions, and hypotonia following a metabolic stressor is the classic presentation of Leigh syndrome (subacute necrotizing encephalomyelopathy). The most common nuclear gene mutation causing Leigh syndrome is SURF1, which encodes an assembly factor crucial for Complex IV (Cytochrome c oxidase).

learningObjective: Correlate periventricular nodular heterotopia with the FLNA gene and its inheritance pattern.
blueprintTopic: Genetic and Developmental Disorders (Malformations of Cortical Development)
vignette: A 16-year-old female is evaluated for new-onset, medication-refractory focal seizures. Her cognitive development and neurological examination are completely normal. An MRI of the brain reveals multiple small, nodular foci of tissue that are isointense to gray matter lining the walls of the lateral ventricles bilaterally. Family history is notable; her mother also has epilepsy, and her mother suffered three mid-trimester miscarriages, all of which were confirmed to be male fetuses.
leadIn: A mutation in which of the following genes is the most likely etiology of this patient's condition?

options.rationale: This option cause classic Miller-Dieker lissencephaly (autosomal).
This option cause X-linked lissencephaly with ambiguous genitalia in males.
This option cause X-linked lissencephaly (smooth brain) in males and subcortical band heterotopia ("double cortex") in females due to X-inactivation.

The MRI findings describe periventricular nodular heterotopia (PVNH). In familial cases, this is most commonly caused by a mutation in the FLNA (Filamin A) gene on chromosome Xq28, which regulates actin cytoskeleton stabilization for neuronal migration. It is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern. Crucially, it is typically lethal in males in utero (explaining the mother's history of recurrent male miscarriages), meaning it presents almost exclusively in females.

learningObjective: Diagnose Niemann-Pick Type C based on vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and cataplexy.
vignette: A 7-year-old boy presents to the clinic with progressive school failure, dysarthria, and frequent falls. The parents report that he seems physically clumsy and occasionally collapses to the floor when he laughs at a joke or is startled. When tracking objects during the neurological exam, he has full horizontal eye movements but is completely unable to look upward or downward. A review of his medical records indicates he had unexplained, prolonged neonatal jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly that eventually resolved.
leadIn: Which of the following is the primary pathophysiologic defect in this patient's disorder?

options.text: Deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme galactocerebrosidase
options.rationale: This option describes Krabbe disease.

options.text: Defect in intracellular cholesterol ester and sphingolipid transport
options.rationale: The classic clinical triad of vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, gelastic cataplexy (collapsing when laughing), and progressive ataxia/dementia in a school-aged child with a history of neonatal hepatosplenomegaly is diagnostic of Niemann-Pick Type C. This is caused by mutations in the NPC1 or NPC2 genes, which results in a fatal defect in intracellular transport of unesterified cholesterol and lipids out of the lysosome.

options.text: Deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid sphingomyelinase
options.rationale: This option describes Niemann-Pick Type A and B. Type A presents in infancy with severe regression, massive organomegaly, and a cherry-red macula.

options.text: Deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme hexosaminidase A
options.rationale: This option describes Tay-Sachs disease.

learningObjective: Correlate Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome (Abetalipoproteinemia) with vitamin E deficiency and peripheral neuropathy.
vignette: A 10-year-old boy is evaluated for progressive clumsiness and severe, generalized weakness. He has a history of failure to thrive, steatorrhea, and chronic fat malabsorption since infancy. Neurological examination reveals severe sensory ataxia, absent deep tendon reflexes, and a profound loss of vibratory and position sense in the lower extremities. Ophthalmologic examination reveals atypical retinitis pigmentosa. A peripheral blood smear demonstrates numerous spiculated red blood cells (acanthocytes).
leadIn: This patient’s neurological deterioration is most directly caused by a genetic mutation affecting which of the following?

options.rationale: This option causes Friedreich Ataxia (ataxia, absent reflexes, cardiomyopathy, normal blood smear/lipids).
This option causes Ataxia-Telangiectasia (ataxia, immune deficiency, telangiectasias, normal blood smear/lipids).

This option causes Refsum disease (ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa, sensorineural hearing loss, elevated phytanic acid). -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- HARD (5 Questions)

The clinical picture of severe fat malabsorption, acanthocytosis, atypical retinitis pigmentosa, and a profound spinocerebellar/posterior column neuropathy (mimicking Friedreich ataxia or Vitamin E deficiency) is diagnostic of Abetalipoproteinemia (Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome). It is caused by an autosomal recessive mutation in the MTTP gene, completely abrogating the assembly of apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins (chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL) and leading to a severe, secondary fat-soluble vitamin (especially Vitamin E) deficiency that destroys the posterior columns and peripheral nerves.

learningObjective: Diagnose Unverricht-Lundborg disease (EPM1).
blueprintTopic: Epilepsy and Episodic Disorders (Progressive Myoclonic Epilepsies)
vignette: A 13-year-old adolescent of Scandinavian descent is evaluated for a progressive seizure disorder. He initially developed brief, shock-like muscle jerks that are violently exacerbated by loud noises, sudden movements, or photic stimulation. He subsequently began experiencing generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Unlike many other patients with severe early-onset epilepsies, his cognitive function has remained relatively intact, and his primary disability stems from his severe action myoclonus and ataxia. Brain MRI is normal.
leadIn: Which of the following genetic/molecular abnormalities is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?

options.text: Mutation in the CLN3 gene leading to fingerprint body accumulation
options.rationale: This option describes Juvenile Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis (Batten disease), which features vision loss, severe dementia, and myoclonus.

options.text: Mutation in the EPM1 gene encoding cystatin B
options.rationale: The patient has Unverricht-Lundborg disease (Baltic myoclonus), a progressive myoclonic epilepsy (PME) characterized by severe, stimulus-sensitive action myoclonus, ataxia, and generalized seizures, but notable for relatively preserved cognition and a lack of early dementia compared to other PMEs. It is caused by an autosomal recessive mutation in the EPM1 gene on chromosome 21q22.3, which encodes cystatin B, a cysteine protease inhibitor.

options.text: Accumulation of PAS-positive polyglucosan inclusions (Lafora bodies)
options.rationale: This option describes Lafora body disease, a severe PME that prominently features early, rapid, and severe cognitive decline/dementia and occipital seizures (transient blindness).

options.text: A maternally inherited mitochondrial DNA point mutation in the MT-TK gene
options.rationale: This option describes MERRF (Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Red Fibers), which features myoclonus, ataxia, short stature, and deafness.

learningObjective: Identify the underlying molecular defect in Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia.
vignette: A 15-year-old adolescent is brought to the emergency department after a sudden, severe headache followed by left-sided hemiparesis and lethargy. Brain MRI and MR angiography confirm an intraparenchymal hemorrhage secondary to a ruptured cerebral arteriovenous malformation (AVM). Medical history is significant for severe, recurrent episodes of epistaxis requiring cauterization, and physical examination reveals multiple small, blanching red macules on his lips, oral mucosa, and fingertips.
leadIn: The defective gene in this patient's underlying disorder most likely encodes for a protein involved in which of the following cellular signaling pathways?

options.rationale: This option is the pathway disrupted in Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.

The triad of epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, and visceral AVMs (including cerebral AVMs causing stroke/hemorrhage) is diagnostic of Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome). The disorder is autosomal dominant, most commonly caused by mutations in the ENG (endoglin) gene (HHT1) or ACVRL1 gene (HHT2). Both of these encode receptor proteins that are critical modulators of the Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) signaling pathway, which is essential for normal vascular development and capillary bed formation.

options.text: Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) receptor signaling
options.rationale: This option is heavily targeted by oncology drugs (e.g., bevacizumab) to prevent angiogenesis, but is not the primary monogenic defect in HHT.
This option is the pathway disrupted in CADASIL (leading to subcortical strokes and dementia).

learningObjective: Diagnose Tangier disease based on neuropathy and pathognomonic tonsillar findings.
vignette: An 8-year-old child presents to the neurology clinic with progressive, symmetric muscle weakness and loss of pain and temperature sensation in the upper extremities. Proprioception and vibratory sense are entirely preserved (dissociated sensory loss). A routine examination of the oropharynx reveals strikingly enlarged, lobulated, bright yellow-orange palatine tonsils. A comprehensive lipid panel is ordered.
leadIn: A mutation in which of the following genes is the root cause of this patient's presentation?

options.rationale: A peripheral neuropathy (often a dissociated sensory loss resembling syringomyelia) combined with the pathognomonic finding of huge, yellow-orange tonsils points exclusively to Tangier disease. This is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the ABCA1 gene, which is essential for cholesterol efflux from cells to form HDL. The lack of HDL results in massive accumulation of cholesterol esters in the reticuloendothelial system (creating the orange tonsils/hepatosplenomegaly) and peripheral nerves.
This option mutations cause Familial Amyloid Polyneuropathy (severe autonomic dysfunction and sensorimotor neuropathy in adults).
This option mutations cause Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A, a demyelinating neuropathy without orange tonsils or lipid defects.
This option mutations cause Fabry disease (X-linked, burning pain in hands/feet, angiokeratomas).

learningObjective: Identify the clinical features and classification of Dejerine-Sottas syndrome.
leadIn: Charcot-Marie-Tooth Type 3 (CMT3), historically known as Dejerine-Sottas syndrome, is a severe hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy. Which of the following features specifically distinguishes CMT3 from the much more common CMT Type 1A?

options.text: Complete sparing of myelin, presenting as a purely axonal degeneration with completely normal nerve conduction velocities
options.rationale: This option describes CMT Type 2, which is the axonal form of CMT.

options.text: Onset in early infancy with severe, rapid progression, marked hypotonia, and massive hypertrophy of peripheral nerves ("onion bulb" formation)
options.rationale: CMT3 (Dejerine-Sottas syndrome) is distinguished by its severe, early-onset presentation in infancy. Unlike CMT1A (which presents later in childhood/adolescence with slow progression), CMT3 causes severe delayed motor milestones, profound generalized weakness, and massively hypertrophied peripheral nerves due to relentless demyelination and remyelination cycles creating thick "onion bulb" structures on nerve biopsy.

options.text: Predominant involvement of unmyelinated C-fibers leading to severe, life-threatening dysautonomia and insensitivity to pain
options.rationale: This option describes Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy Type III (Riley-Day syndrome/Familial Dysautonomia).

options.text: X-linked recessive inheritance with prominent central nervous system involvement and intellectual disability
options.rationale: This option describes features not typical of CMT3. (CMTX is X-linked, but does not typically cause severe ID).

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation of 18q deletion syndrome (De Grouchy syndrome).
vignette: A newborn male is evaluated in the nursery for multiple congenital anomalies. Physical examination reveals microcephaly, deep-set eyes, a depressed mid-face, a protruded mandible, and atresia of the external ear canals. The infant's legs exhibit a highly unusual posture: they are held in constant flexion, external rotation, and extreme abduction, resembling a "frog-like" position.
leadIn: Which of the following cytogenetic abnormalities is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option features overlapping fingers, prominent occiput, micrognathia, and rocker-bottom feet.

options.text: Deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-)
options.rationale: This option features a high-pitched cry and moon facies, not the classic frog-leg posture or ear canal atresia.

options.text: Deletion of the long arm of chromosome 18 (18q-)
options.rationale: The classic description of a neonate with mid-face hypoplasia, ear canal atresia, deep-set eyes, and a highly distinct "frog-like" posture of the lower extremities strongly points to 18q deletion syndrome (De Grouchy syndrome).
This option features elfin facies, hypercalcemia, and supravalvular aortic stenosis. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- VERY HARD (3 Questions)

learningObjective: Diagnose Molybdenum cofactor deficiency / sulfite oxidase deficiency.
vignette: A 4-day-old neonate presents with severe encephalopathy, profound hypertonia, and medically intractable myoclonic seizures. Routine metabolic panels, serum ammonia, and CSF glucose levels are all within normal limits. An ophthalmologic examination reveals bilateral dislocation of the lenses (ectopia lentis). A specialized urine test is ordered and detects massively elevated levels of a specific biomarker, confirming a fatal defect in the enzyme sulfite oxidase.
leadIn: Which of the following compounds is abnormally elevated in this patient's urine?

options.rationale: This option accumulates in Alkaptonuria (dark urine, ochronosis).
This option is the classic marker for Tyrosinemia Type 1.
This option is massively elevated in Canavan disease (macrocephaly, leukodystrophy).

Intractable neonatal seizures, hypertonia, and uniquely dislocated lenses (ectopia lentis) in a newborn are pathognomonic for Sulfite Oxidase Deficiency or Molybdenum Cofactor Deficiency. (Molybdenum is a required cofactor for sulfite oxidase). Because sulfite cannot be converted to sulfate, it reacts with cysteine to form S-sulfocysteine, which accumulates to toxic levels and is massively elevated in the urine.

learningObjective: Identify the enzyme defect in Cerebrotendinous Xanthomatosis (CTX).
vignette: A 28-year-old man presents to the neurology clinic with progressive cerebellar ataxia, spastic paraparesis, and a decline in executive functioning. He has a long-standing history of intractable diarrhea since early childhood and underwent bilateral cataract extractions at age 14. Physical examination is notable for large, firm, nodular masses embedded within bilateral Achilles tendons. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain reveals symmetric T2 hyperintensities in the dentate nuclei of the cerebellum.
leadIn: This patient's lipid storage disorder is caused by a deficiency in which of the following enzymes?

options.rationale: This option is deficient in Krabbe disease.
