The classic pentad of chronic childhood diarrhea, juvenile cataracts, tendon xanthomas (especially Achilles), progressive ataxia/spasticity, and cognitive decline in early adulthood is diagnostic of Cerebrotendinous Xanthomatosis (CTX). CTX is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the CYP27A1 gene, which encodes the mitochondrial enzyme 27-sterol hydroxylase. This defect halts bile acid synthesis, leading to massive deposition of cholesterol and cholestanol in the brain and tendons.
This option is deficient in Metachromatic Leukodystrophy.
This option is deficient in Refsum disease, a peroxisomal disorder that causes retinitis pigmentosa, ataxia, and neuropathy (without tendon xanthomas or cataracts).

learningObjective: Identify the genetic defect and molecular mechanism of NARP syndrome.
leadIn: A 35-year-old female presents with progressive neurogenic muscle weakness, sensory ataxia, and night blindness progressing to severe visual loss due to retinitis pigmentosa. Her maternal grandmother and mother suffered from a milder constellation of similar symptoms. A genetic workup confirms a diagnosis of NARP (Neurogenic muscle weakness, Ataxia, and Retinitis Pigmentosa) syndrome. This condition is caused by a specific mutation in the ATP6 gene.

options.rationale: , and D are incorrect because the ATP6 mutation responsible for NARP is strictly a mitochondrial DNA mutation, not a nuclear DNA mutation. (Note: While some mitochondrial proteins are encoded by nuclear DNA, the ATP6 gene involved in NARP is entirely mitochondrial). -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Epilepsy and Episodic Disorders Board-Style Questions - Set 7 (25) Here is a new set of 25 high-yield, board-style questions focused exclusively on Epilepsy and Episodic Disorders, crafted strictly according to your Operational Model. These questions emphasize novel concepts, distinct electroclinical syndromes, epilepsy localization, and neuropharmacology not covered in previous sets.

NARP is caused by point mutations (most commonly m.8993T>G) in the mitochondrial ATP6 gene, which encodes a subunit of complex V. It is inherited maternally and is not encoded on nuclear chromosome 15.

, and D are incorrect because the ATP6 mutation responsible for NARP is strictly a mitochondrial DNA mutation, not a nuclear DNA mutation. (Note: While some mitochondrial proteins are encoded by nuclear DNA, the ATP6 gene involved in NARP is entirely mitochondrial). -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Epilepsy and Episodic Disorders Board-Style Questions - Set 7 (25) Here is a new set of 25 high-yield, board-style questions focused exclusively on Epilepsy and Episodic Disorders, crafted strictly according to your Operational Model. These questions emphasize novel concepts, distinct electroclinical syndromes, epilepsy localization, and neuropharmacology not covered in previous sets.

NARP is a classic mitochondrial encephalomyopathy. Like MELAS and MERRF, it is caused by a mutation in the Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), specifically the MT-ATP6 gene, which encodes a subunit of ATP synthase (Complex V). Because it is located in the mitochondrial genome, it is passed strictly through maternal inheritance and is subject to heteroplasmy, explaining the variable phenotypic severity seen among generations in the maternal lineage.

learningObjective: Diagnose Lafora body disease based on clinical presentation and histopathologic findings.
blueprintTopic: Epilepsy and Episodic Disorders (Progressive Myoclonic Epilepsies)
vignette: A 16-year-old adolescent is evaluated for progressive cognitive decline, dysarthria, and multiple seizure types, including massive myoclonic jerks and occipital seizures presenting as transient blindness. Her development was completely normal until age 13. A skin biopsy is performed to evaluate for a suspected genetic disorder.
leadIn: Which of the following histopathological findings is most likely to be present in this patient's sweat gland ducts?

options.rationale: This option are seen in Alexander disease or pilocytic astrocytomas.

The patient’s clinical presentation of adolescent-onset progressive myoclonic epilepsy, cognitive decline, and occipital seizures is classic for Lafora body disease. It is an autosomal recessive disorder (EPM2A gene mutation encoding laforin). The hallmark histopathological finding is Lafora bodies, which are PAS-positive intracellular polyglucosan inclusions that can be found in the brain, sweat glands, liver, and skeletal muscle.
This option are seen in Parkinson disease and Dementia with Lewy bodies.
This option are the classic electron microscopy finding for Late Infantile Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis (Batten disease).

learningObjective: Identify the clinical features and genetic mechanism of Autosomal Dominant Nocturnal Frontal Lobe Epilepsy (ADNFLE).
vignette: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for unusual nighttime events. His parents report that shortly after falling asleep, he suddenly sits up, exhibits thrashing and bicycling movements of his arms and legs, and occasionally displays dystonic posturing. He is fully aware during the events but cannot control his movements. An overnight video-EEG captures several of these brief episodes, which show prominent movement artifact but subtle anterior epileptiform discharges. His father had similar episodes as a child.
leadIn: A mutation affecting which of the following receptors is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?

options.rationale: This option is the target in autoimmune anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, not the genetic locus for ADNFLE.
This option mutations (KCNQ2/3) cause benign familial neonatal seizures.
This option mutations (GABRG2) are associated with GEFS+ (Generalized Epilepsy with Febrile Seizures Plus).

The presentation of brief, hyperkinetic, bizarre nocturnal seizures with preserved awareness and a strong family history is classic for Autosomal Dominant Nocturnal Frontal Lobe Epilepsy (ADNFLE). It is classically associated with mutations in the CHRNA4 or CHRNB2 genes, which encode subunits of the neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.

learningObjective: Diagnose pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy and identify its underlying genetic defect.
vignette: A term neonate develops intractable, generalized tonic-clonic seizures within hours of birth. The seizures are unresponsive to phenobarbital, phenytoin, and levetiracetam. An EEG demonstrates continuous multifocal epileptiform discharges. The neonatologist administers an intravenous infusion of a specific vitamin during continuous EEG monitoring, which results in the immediate cessation of clinical seizures and normalization of the EEG background within minutes.
leadIn: This patient's condition is caused by an autosomal recessive mutation in which of the following genes?

options.rationale: This option causes Rett syndrome.
This option causes Dravet syndrome, which presents slightly later (first year) with prolonged febrile seizures.

The clinical scenario of early neonatal status epilepticus that is completely refractory to standard anti-seizure medications but exquisitely responsive to intravenous Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is diagnostic of Pyridoxine-Dependent Epilepsy. This is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the ALDH7A1 gene, which encodes the protein antiquitin.
This option causes GLUT1 deficiency syndrome, characterized by low CSF glucose and responsiveness to the ketogenic diet.

learningObjective: Differentiate early childhood occipital epilepsy (Panayiotopoulos syndrome) from late-onset (Gastaut type).
vignette: A 9-year-old girl is evaluated for recurrent brief episodes of visual disturbances. She describes seeing brightly colored, circular flashing lights in her left visual field that last for 1 to 2 minutes. Occasionally, these visual symptoms are followed by forced deviation of her eyes to the left and clonic jerking of her left arm. She does not experience prominent nausea or vomiting during these events. An interictal EEG reveals right occipital spike-and-wave discharges that attenuate when she opens her eyes.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option can cause visual auras, but the aura typically lasts 15-60 minutes (gradual build-up) followed by a severe headache, and the EEG lacks highly epileptogenic focal occipital spikes that spread to hemiclonic motor activity.

This option occurs in younger children (age 4-8) and is defined by massive autonomic symptoms (severe retching, vomiting, pallor, syncope) and prolonged seizures, rather than brief visual hallucinations.

Late-onset childhood occipital epilepsy (Gastaut type) typically begins after age 8 and is characterized by brief, frequent visual auras (elementary visual hallucinations like colored circles), which may spread to cause hemiclonic motor seizures. The EEG shows characteristic occipital spikes that attenuate with eye opening.
This option presents with staring spells and 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges.

learningObjective: Localize a focal seizure presenting with the classic "fencing posture."
vignette: A 25-year-old patient with medically refractory epilepsy is admitted to the epilepsy monitoring unit. During a typical seizure, he abruptly awakens from sleep, forcefully extends his right arm upward and outward, flexes his left arm, and turns his head and eyes to the right, resembling a "fencer's posture." He remains fully aware during the initial part of this sequence, which lasts for 15 seconds before secondarily generalizing.
leadIn: This seizure semiology most strongly localizes the epileptogenic zone to which of the following cortical regions?

options.rationale: This option produces auras of rising epigastric sensation, olfactory hallucinations, and prominent oral/manual automatisms with altered awareness.
This option would produce focal clonic jerking of the left face, arm, or leg (Jacksonian march), rather than the complex postural fencing movement.

The "fencing posture" (asymmetric tonic posturing with head/eye version looking toward the extended arm) is the classic semiology for seizures originating in the Supplementary Motor Area (SMA). The extended arm is typically contralateral to the seizure focus, so right arm extension indicates a left SMA focus. These seizures are notably brief, abrupt, and frequently occur during sleep.
This option produces episodic focal somatosensory symptoms (tingling, numbness).

learningObjective: Anticipate the pharmacokinetic interaction between valproic acid and carbamazepine.
vignette: A 15-year-old boy with focal epilepsy is currently well-controlled on a stable dose of carbamazepine. He is diagnosed with a comorbid mood disorder, and his psychiatrist initiates valproic acid therapy. Two weeks later, the patient returns to the neurology clinic complaining of severe dizziness, double vision, and unsteady gait. A serum carbamazepine level is drawn and returns perfectly within the normal therapeutic range.
leadIn: Which of the following mechanisms best explains this patient's acute neurological toxicity?

options.text: Inhibition of epoxide hydrolase by valproic acid
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is metabolized in the liver to an active and highly toxic metabolite, carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide, which is then broken down by epoxide hydrolase. Valproic acid directly inhibits epoxide hydrolase. This leads to a massive accumulation of the toxic epoxide metabolite (causing diplopia, ataxia, and dizziness) while the parent serum carbamazepine level remains deceptively normal.

options.text: Autoinduction of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
options.rationale: This option lowers carbamazepine levels over the first 3-5 weeks of monotherapy; it does not explain toxicity upon adding valproate.

options.text: Synergistic blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels
options.rationale: This option is a pharmacodynamic concept, but the classic pharmacokinetic interaction requiring dose adjustment here is the epoxide buildup.

options.text: Displacement of carbamazepine from plasma binding proteins
options.rationale: This option occurs with highly protein-bound drugs, but the toxicity here is distinctly driven by the epoxide metabolite accumulation.

learningObjective: Localize mesial temporal lobe seizures based on classic auras and automatisms.
vignette: A 17-year-old adolescent describes episodes where she suddenly experiences a strange, "rising" sensation in her stomach followed by a profound feeling of fear and a strong smell of burning rubber. Witnesses report that she then stops talking, stares blankly, and repeatedly smacks her lips and picks at her clothing for about two minutes. She is confused and tired for 15 minutes afterward.
leadIn: Which of the following anatomical structures is most likely the site of seizure onset in this patient?

options.rationale: This option produces simple somatosensory auras.

The sequence of a rising epigastric aura, emotional changes (fear/terror), olfactory hallucinations, behavioral arrest, and oro-alimentary automatisms (lip smacking) with post-ictal confusion is the textbook presentation of Mesial Temporal Lobe Epilepsy. The epileptogenic zone heavily involves the amygdala and hippocampus.
This option seizures often present with hypermotor or bizarre behaviors, but lack the classic visceral/epigastric aura and prolonged postictal confusion of the temporal lobe.
This option lesions (hamartomas) produce gelastic (laughing) seizures.

learningObjective: Recognize the interaction between estrogen-containing contraceptives and lamotrigine clearance.
vignette: A 19-year-old female with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy has been seizure-free for two years on a stable monotherapy dose of lamotrigine. She recently visited her gynecologist and was started on an oral contraceptive pill containing ethinyl estradiol and a progestin. Three months later, she suffers a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She reports 100% adherence to both of her medications.
leadIn: What is the most likely cause of her breakthrough seizure?

options.text: Competitive inhibition of lamotrigine absorption in the gut
options.rationale: This option are incorrect mechanisms for the lamotrigine-estrogen interaction.

options.text: Estrogen-mediated displacement of lamotrigine from albumin
options.rationale: This option are incorrect mechanisms for the lamotrigine-estrogen interaction.

options.text: Pro-convulsant effects of ethinyl estradiol on the motor cortex
options.rationale: This option is not the primary mechanism of breakthrough seizures in this context; the pharmacokinetic drug interaction is the overriding factor.

options.text: Increased glucuronidation and clearance of lamotrigine
options.rationale: Ethinyl estradiol is a potent inducer of the UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) enzyme system in the liver. Lamotrigine is primarily metabolized via glucuronidation. Adding an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive can increase lamotrigine clearance by >50%, resulting in sub-therapeutic levels and breakthrough seizures unless the lamotrigine dose is significantly increased.

learningObjective: Identify risk factors for the recurrence of febrile seizures.
leadIn: A 14-month-old infant is evaluated in the emergency department after a 2-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the setting of acute otitis media and a fever of 38.5°C (101.3°F). The parents are highly anxious and ask about the likelihood of this happening again. Which of the following factors places this child at the highest risk for a recurrent febrile seizure in the future?

options.text: Prolonged duration of the fever (greater than 48 hours) prior to the seizure
options.rationale: This option represent the opposite of the known risk factors; a lower peak temp and a brief time between fever onset and seizure indicate a lower seizure threshold, predicting higher recurrence risk.

options.text: A peak fever greater than 40.0°C (104°F) during the illness
options.rationale: This option represent the opposite of the known risk factors; a lower peak temp and a brief time between fever onset and seizure indicate a lower seizure threshold, predicting higher recurrence risk.
This option is not a major independent predictor of recurrence.

options.text: Age younger than 18 months at the time of the first febrile seizure
options.rationale: Major risk factors for the recurrence of febrile seizures include young age at onset (<18 months), a family history of febrile seizures, a lower peak temperature precipitating the seizure, and a shorter duration of fever prior to the seizure.

learningObjective: Differentiate Benign Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy from other early epileptic encephalopathies.
vignette: A 14-month-old boy is brought to the neurologist because he has started having brief, sudden jerks of his head and arms. The parents note these episodes almost exclusively occur when he is very drowsy, falling asleep, or just waking up. They do not occur in clusters. His birth history and developmental milestones are completely normal. An interictal EEG is performed and shows a completely normal background without slowing or disorganization.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely prognosis for this patient's condition?

options.text: Development of refractory status epilepticus requiring hemispherectomy
options.rationale: This option describes the trajectory of Rasmussen encephalitis.
This option is the common prognosis for severe epileptic encephalopathies like West Syndrome or Ohtahara syndrome, which feature chaotic EEGs and developmental regression.

options.text: Spontaneous resolution within the first few years of life
options.rationale: The presentation of brief myoclonic jerks exclusively provoked by drowsiness or sleep transitions in a developmentally normal infant with a normal interictal EEG is classic for Benign Myoclonic Epilepsy of Infancy. True to its name, the condition is easily treated (often with valproic acid) and typically resolves spontaneously within the first 1 to 2 years after onset.

options.text: Lifelong necessity for vagus nerve stimulation
options.rationale: This option is indicated for highly refractory epilepsies, whereas this syndrome is benign.

learningObjective: Recognize the phenomenon of autoinduction associated with carbamazepine.
leadIn: When initiating therapy with carbamazepine for focal epilepsy, neurologists must carefully titrate the dose over several weeks. This slow titration is clinically necessary because carbamazepine specifically induces the hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes responsible for its own metabolism. How long does this process of "autoinduction" typically take to reach completion?

options.rationale: , and D represent incorrect timeframes for the completion of hepatic autoinduction.
, and D represent incorrect timeframes for the completion of hepatic autoinduction.

Carbamazepine undergoes autoinduction, meaning it induces the CYP3A4 enzymes that metabolize it. This process begins within days but takes approximately 3 to 5 weeks at a stable dose to reach completion. Therefore, a dose that provides therapeutic levels in week 1 may become sub-therapeutic by week 4, necessitating careful monitoring and upward titration.

CYP3A4 autoinduction by carbamazepine is largely complete within 3–5 weeks of reaching a stable dose; serum levels then plateau. A 1–2 year time course would be inconsistent with the known pharmacokinetics of enzyme induction.

learningObjective: Diagnose LGI1 autoimmune encephalitis based on classic seizure semiology.
vignette: A 62-year-old man presents with rapidly progressive cognitive decline, confusion, and new-onset seizures. The seizures are highly distinctive, characterized by very brief, sudden, dystonic posturing of the right side of his face and his right arm. These episodes occur up to 40 times a day and last only a few seconds. Laboratory evaluation reveals a serum sodium level of 124 mEq/L.
leadIn: This patient's syndrome is mediated by autoantibodies directed against a protein complex associated with which of the following?

options.rationale: The classic triad of faciobrachial dystonic seizures (brief, frequent posturing of face and arm), limbic encephalitis (cognitive decline/amnesia), and severe hyponatremia is pathognomonic for anti-LGI1 encephalitis. LGI1 is a protein tightly complexed with Voltage-Gated Potassium Channels (VGKC) in the central nervous system.
This option is the target in Neuromyelitis Optica (NMO).
This option is a target in a variant of Myasthenia Gravis.
This option are targeted in anti-NMDAR encephalitis, which classically presents in young women with psychiatric symptoms, autonomic instability, and orofacial dyskinesias.

learningObjective: Correlate anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis with its associated paraneoplastic trigger.
vignette: A 22-year-old previously healthy woman is admitted to the intensive care unit for new-onset seizures, extreme autonomic instability (tachycardia, hyperthermia), and continuous chewing and lip-smacking movements (orofacial dyskinesias). Her family reports that two weeks prior, she exhibited bizarre behavior, paranoia, and severe anxiety, leading to a brief psychiatric admission. Continuous EEG monitoring reveals an "extreme delta brush" pattern.
leadIn: A comprehensive imaging workup should specifically prioritize the evaluation of which of the following organs?

options.rationale: This option should be screened for small cell lung cancer in patients with anti-Hu or Lambert-Eaton syndromes.
This option is associated with Hashimoto encephalopathy (SREAT), which presents with myoclonus and elevated TPO antibodies, but lacks the extreme delta brush and dyskinesias of NMDAR.

The presentation of a young woman with a viral prodrome followed by acute psychiatric symptoms, autonomic instability, orofacial dyskinesias, seizures, and an "extreme delta brush" EEG is the textbook description of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. In roughly 50% of young adult female patients, this is a paraneoplastic syndrome triggered by an occult ovarian teratoma containing neural tissue.
This option are not a classic primary site for tumors triggering this specific encephalitis.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation and metabolic etiology of Early Myoclonic Encephalopathy (EME).
vignette: A 10-day-old neonate is evaluated in the NICU for profound hypotonia and frequent, erratic, migrating myoclonic jerks involving the face and limbs. The myoclonus is nearly continuous. An EEG is obtained and demonstrates a profound burst-suppression pattern. An extensive metabolic workup is initiated.
leadIn: Which of the following underlying etiologies is most frequently associated with this specific epileptic syndrome?

options.rationale: This option typically presents with microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, and sensorineural hearing loss, but is not the primary driver of EME.
This option causes Dravet syndrome, which presents later in the first year of life.
This option are the primary cause of Ohtahara syndrome.

options.text: Inborn errors of metabolism (e.g., nonketotic hyperglycinemia)
options.rationale: Early Myoclonic Encephalopathy (EME) presents in the neonatal period with erratic, fragmented myoclonus and a burst-suppression EEG pattern. Unlike Ohtahara syndrome (which presents with tonic spasms and is usually due to structural brain malformations), EME is most commonly caused by underlying inborn errors of metabolism, particularly nonketotic hyperglycinemia or amino/organic acidopathies.

learningObjective: Select the appropriate targeted therapy for infantile spasms in a patient with Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.
blueprintTopic: Epilepsy and Episodic Disorders / Neurocutaneous Syndromes
vignette: A 5-month-old female infant presents with clusters of sudden symmetric forward flexion of her head and trunk. Physical examination reveals three hypomelanotic macules on her torso. MRI of the brain demonstrates multiple subependymal nodules. She is diagnosed with infantile spasms secondary to Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC).
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic treatment for this specific patient?

options.rationale: This option is first-line for non-TSC infantile spasms.
This option is a sodium channel blocker used for focal seizures and status epilepticus, and can worsen epileptic spasms.

While Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and oral corticosteroids are first-line treatments for idiopathic infantile spasms, Vigabatrin is the specific drug of choice and highly efficacious first-line treatment for infantile spasms caused by Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC). It works by irreversibly inhibiting GABA transaminase.
This option is the treatment for childhood absence epilepsy.

learningObjective: Identify the appropriate second-line therapy for pediatric status epilepticus.
vignette: A 6-year-old child with a history of epilepsy is brought to the emergency department by EMS. He has been experiencing continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity for the past 20 minutes. EMS administered two doses of intravenous lorazepam en route, but the patient continues to seize upon arrival. His airway is secure, and hemodynamics are stable.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacologic management?

options.rationale: This option is used for absence epilepsy and is unavailable/inappropriate for acute status epilepticus.

The patient is in established status epilepticus and has failed first-line therapy with benzodiazepines (lorazepam). According to standard protocols, the immediate next step is the administration of a second-line intravenous anti-seizure medication, most commonly fosphenytoin, phenytoin, levetiracetam, or valproic acid, loaded sequentially.
This option is a first-line benzodiazepine, but since the patient already received adequate lorazepam, a longer-acting second-line agent is required.
This option or continuous midazolam/pentobarbital infusions are reserved for refractory status epilepticus (failing both first and second-line agents) and require intubation.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical sequence of Hemiconvulsion-Hemiplegia-Epilepsy (HHE) syndrome.
vignette: A 2-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a severe, unilateral right-sided clonic seizure that lasts for 45 minutes in the setting of a high fever. The seizure is eventually aborted with intravenous fosphenytoin. Upon waking, the child has a profound flaccid paralysis of the right arm and leg. An MRI of the brain obtained acutely shows cytotoxic edema in the left cerebral hemisphere.
leadIn: If this child develops Hemiconvulsion-Hemiplegia-Epilepsy (HHE) syndrome, follow-up neuroimaging one year later is most likely to reveal which of the following?

options.text: Severe global atrophy of the left cerebral hemisphere
options.rationale: HHE syndrome is characterized by a prolonged, unilateral clonic seizure (hemiconvulsion) in an infant or toddler, followed immediately by flaccid hemiplegia. The prolonged focal status epilepticus causes severe excitotoxic injury. Over months to years, this results in dramatic unilateral cerebral atrophy of the affected hemisphere and the subsequent development of intractable focal epilepsy.

options.text: An actively enhancing astrocytoma in the left frontal lobe
options.rationale: This option describes a neoplastic process, not post-ictal atrophic changes.

options.text: A large cavernous malformation in the left basal ganglia
options.rationale: This option is a vascular malformation that causes isolated seizures/hemorrhage but is not the consequence of HHE excitotoxic injury.
This option is the hallmark of premature hypoxic-ischemic injury.

learningObjective: Classify a complex febrile seizure based on duration and focal features.
leadIn: Febrile seizures are the most common neurological disorder of infants and young children. Distinguishing between simple and complex febrile seizures is critical for determining the need for further diagnostic workup. Which of the following clinical features explicitly classifies an event as a complex febrile seizure?

options.text: The seizure is a generalized tonic-clonic event lasting 5 minutes
options.rationale: , and D are typical features of a simple febrile seizure (generalized, <15 mins, solitary event in 24 hours, often occurring with a rapidly rising high fever, followed by normal post-ictal sleep).

options.text: The child experiences a post-ictal period of sleepiness lasting 30 minutes
options.rationale: , and D are typical features of a simple febrile seizure (generalized, <15 mins, solitary event in 24 hours, often occurring with a rapidly rising high fever, followed by normal post-ictal sleep).

options.text: The seizure has focal motor features or lasts longer than 15 minutes
options.rationale: A complex febrile seizure is defined by any of the following features: focal onset, duration greater than 15 minutes, or occurrence more than once within a 24-hour period. These features increase the risk of underlying pathology and subsequent epilepsy, often warranting further investigation.

options.text: The fever reaches a peak of 40.5°C (104.9°F) just prior to the seizure
options.rationale: Peak temperature does not classify a febrile seizure as simple or complex. Classification depends on duration (>15 minutes), focality, or recurrence within 24 hours.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical utility of the ketogenic diet and its absolute contraindication.
vignette: A 3-year-old child with medically refractory epilepsy is being evaluated for initiation of the ketogenic diet. The child has generalized tonic-clonic and myoclonic seizures. Before starting the diet, the neurologist orders a comprehensive metabolic panel and an acylcarnitine profile.
leadIn: The ketogenic diet is absolutely contraindicated if the patient has an underlying defect in which of the following metabolic pathways?

options.rationale: This option defects, specifically glucose transporter 1 (GLUT-1) deficiency, are the primary indication for the ketogenic diet, as ketones bypass the defective transporter.
This option are not the absolute, direct contraindications that fatty acid oxidation defects are, though high-protein versions of the diet must be modified for urea cycle disorders.

The ketogenic diet mimics the fasting state, forcing the brain to rely on ketone bodies (derived from fat) rather than glucose for energy. If a patient has a fatty acid oxidation defect (e.g., MCAD deficiency, carnitine deficiency), they cannot metabolize fats to create ketones. Placing them on a high-fat, low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet will precipitate a lethal metabolic crisis (hypoketotic hypoglycemia, coma, and death).
This option are not the absolute, direct contraindications that fatty acid oxidation defects are, though high-protein versions of the diet must be modified for urea cycle disorders.

learningObjective: Identify the side effect profile of topiramate.
leadIn: Topiramate is a broad-spectrum anti-seizure medication frequently utilized for both epilepsy and migraine prophylaxis in pediatric and adult patients. Which of the following represents a classic triad of adverse effects that patients must be counseled on prior to starting this medication?

options.text: Aplastic anemia, hyponatremia, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome
options.rationale: This option describes severe idiosyncratic reactions primarily associated with Carbamazepine.

options.text: Kidney stones, cognitive slowing, and acute angle-closure glaucoma
options.rationale: Topiramate is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. It famously causes weight loss, but its concerning adverse effect profile includes a significant risk for nephrolithiasis (kidney stones), cognitive dulling/word-finding difficulties ("dopamax"), and acute angle-closure glaucoma. Paresthesias are also very common.

options.text: Weight gain, hepatotoxicity, and polycystic ovarian syndrome
options.rationale: This option describes the classic side effect profile of Valproic acid.

options.text: Gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, and cerebellar ataxia
options.rationale: This option describes the classic side effect profile of Phenytoin.

learningObjective: Diagnose Sialidosis Type 1 (Cherry-Red Spot Myoclonus Syndrome).
blueprintTopic: Epilepsy and Episodic Disorders / Genetic Disorders
vignette: A 15-year-old girl is evaluated for worsening clumsiness and visual difficulties. Her parents report she has started experiencing sudden, shock-like jerks of her arms when she tries to reach for objects (action myoclonus). Her cognitive development and school performance have remained entirely normal. A fundoscopic examination reveals bilateral cherry-red spots in the maculae.
leadIn: A deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely responsible for this presentation?

options.rationale: This option causes Niemann-Pick Type A, presenting in infancy with hepatosplenomegaly, regression, and cherry-red spots.
This option causes Metachromatic Leukodystrophy, a demyelinating disorder without cherry-red spots.

The presentation of action myoclonus, ataxia, visual deterioration, and cherry-red spots presenting in adolescence with preserved intellect is the classic hallmark of Sialidosis Type 1 (Cherry-Red Spot Myoclonus Syndrome). It is caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-neuraminidase.
This option deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease, which presents in infancy with cherry-red spots but features profound cognitive and motor regression.

learningObjective: Recall normal pediatric EEG maturation regarding the posterior dominant rhythm.
leadIn: The electroencephalogram (EEG) of a healthy child undergoes predictable maturational changes from infancy through adolescence. A key milestone in this maturation is the frequency of the posterior dominant rhythm (PDR) during relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed. By what age does a healthy child's PDR typically reach the normal adult "alpha" frequency of 8 Hz?

options.rationale: The posterior dominant rhythm (PDR) starts at roughly 3-4 Hz in neonates, reaches 5-6 Hz by 1 year of age, and classically reaches the adult lower-limit alpha frequency of 8 Hz by 3 years of age.
, and D are incorrect maturational milestones. Knowing that an 8 Hz PDR is expected by age 3 is essential for distinguishing normal maturation from abnormal background slowing in toddlers.
By age 12 the PDR has long since reached the adult alpha range (~9–10 Hz). The 8 Hz milestone is achieved much earlier — typically around 3 years; waiting until 12 would be abnormally delayed.
, and D are incorrect maturational milestones. Knowing that an 8 Hz PDR is expected by age 3 is essential for distinguishing normal maturation from abnormal background slowing in toddlers.

learningObjective: Recognize the risk of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome with rapid lamotrigine titration.
vignette: A 12-year-old boy with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is currently taking valproic acid. His neurologist decides to add lamotrigine as adjunctive therapy. Because the parents misunderstood the instructions, they escalate the lamotrigine dose to the maximum target over 5 days instead of the recommended 8 weeks.
leadIn: This dosing error places the patient at the highest immediate risk for developing which of the following complications?

options.rationale: Lamotrigine carries a black box warning for severe, life-threatening skin rashes, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN). The risk is significantly increased by rapid dose escalation, use in pediatric patients (<16 years), and concurrent use of Valproic acid (which inhibits lamotrigine's metabolism, doubling its half-life). Extremely slow titration is mandatory in this specific clinical scenario.
This option are idiosyncratic, black-box warning side effects of Valproic acid, not the primary acute risk of rapid lamotrigine titration.
This option might occur with rapid withdrawal of anti-seizure medications, but rapid loading here primarily risks severe rash.
This option are idiosyncratic, black-box warning side effects of Valproic acid, not the primary acute risk of rapid lamotrigine titration.

learningObjective: Correlate Gelastic seizures with a hypothalamic hamartoma.
blueprintTopic: Epilepsy and Episodic Disorders / Brain Tumors
vignette: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician because his parents note he has been experiencing frequent episodes of inappropriate, unprovoked laughter. These episodes sound mechanical or forced, last for 10 to 20 seconds, and occur multiple times a day. Additionally, the pediatrician notes the child has enlarged testicles, pubic hair, and an advanced bone age.
leadIn: A high-resolution MRI of the brain is most likely to reveal a mass in which of the following locations?

options.rationale: This option is the location for medulloblastomas, causing ataxia and hydrocephalus.
This option tumors classically cause Parinaud syndrome (upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation).

The presentation of gelastic (laughing) seizures coupled with central precocious puberty in a young child is the pathognomonic presentation of a Hypothalamic Hamartoma. This is a benign, non-neoplastic malformation located in the region of the tuber cinereum of the hypothalamus.
This option is the location for ependymomas, presenting with signs of increased intracranial pressure and ataxia.

learningObjective: Differentiate Sandifer syndrome from epileptic seizures.
vignette: A 3-month-old infant is evaluated for recurrent episodes of sudden body stiffening. The parents state that the baby will frequently arch his back tightly, extend his neck backward (opisthotonos), and turn his head to the side. Upon detailed history taking, the parents note these events occur almost exclusively 10 to 15 minutes after feeding and are accompanied by irritability and crying. An EEG is performed and is completely normal during several of these events.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?

options.text: Initiation of anti-reflux medication and feeding modifications
options.rationale: The infant is exhibiting Sandifer syndrome, a non-epileptic paroxysmal disorder that is a behavioral response to the pain of severe gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). The opisthotonic posturing and neck extension typically occur during or just after feeding. Because it is non-epileptic (normal EEG during the event), the correct treatment targets the underlying GERD with anti-reflux medications and feeding modifications.

options.text: Prescription of daily valproic acid therapy
options.rationale: This option is an anti-seizure medication, which is inappropriate for a non-epileptic condition.

options.text: Genetic testing for a voltage-gated sodium channel mutation
options.rationale: This option evaluates for Dravet syndrome, which presents with prolonged febrile seizures, not post-prandial back arching. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- High-Yield Child Neurology Board Review Questions - Set 6 (25) Here is a brand new set of 25 very high-yield board-style questions focused exclusively on Child Neurology, drawn directly from the ABPN Content Specifications, “Board Review” resources, and pediatric texts in the provided sources. These questions cover entirely novel concepts and diagnoses to ensure no redundancy with your previous sets.
This option is the treatment for infantile spasms (West syndrome), which usually occur in clusters upon waking and feature a highly abnormal EEG (hypsarrhythmia).

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation of a Vein of Galen malformation in a neonate.
vignette: A 2-day-old term neonate is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for worsening respiratory distress, tachycardia, and hepatomegaly. Echocardiography reveals a structurally normal heart but severe high-output cardiac failure. Auscultation of the infant's skull reveals a loud, continuous cranial bruit.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely underlying neurologic abnormality driving this patient's systemic symptoms?

options.rationale: This option presents with seizures or focal hemorrhage, not systemic heart failure.
This option is an occlusive cerebrovascular disease presenting with strokes or TIAs, not high-output heart failure.
This option involves a capillary-venous malformation (port-wine stain) and leptomeningeal angioma, but does not cause massive arteriovenous shunting resulting in high-output heart failure.

A Vein of Galen malformation is an arteriovenous shunt located deep in the brain. In the neonatal period, it classically presents with profound high-output congestive heart failure (due to the massive shunting of blood) and a cranial bruit. It can also lead to progressive macrocephaly due to hydrocephalus from increased venous pressure.

learningObjective: Diagnose GLUT-1 deficiency syndrome based on early-onset seizures and CSF findings.
vignette: A 4-month-old infant is evaluated for recurrent seizures, developmental delay, and a complex movement disorder. The parents note the seizures occur most frequently just before feeding. A lumbar puncture is performed, revealing a normal white blood cell count and normal protein, but a markedly low cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) glucose level. Simultaneous serum blood glucose is completely normal.
leadIn: A mutation in which of the following genes is most likely responsible for this condition?

options.rationale: This option causes Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.
This option causes Rett syndrome.
This option causes Dravet syndrome (severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy).

Early-onset seizures (often provoked by fasting), developmental delay, and the pathognomonic finding of low CSF glucose (hypoglycorrhachia) with a normal serum glucose define GLUT-1 deficiency syndrome. It is caused by a mutation in the SLC2A1 gene, which impairs glucose transport across the blood-brain barrier. It is highly responsive to the ketogenic diet.

learningObjective: Correlate holoprosencephaly with Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome).
vignette: A newborn is evaluated in the nursery for severe midline facial defects, including a central cleft lip, hypotelorism (closely spaced eyes), and a single central incisor. Polydactyly is also noted on the hands. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain reveals failure of the cerebral hemispheres to separate, resulting in a single, fused lateral ventricle and fused thalami.
leadIn: This severe brain malformation is most classically associated with which of the following chromosomal abnormalities?

options.rationale: This option typically presents with prominent occiput, overlapping fingers, and rocker-bottom feet.

The patient’s clinical and radiologic presentation (midline facial defects, polydactyly, and holoprosencephaly) is the classic hallmark of Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome). Holoprosencephaly is a disorder of forebrain cleavage.
This option presents with a webbed neck, shield chest, and coarctation of the aorta.
This option features upslanting palpebral fissures, a single palmar crease, and atrioventricular septal defects.

learningObjective: Identify the specific biochemical marker and imaging features of Canavan disease.
leadIn: A 6-month-old infant presents with profound macrocephaly, hypotonia, and poor head control. Brain MRI demonstrates diffuse, symmetric white matter T2 hyperintensities with prominent involvement of the subcortical U-fibers. Which of the following biochemical markers is characteristically elevated in the urine of patients with this specific disorder?

options.rationale: This option is elevated in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.
This option is elevated in molybdenum cofactor deficiency/sulfite oxidase deficiency (presenting with dislocated lenses and intractable neonatal seizures).
This option is elevated in Glutaric aciduria type 1.

The triad of macrocephaly, hypotonia, and a leukodystrophy involving the subcortical U-fibers points to Canavan disease. It is caused by a deficiency in aspartoacylase, which leads to a diagnostic accumulation of N-acetylaspartic acid (NAA) in the urine, blood, and brain (visible as a massive NAA peak on MR spectroscopy).

learningObjective: Diagnose Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM) and select appropriate initial therapy.
vignette: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of extreme lethargy, bilateral leg weakness, and urinary retention. She had a resolving upper respiratory infection two weeks ago. On exam, she is highly encephalopathic with bilateral Babinski signs. MRI of the brain and spine reveals multiple, large, asymmetric, poorly marginated T2-hyperintense lesions in the deep white matter, basal ganglia, and spinal cord.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy for this condition?

options.rationale: This option is a treatment for chronic spasticity.

Acute onset of polyfocal neurologic deficits accompanied by encephalopathy following a viral illness, with MRI showing large, asymmetric, "fluffy" white and gray matter lesions, is classic for Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM). The first-line treatment is high-dose intravenous corticosteroids to suppress the post-infectious autoimmune cascade.
This option is a disease-modifying therapy for relapsing-remitting Multiple Sclerosis, not acute ADEM.
This option is the treatment for HSV encephalitis, which classically localizes to the medial temporal lobes, not multifocal diffuse lesions.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation and MRI findings of a Diffuse Intrinsic Pontine Glioma (DIPG).
vignette: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 1-month history of worsening gait instability, double vision, and difficulty swallowing. Physical exam reveals a right abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy, right facial nerve (CN VII) weakness, and left-sided spastic hemiparesis. MRI shows a large, expansile, T2-hyperintense mass centering in the pons and encasing the basilar artery.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option arises in the suprasellar region and causes visual field defects and endocrine dysfunction.
This option typically arises from the ependymal lining of the 4th ventricle, causing obstructive hydrocephalus.
This option arises from the cerebellar vermis and presents heavily with ataxia and signs of increased ICP (headache, vomiting).

The presentation of multiple cranial nerve palsies (VI, VII), long tract signs (hemiparesis), and ataxia, coupled with an expansile mass in the pons, is the classic presentation of a brainstem glioma (Diffuse Intrinsic Pontine Glioma / DIPG). It carries a very poor prognosis.

learningObjective: Differentiate transient neonatal myasthenia gravis from congenital forms based on maternal history.
vignette: A newborn is noted to have a feeble cry, poor suckling, and diffuse hypotonia shortly after birth. The mother has a history of intermittent ptosis, diplopia, and proximal muscle weakness that worsens toward the evening.
leadIn: The infant's symptoms are primarily mediated by which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: Genetic mutation in the muscle-specific tyrosine kinase (MuSK) gene
options.rationale: This option describes a genetic etiology that would cause Congenital Myasthenic Syndrome (which is not autoimmune and mothers are unaffected).

options.text: Ingestion and systemic circulation of Clostridium botulinum spores
options.rationale: This option causes infant botulism, which generally presents between 1 and 6 months of age following environmental exposure (e.g., honey/soil), not immediately at birth.

options.text: Transplacental transfer of maternal acetylcholine receptor antibodies
options.rationale: Transient neonatal myasthenia gravis occurs in up to 15-20% of infants born to mothers with Myasthenia Gravis. It is caused by the passive transplacental transfer of maternal IgG acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies. The symptoms are transient and spontaneously resolve over weeks as the maternal antibodies clear.

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of anterior horn cells
options.rationale: This option describes the pathophysiology of poliomyelitis.

learningObjective: Identify the genetic mechanism underlying Angelman syndrome.
leadIn: A 4-year-old girl is evaluated for severe intellectual disability, an unsteady, wide-based, stiff-legged gait, and frequent, inappropriate bursts of laughter. She also has a history of epilepsy. This clinical syndrome is most commonly caused by which of the following genetic mechanisms?

options.text: Expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat on the X chromosome
options.rationale: This option describes Fragile X syndrome.
This option causes Prader-Willi syndrome (hypotonia, obesity, hyperphagia).
This option describes Edwards syndrome.

Angelman syndrome is characterized by severe intellectual disability, severe speech impairment, ataxia, seizures, and a unique happy demeanor with inappropriate laughter ("happy puppet"). It is caused by a loss of expression of imprinted genes on the maternal chromosome 15q11-q13.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical features and age of onset of Epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome).
vignette: A 3-year-old boy, who previously had normal development, begins experiencing sudden "drop attacks" where he abruptly loses postural tone and falls to the floor, frequently sustaining facial injuries. He also has episodes of rhythmic jerking of his arms. An EEG reveals bilateral synchronous 2-3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges with biparietal rhythmic theta activity.
leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option presents in infancy (4-8 months) with infantile spasms and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.

Epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome) presents in early childhood (ages 1 to 5) with myoclonic and atonic seizures (drop attacks). The EEG is highly characteristic, showing synchronous spike-and-wave discharges accompanied by prominent biparietal rhythmic theta activity.
This option presents in school-aged children with nocturnal focal facial motor seizures and independent centrotemporal spikes.
This option presents in adolescence with early morning myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

learningObjective: Diagnose Alternating Hemiplegia of Childhood and recognize its association with ATP1A2.
vignette: A 12-month-old infant is evaluated for recurrent episodes of weakness. The parents report episodes where the child suddenly develops flaccid paralysis of the right arm and leg, lasting hours to days. In other episodes, the paralysis involves the left side of the body instead. These events are often accompanied by abnormal eye movements and autonomic instability. The episodes completely resolve after a period of sleep.
leadIn: This condition is most strongly associated with mutations in genes encoding which of the following proteins?

options.rationale: This option mutations cause Gaucher disease.
This option mutations cause Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
This option mutations cause familial hemiplegic migraine type 1 or episodic ataxias.

The clinical picture of early-onset, recurrent episodes of alternating hemiplegia (swapping sides), oculomotor abnormalities, and complete temporary relief following sleep is the hallmark of Alternating Hemiplegia of Childhood (AHC). It is heavily linked to mutations in the ATP1A2 gene, which encodes the alpha-2 subunit of the sodium/potassium-transporting ATPase.

learningObjective: Identify the clinical triggers and distinctive neuroimaging findings of Glutaric Aciduria Type I.
leadIn: A 15-month-old child presents with acute encephalopathy and severe dystonia following a mild viral gastrointestinal illness. Brain MRI demonstrates widely open, widened sylvian fissures (opercula) with a "bat-wing" appearance, alongside hyperintensities in the bilateral basal ganglia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Glutaric aciduria type I classically presents with macrocephaly, a distinctive "bat-wing" appearance of widened sylvian fissures on MRI, and an acute encephalopathic crisis with striatal necrosis (basal ganglia involvement) leading to severe dystonia, often triggered by a minor illness.
This option presents with alopecia, eczematous skin rash, seizures, and hearing loss.
This option presents acutely in neonates with sweet-smelling urine and massive brain edema (especially brainstem).
This option is a leukodystrophy presenting with extreme irritability, hypertonia, and white matter disease sparing U-fibers.

learningObjective: Correlate epidermal nevi with hemimegalencephaly in Epidermal Nevus Syndrome.
vignette: A 2-year-old child presents with intractable focal seizures. Physical examination reveals raised, hyperpigmented, verrucous skin lesions in a linear pattern following the lines of Blaschko on the left side of his body. MRI of the brain demonstrates asymmetric enlargement of the entire left cerebral hemisphere.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option presents with café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas.

Epidermal nevus syndrome is a sporadic neurocutaneous disorder defined by the presence of linear epidermal nevi (following Blaschko lines) associated with central nervous system anomalies. The most classic CNS anomaly associated with this syndrome is ipsilateral hemimegalencephaly, which frequently causes intractable epilepsy and intellectual disability.
This option presents in female neonates with linear vesicles that progress to hyperpigmented whorls, but hemimegalencephaly is not the defining feature.
This option presents with ash-leaf spots, facial angiofibromas, and cortical tubers.

learningObjective: Identify the primary anatomic etiology of obstructive sleep apnea in children.
vignette: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the clinic due to behavioral issues, hyperactivity, and poor attention in school. His parents report that he is a restless sleeper, snores loudly, and frequently sleeps with his neck hyperextended. He is at the 40th percentile for weight and body mass index.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely underlying anatomic cause of this patient's sleep disturbance?

options.rationale: This option causes inspiratory stridor in infants but typically improves by age 1-2 years.
This option can cause airway obstruction in neonates, but adenotonsillar hypertrophy is vastly more common in a normal 5-year-old.
This option is a CNS lesion causing gelastic (laughing) seizures and precocious puberty.

In children (particularly preschool and early school age), Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) frequently masquerades as ADHD (hyperactivity, inattention) rather than daytime sleepiness. Unlike adults, where obesity is the primary driver, the most common anatomic cause of pediatric OSA is adenotonsillar hypertrophy.

learningObjective: Recognize the association between right-to-left cardiac shunts and pediatric brain abscesses.
leadIn: A 6-year-old boy with a history of uncorrected Tetralogy of Fallot presents with fever, new-onset focal seizures, and a right-sided hemiparesis. A CT scan of the head with contrast reveals a ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding vasogenic edema in the left frontal lobe. The pathogenesis of this lesion is most directly related to which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: Right-to-left shunting of venous blood bypassing pulmonary phagocytic filtration
options.rationale: Children with cyanotic congenital heart disease (like Tetralogy of Fallot) have a right-to-left shunt. This allows venous blood to bypass the pulmonary capillary bed, which normally filters out circulating bacteria. Consequently, bacteria can enter the systemic cerebral circulation directly, dramatically increasing the risk of hematogenous brain abscesses.
This option typically causes abscesses in the adjacent temporal lobe or cerebellum, but the heart defect strongly points to hematogenous seeding.

options.text: Retrograde venous spread from a facial infection via the cavernous sinus
options.rationale: This option are incorrect mechanisms for this specific, highly-tested association.

options.text: Autoimmune vasculitis secondary to chronic hypoxemia
options.rationale: This option are incorrect mechanisms for this specific, highly-tested association.

learningObjective: Identify arterial dissection as a cause of stroke in a pediatric patient following mild trauma.
vignette: A 14-year-old adolescent presents to the ED with acute onset of expressive aphasia and right-sided hemiparesis. The parents note that he was at an amusement park riding a high-speed roller coaster earlier in the day. He now complains of sharp neck pain on the left side, and a left-sided Horner syndrome is noted on physical exam.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his acute neurologic presentation?

options.text: Cardioembolic stroke from a patent foramen ovale
options.rationale: This option causes embolic strokes but without the classic preceding neck trauma or ipsilateral Horner syndrome.
This option causes subarachnoid hemorrhage, presenting with "the worst headache of life" rather than acute ischemic stroke and isolated neck pain/Horner syndrome.

Blunt neck trauma, severe neck extension, or chiropractic manipulation (or roller coasters) can cause a dissection of the cervical internal carotid artery. This classically presents with neck pain, ipsilateral Horner syndrome (due to disruption of sympathetic fibers wrapping the carotid), and ischemic stroke in the MCA territory (aphasia, hemiparesis).
This option causes an epidural hematoma.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation and genetic etiology of Charcot-Marie-Tooth Type 1A.
leadIn: A 12-year-old boy presents with slowly progressive clumsiness and frequent ankle sprains. Examination reveals bilateral pes cavus (high-arched feet), a "stork leg" or "inverted champagne bottle" deformity due to distal calf muscle atrophy, and absent deep tendon reflexes at the ankles. Nerve conduction studies show symmetric, markedly slowed conduction velocities. This disorder is most commonly caused by a duplication of which of the following genes?

options.rationale: This option mutations cause Duchenne/Becker Muscular Dystrophy.

The clinical picture of pes cavus, distal atrophy, and areflexia with severely slowed nerve conduction velocities defines Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease Type 1 (a demyelinating hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy). The vast majority of CMT1 cases (CMT1A) are caused by a duplication of the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17.
This option mutations cause Spinal Muscular Atrophy.
This option mutations cause Friedreich Ataxia.

learningObjective: Diagnose benign familial neonatal seizures and its genetic/clinical characteristics.
vignette: A 5-day-old neonate begins having brief, focal clonic seizures that migrate from one side of the body to the other, sometimes accompanied by apnea. The infant was born at full term with no perinatal complications. The interictal EEG is entirely normal, and the infant is thriving. The father reports that he himself had seizures as a newborn that resolved on their own after a few months without treatment.
leadIn: A mutation in which of the following ion channels is most strongly associated with this familial syndrome?

options.rationale: This option is associated with Dravet syndrome and GEFS+.
This option mutations are associated with Myotonia Congenita.
This option mutations are associated with childhood absence epilepsy (T-type channels).

Benign familial neonatal seizures ("fifth day fits") typically present around day 5 of life with focal clonic or apneic seizures in an otherwise healthy infant. They are self-limiting and have an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. They are most commonly caused by mutations in the KCNQ2 or KCNQ3 genes, which encode voltage-gated potassium channels.

learningObjective: Identify the severe neonatal presentation of congenital myotonic dystrophy and its maternal transmission bias.
vignette: A neonate born at 36 weeks gestation presents with profound generalized hypotonia, poor suck, respiratory distress requiring mechanical ventilation, and bilateral clubfeet (arthrogryposis). Facial examination reveals an inverted V-shaped upper lip and severe facial diplegia. The mother has a history of early-onset cataracts and a notably "long, narrow" facial structure, though she has never been formally diagnosed with a neurologic condition.
leadIn: The genetic mutation responsible for this infant's condition is an expansion of a trinucleotide repeat (CTG). This severe congenital form is almost exclusively inherited via which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: Paternal transmission due to massive expansion of the repeat during spermatogenesis
options.rationale: This option is incorrect as paternal transmission of myotonic dystrophy typically does not expand enough to cause the severe congenital form (though paternal expansion is seen in Huntington disease).

options.text: Maternal transmission due to massive expansion of the repeat during oogenesis
options.rationale: The infant has Congenital Myotonic Dystrophy (Type 1), characterized by profound hypotonia, facial diplegia (tenting of the upper lip), respiratory failure, and arthrogryposis. Due to genetic anticipation, the trinucleotide CTG repeat expands in successive generations. Massive, severe expansions capable of causing the congenital form almost exclusively occur during maternal transmission (oogenesis).

options.text: Spontaneous de novo mutation early in embryogenesis
options.rationale: This option are incorrect; Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1 is an autosomal dominant disorder.

options.text: Autosomal recessive inheritance requiring mutations from both parents
options.rationale: This option are incorrect; Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1 is an autosomal dominant disorder.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical stigmata and neurologic manifestations of late congenital syphilis.
vignette: An 8-year-old boy, who recently immigrated from a region with poor prenatal care, is evaluated for progressive hearing loss and behavioral changes. Physical examination is notable for a saddle nose deformity, anterior bowing of the tibias (saber shins), and widely spaced, barrel-shaped, notched central incisors.
leadIn: These findings are classic late manifestations of an in utero infection with which of the following pathogens?

options.rationale: This option presents with cataracts, sensorineural hearing loss, and patent ductus arteriosus.
This option classically presents with periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, and petechial rash.

The clinical findings of sensorineural hearing loss, interstitial keratitis, and notched teeth (Hutchinson teeth) make up the classic Hutchinson triad of late congenital syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum. Other stigmata include saber shins and saddle nose deformity.
This option classically presents with chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications.

learningObjective: Identify the clinical presentation and genetic defect of Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease.
leadIn: A 6-month-old male infant presents with prominent pendular nystagmus, titubation (head bobbing), and severe central hypotonia. MRI of the brain reveals an almost complete absence of normal myelin (hypomyelination) throughout the cerebral hemispheres. This condition is caused by an X-linked mutation affecting which of the following structural myelin proteins?

options.rationale: This option is mutated in Alexander disease.
This option is deficient in Metachromatic Leukodystrophy.
This option is deficient in Krabbe disease.

Pendular nystagmus in early infancy, titubation, and an MRI showing classic hypomyelination (rather than demyelination) are hallmarks of Pelizaeus-Merzbacher Disease (PMD). It is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the PLP1 gene, which is a major structural protein of CNS myelin.

learningObjective: Diagnose lead encephalopathy and identify its classic hematologic finding.
vignette: A 3-year-old boy living in a home built in 1950 presents to the emergency department with acute irritability, persistent vomiting, and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. The parents report he has been increasingly clumsy and complaining of abdominal pain over the last month. A complete blood count reveals a microcytic anemia.
leadIn: Which of the following findings on a peripheral blood smear would most strongly support the underlying toxicological diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option are seen in patients with functional or surgical asplenia (e.g., Sickle cell disease).

options.text: Basophilic stippling of red blood cells
options.rationale: The child presents with acute lead encephalopathy (seizures, vomiting, severe irritability) preceded by chronic symptoms (abdominal pain, clumsiness) in the setting of an older home (lead paint risk). Lead poisoning interferes with heme synthesis, leading to a microcytic anemia. A classic finding on the peripheral blood smear is basophilic stippling of the red blood cells (aggregation of ribosomes).
This option are seen in G6PD deficiency.
This option are seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemias (e.g., HUS, TTP).

learningObjective: Recognize the classic dysmorphic features of Trisomy 18.
vignette: A newborn is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for severe hypotonia, a weak cry, and a structural congenital heart defect. Physical examination reveals a prominently enlarged occiput, micrognathia (small jaw), low-set malformed ears, overlapping fingers (index finger overlapping the middle finger, and pinky overlapping the ring finger), and distinct "rocker-bottom" feet.
leadIn: What is the most likely karyotype of this patient?

options.rationale: The constellation of a prominent occiput, micrognathia, overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, and congenital heart disease is the classic, highly-tested phenotype for Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome).
This option features holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, and cutis aplasia.
This option features upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat facial profile, and a single palmar crease.
This option features a webbed neck, cystic hygroma, and primary amenorrhea later in life.

learningObjective: Correlate Parinaud syndrome with a mass in the pineal region.
vignette: A 10-year-old boy complains of worsening morning headaches and double vision. Neurologic examination is remarkable for impaired upward conjugate gaze, pupils that constrict to accommodation but not to light (light-near dissociation), and bilateral upper eyelid retraction (Collier sign).
leadIn: Neuroimaging is most likely to reveal a mass in which of the following anatomical locations?

options.rationale: The triad of an upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation (pupils accommodate but do not react to light), and eyelid retraction represents Parinaud syndrome (dorsal midbrain syndrome). It is caused by compression of the superior colliculus and the pretectal area of the midbrain. The most common cause in a child is a mass in the pineal region (e.g., a pinealoma or germinoma).
This option typically compresses the optic chiasm, causing a bitemporal hemianopsia.
This option causes truncal/gait ataxia.
This option mass would cause lower cranial nerve palsies and long-tract signs.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical triad of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and its biochemical defect.
vignette: A 2-year-old boy presents with profound developmental delay and new-onset involuntary choreoathetoid movements. The parents report that he has a disturbing tendency to bite his own lips and fingers, often causing significant tissue damage. Laboratory tests show markedly elevated serum uric acid levels.
leadIn: A deficiency in which of the following enzymes is responsible for this condition?

options.rationale: This option is deficient in Biotinidase deficiency (alopecia, rash, hearing loss, seizures).
This option is deficient in Phenylketonuria (PKU).

The triad of severe hyperuricemia, choreoathetosis/dystonia, and compulsive self-mutilating behavior (biting lips/fingers) in a male toddler is diagnostic for Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. It is an X-linked recessive disorder of purine metabolism caused by a deficiency in the HGPRT enzyme.
This option is deficient in Niemann-Pick disease (hepatosplenomegaly, cherry-red spot).

learningObjective: Identify FDA-approved abortive treatments for pediatric migraine.
vignette: An 8-year-old girl is evaluated for recurrent migraines. She experiences severe, throbbing, unilateral headaches accompanied by nausea and photophobia, occurring twice a month. Her pediatrician has already tried optimizing her sleep and hydration, and she has failed to get adequate relief from high-dose ibuprofen and acetaminophen during attacks.
leadIn: Which of the following medications is a targeted, FDA-approved acute abortive therapy for migraines in children of this age group?

options.rationale: Triptans are the first-line targeted abortive therapy for pediatric migraines that do not respond to NSAIDs or acetaminophen. Rizatriptan is FDA-approved for acute abortive therapy of migraines in children aged 6 to 17 years. Almotriptan and Zolmitriptan nasal spray are also approved for adolescents (ages 12-17).

This option is used as a prophylactic agent for cluster headaches or bipolar disorder. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Pediatric Neurology Case Studies - Set 5 (25)
This option is an older abortive agent with significant side effects (nausea, vasoconstriction) and is rarely used as first-line in pediatrics.
This option is a calcium-channel blocker used occasionally for migraine or cluster headache prophylaxis, not acute abortive therapy.

learningObjective: Identify the clinical presentation and genetic mutation associated with Dravet syndrome (severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy).
vignette: A 14-month-old boy is evaluated for recurrent, prolonged seizures. His first seizure occurred at 6 months of age during a febrile illness and lasted for 20 minutes. Since then, he has experienced multiple febrile and afebrile generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Recently, his parents have noted brief jerking movements of his extremities and staring spells. His development, initially normal, has begun to plateau.
leadIn: A mutation in which of the following genes is the most likely cause of this patient's epilepsy?

options.rationale: This option mutations cause GLUT1 deficiency syndrome, presenting with early-onset seizures, microcephaly, and low CSF glucose.
This option mutations are associated with benign familial neonatal seizures, an autosomal dominant condition presenting in the first week of life that spontaneously resolves.

Severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy, or Dravet syndrome, typically presents in the first year of life with prolonged febrile seizures, followed by the development of multiple seizure types (myoclonic, atypical absence, tonic) and developmental plateauing. It is strongly associated with mutations in the SCN1A gene, representing the severe end of the generalized epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+) spectrum.
This option mutations are associated with paroxysmal kinesiogenic dyskinesia and benign familial infantile convulsions.

learningObjective: Diagnose CADASIL based on a characteristic clinical history and neuroimaging pattern.
vignette: A 42-year-old man presents to the neurology clinic with progressive memory impairment, executive dysfunction, and apathy. His medical history is notable for frequent migraine headaches with aura since his twenties and two prior ischemic strokes without identifiable cardiovascular risk factors. His father died at age 55 after years of severe dementia and multiple strokes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain reveals extensive, symmetric white matter hyperintensities on T2-weighted sequences.
leadIn: Which of the following specific regions is characteristically involved on this patient's MRI?

options.rationale: This option atrophy/hypoplasia is seen in Dandy-Walker or Joubert syndrome.

The clinical triad of migraines with aura, early-onset recurrent strokes without vascular risk factors, and progressive dementia with a strong autosomal dominant family history is highly suspicious for Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL). A classic MRI finding for CADASIL is extensive white matter disease with characteristic extension into the anterior temporal poles.
This option is the classic initial site of demyelination in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD).
This option are classically involved in Canavan and Alexander diseases, and spared in Krabbe and Metachromatic Leukodystrophy.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation, EEG findings, and specific biochemical marker of Nonketotic Hyperglycinemia (NKH).
vignette: A 3-day-old neonate is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit for profound lethargy, hypotonia, and apneic episodes. The infant also exhibits frequent, intractable myoclonic seizures and persistent hiccups. Laboratory evaluation shows normal serum ammonia, a normal anion gap, and no evidence of metabolic acidosis. An electroencephalogram (EEG) demonstrates a burst suppression pattern.
leadIn: Which of the following cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings will most specifically confirm this patient's diagnosis?

options.text: Low CSF glucose with a normal serum glucose
options.rationale: This option is characteristic of GLUT1 deficiency syndrome, caused by a defect in glucose transport across the blood-brain barrier.

options.text: A CSF-to-plasma glycine ratio greater than 0.06
options.rationale: The presentation of early neonatal encephalopathy, unremitting seizures, apnea, and characteristic hiccups without acidosis or hyperammonemia strongly points to glycine encephalopathy (nonketotic hyperglycinemia). The diagnosis depends on the simultaneous measurement of CSF and plasma glycine levels, with a CSF-to-plasma glycine ratio >0.06 being diagnostic.

options.text: Elevated CSF lactate with a normal serum glucose
options.rationale: This option is typical of mitochondrial disorders (e.g., Leigh syndrome or MELAS).
This option is the hallmark of Guillain-Barré syndrome.

learningObjective: Identify the deficient enzyme in Pompe disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type II).
leadIn: A 6-week-old infant presents with profound generalized hypotonia, a large tongue, and a significantly enlarged heart resulting in congestive heart failure. Laboratory studies reveal markedly elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels, but serum glucose levels remain normal during fasting. Muscle biopsy shows vacuoles distended with glycogen. This presentation is caused by a deficiency of which of the following enzymes?

options.rationale: Pompe disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type II) is caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid maltase (alpha-1,4-glucosidase). It classically presents in early infancy with severe hypotonia, massive cardiomegaly, hepatomegaly, and heart failure, notably without the hypoglycemia seen in other glycogen storage diseases.
This option is deficient in Tarui disease (GSD Type VII), presenting similarly to McArdle disease but with associated hemolytic anemia.
This option is deficient in von Gierke disease (GSD Type I), which presents with severe hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly, but not massive early cardiomegaly or primary muscle weakness.
This option is deficient in McArdle disease (GSD Type V), which presents in older children/adolescents with exercise-induced cramping and myoglobinuria.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical history, delayed presentation, and classic EEG findings of Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE).
vignette: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the neurology clinic by his parents due to a progressive decline in school performance and behavioral changes over the past six months. Recently, he has developed involuntary, sudden, shock-like muscle jerks (myoclonus) and gait unsteadiness. His medical history is notable for immigrating to the United States at age 4; his parents report he had a severe, generalized rash and high fever at 1 year of age.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely finding on this patient's electroencephalogram (EEG)?

options.rationale: This option is the classic finding for Childhood Absence Epilepsy.

options.text: Periodic slow-wave complexes at regular intervals
options.rationale: The patient's history of a presumed measles infection in early infancy followed years later (typically 2-12 years) by behavioral changes, cognitive decline, and myoclonus is classic for Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE). The pathognomonic EEG finding for SSPE is periodic slow-wave or high-amplitude complexes occurring at regular intervals (often 1-2 seconds) against a suppressed background.
This option is the defining EEG feature of Landau-Kleffner syndrome (acquired epileptic aphasia).
This option is the highly chaotic pattern seen in West syndrome (infantile spasms).

learningObjective: Localize the lesion responsible for internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO).
leadIn: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is a disorder of conjugate horizontal gaze characterized by an inability to adduct the eye ipsilateral to the lesion, coupled with abducting nystagmus in the contralateral eye. This classic neuro-ophthalmologic sign localizes to a lesion in which of the following structures?

options.rationale: This option drive voluntary saccades to the contralateral side; destructive lesions cause gaze preference toward the side of the lesion.

Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) is caused by a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), the heavily myelinated tract that connects the contralateral abducens (CN VI) nucleus to the ipsilateral medial rectus subnucleus of the oculomotor (CN III) nerve.
This option is involved in vertical gaze; compressive lesions here (e.g., pinealoma) result in Parinaud syndrome (upgaze palsy).
This option acts as the horizontal gaze center; a lesion here causes an ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy (neither eye can look toward the side of the lesion).

learningObjective: Identify the inheritance pattern, biochemical defect, and clinical features of Menkes disease.
leadIn: A 9-month-old male infant presents with profound developmental regression, severe hypotonia, and refractory myoclonic seizures. Physical examination is striking for pale, brittle, twisted "steel wool" hair and prominent, sagging jowls. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates low serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels. What is the inheritance pattern of this disorder?

options.rationale: The infant has Menkes disease (kinky hair disease), which is an X-linked recessive disorder of copper transport caused by mutations in the ATP7A gene. The lack of copper transport across the blood-brain barrier and intestinal mucosa leads to neurodegeneration, seizures, and characteristic brittle, twisted hair.
This option describes disorders with maternal inheritance, such as MELAS or MERRF.
This option describes conditions like Neurofibromatosis Type 1 and Tuberous Sclerosis.
