This option describes Wilson disease, another copper transport defect (ATP7B), which typically presents in older childhood/adolescence with liver disease or extrapyramidal symptoms, rather than early infancy with kinky hair.

learningObjective: Diagnose the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome based on clinical presentation.
vignette: A 10-year-old girl is evaluated in the emergency department for sudden onset of clumsiness, double vision, and difficulty walking. Her parents state she had a mild diarrheal illness two weeks ago. On neurologic examination, she has severe bilateral ptosis and near-complete restriction of eye movements in all directions. She is severely ataxic when attempting to walk, and her deep tendon reflexes are completely absent in both the upper and lower extremities. Her motor strength is otherwise fully intact.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option presents with fatigable ptosis and ophthalmoplegia but features normal deep tendon reflexes and does not typically cause profound isolated ataxia.
This option commonly follows a viral illness (e.g., Varicella) and presents with acute gait ataxia, but reflexes are preserved and complete external ophthalmoplegia is not characteristic.

options.text: Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome
options.rationale: The classic clinical triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia following a gastrointestinal or respiratory infection is diagnostic of the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS).
This option causes a descending flaccid paralysis with cranial nerve palsies, sluggish pupils, and prominent hypotonia/weakness, typically without pronounced isolated ataxia.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation, physical findings, and specific enzyme defect in Niemann-Pick disease Type A.
vignette: A 10-month-old infant is brought to the metabolic clinic due to loss of motor milestones and difficulty feeding. The child had been developing normally until 6 months of age. On physical examination, the child has severe, diffuse hypotonia and massive hepatosplenomegaly. Ophthalmologic examination reveals a distinct cherry-red spot in the macula bilaterally. A bone marrow aspirate shows numerous lipid-laden macrophages with a foamy cytoplasmic appearance.
leadIn: A deficiency in which of the following enzymes is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?

options.rationale: The combination of early developmental regression, massive hepatosplenomegaly, a cherry-red macula, and the presence of "foamy cells" in the bone marrow points to Niemann-Pick disease Type A, which is caused by a deficiency in sphingomyelinase.
This option is deficient in Tay-Sachs disease, which also presents with a cherry-red spot and regression, but explicitly lacks hepatosplenomegaly.

This option is deficient in Gaucher disease, which presents with massive hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises, and "wrinkled tissue paper" macrophages, but typically lacks the cherry-red macula (and Type 1 lacks early CNS involvement).

This option is deficient in Metachromatic Leukodystrophy, a demyelinating disorder that causes peripheral neuropathy and central white matter disease without massive hepatosplenomegaly or a cherry-red spot.

learningObjective: Identify the clinical and EEG features of Ohtahara syndrome.
vignette: A 3-week-old neonate is admitted to the pediatric neurology service for frequent, abnormal stiffening episodes. The parents report the infant has up to 100 episodes a day where he suddenly stiffens his arms and legs and holds them rigid for a few seconds. He is highly lethargic and feeds poorly. An extended sleep-deprived electroencephalogram (EEG) is obtained.
leadIn: If this patient has Ohtahara syndrome, which of the following patterns will be observed on the EEG?

options.text: Continuous spike-and-wave discharges during slow-wave sleep
options.rationale: This option is the defining EEG feature of Landau-Kleffner syndrome (acquired epileptic aphasia) seen in older children.

options.text: Burst suppression present during both wakefulness and sleep
options.rationale: Ohtahara syndrome (early infantile epileptic encephalopathy) presents in the first few weeks to months of life with intractable tonic spasms. The hallmark EEG finding is a burst suppression pattern that is apparent during both wakefulness and sleep. It is frequently associated with structural brain malformations.
This option is characteristic of Childhood Absence Epilepsy.

options.text: Chaotic, high-voltage slowing with multifocal spikes (hypsarrhythmia)
options.rationale: This option is the classic EEG pattern for West syndrome (infantile spasms), which typically presents slightly later (4 to 8 months of age).

learningObjective: Correlate the clinical presentation of a craniopharyngioma with its anatomic location and typical neuroimaging features.
vignette: An 8-year-old boy is evaluated for headaches, clumsiness, and increased thirst. His parents report that he has been drinking massive amounts of water and waking up multiple times at night to urinate. Additionally, his pediatrician noted that he has fallen off his growth curve over the past year. Confrontational visual field testing demonstrates a bitemporal hemianopsia.
leadIn: Neuroimaging of the brain is most likely to reveal which of the following lesions?

options.text: A calcified cystic mass in the suprasellar region
options.rationale: Headaches, bitemporal hemianopsia (optic chiasm compression), growth failure (pituitary stalk compression), and diabetes insipidus (polyuria/polydipsia) define the classic presentation of a suprasellar tumor, most commonly a craniopharyngioma in a child. Craniopharyngiomas are classically cystic, solid, and calcified on neuroimaging.

options.text: A solid mass in the posterior fossa arising from the cerebellar vermis
options.rationale: This option describes a medulloblastoma, which presents with ataxia and signs of increased intracranial pressure (ICP), not prominent endocrine dysfunction or bitemporal hemianopsia.

options.text: A cystic mass with a mural nodule in the cerebellar hemisphere
options.rationale: This option describes a juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma of the cerebellum, the most common pediatric brain tumor, presenting with ataxia and elevated ICP.

options.text: An enhancing mass within the lateral ventricle
options.rationale: This option describes an intraventricular tumor, such as a choroid plexus papilloma or a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA), which typically presents with obstructive hydrocephalus.

learningObjective: Diagnose cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and recognize the appropriate treatment despite hemorrhagic conversion.
vignette: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department for a severe, progressively worsening headache and two new-onset focal motor seizures involving her right side. Her medical history is notable for recently starting oral contraceptive pills. A non-contrast head CT demonstrates an area of hyperdensity with surrounding edema and petechial hemorrhage in the left parietal lobe that does not conform to a specific arterial territory. An MRI with MR venography confirms an occluded superior sagittal sinus.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.rationale: This option is an acute thrombolytic used strictly for acute arterial ischemic strokes within a rigid time window and is strictly contraindicated if any intracranial hemorrhage is present on CT.
This option would be indicated if the thrombosis was septic (e.g., mastoiditis causing transverse sinus thrombosis), but the history points to an aseptic, hypercoagulable etiology.
This option is used for inflammatory conditions or vasogenic edema associated with tumors, but is not the primary treatment for venous thrombosis.

The patient has a cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CSVT) associated with a hypercoagulable state (OCP use). CSVT often presents with headache, seizures, and venous infarctions that may cross arterial territories and undergo hemorrhagic conversion. The standard of care is systemic anticoagulation, which is indicated even in the presence of hemorrhagic infarcts, as it prevents further thrombosis and does not significantly increase bleeding risk.

learningObjective: Correlate the specific neuroanatomic malformation of schizencephaly with its MRI appearance.
leadIn: A 6-month-old infant is referred to the pediatric neurology clinic for severe global developmental delay and focal motor seizures. A brain MRI is ordered to evaluate for a structural brain malformation. Which of the following MRI descriptions is the defining hallmark of schizencephaly?

options.text: Bilateral, full-thickness cerebrospinal fluid-filled clefts extending from the ependyma of the ventricles to the pial surface
options.rationale: Schizencephaly is a disorder of neuronal migration characterized by the presence of abnormal, full-thickness, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-filled clefts within the cerebral hemispheres that extend from the ventricular ependyma to the pial surface.

options.text: A cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle with complete agenesis of the cerebellar vermis
options.rationale: This option describes Dandy-Walker malformation.

options.text: A completely smooth cerebral cortex lacking gyri and sulci
options.rationale: This option describes lissencephaly (agyria/pachygyria), which also causes severe delay and seizures but presents as a "smooth brain" without clefts.

options.text: Downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum
options.rationale: This option describes a Chiari malformation.

learningObjective: Diagnose Zellweger spectrum disorder based on characteristic clinical findings and lipid marker accumulation.
vignette: A 2-week-old neonate is evaluated in the nursery for profound hypotonia, poor suck, and frequent seizures. Physical examination reveals striking dysmorphic features, including a highly prominent forehead, a large anterior fontanelle, widely spaced eyes (hypertelorism), and a flat occiput. Abdominal palpation demonstrates marked hepatomegaly. Radiographs of the lower extremities reveal calcific stippling (chondrodysplasia punctata) of the patellae.
leadIn: Which of the following compounds is most likely to be elevated in this patient's plasma due to the underlying cellular defect?

options.rationale: This option are elevated in Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD).

The triad of severe neonatal hypotonia, distinct craniofacial dysmorphism (high forehead, flat occiput, hypertelorism), hepatomegaly, seizures, and characteristic bony stippling of the patellae is the classic presentation of Zellweger syndrome (cerebrohepatorenal syndrome). This is a severe defect in peroxisomal biogenesis, which results in the inability to oxidize very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs), leading to elevated VLCFA levels in the plasma.
This option accumulate in mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS, e.g., Hurler syndrome), which typically do not present with seizures and profound hypotonia in the immediate newborn period.
This option is elevated in Phenylketonuria (PKU).

learningObjective: Diagnose Panayiotopoulos syndrome (early childhood occipital epilepsy) based on autonomic seizure features.
vignette: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after his parents found him unresponsive in bed. They report he woke up suddenly, appeared very pale, and began violently retching and vomiting. His eyes deviated strongly to the right side, and he became completely unresponsive. The episode lasted for approximately 25 minutes before he slowly regained consciousness. His neurologic exam is completely normal.
leadIn: Which of the following electroencephalogram (EEG) findings is most strongly associated with this patient's epilepsy syndrome?

options.text: High-voltage occipital spikes that disappear with eye opening
options.rationale: The patient’s presentation is classic for early childhood occipital epilepsy (Panayiotopoulos syndrome), which occurs around age 4-8 years. Seizures often occur in sleep, are typically prolonged, and are distinctly characterized by marked prominent autonomic symptoms (pallor, severe retching, vomiting) and tonic eye deviation. The hallmark EEG finding is high-voltage occipital spikes that attenuate (disappear) with eye opening.

options.text: Continuous spike-and-wave discharges during slow-wave sleep
options.rationale: This option is seen in Landau-Kleffner syndrome, which presents with language regression.

options.text: Bilateral independent centrotemporal spikes activated by sleep
options.rationale: This option is the classic finding for Benign Epilepsy with Centrotemporal Spikes (BECTS / Rolandic Epilepsy), which presents with focal facial twitching and drooling, without the massive autonomic storm.

options.text: 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave complexes provoked by hyperventilation
options.rationale: This option is the finding for Childhood Absence Epilepsy, which features brief staring spells, not prolonged autonomic seizures.

learningObjective: Identify the classic MRI sign associated with neurologic Wilson disease.
vignette: A 16-year-old boy is evaluated in the neurology clinic for progressively worsening handwriting, dysarthria, and new-onset involuntary twisting movements of his right arm. His parents also note that he has been uncharacteristically aggressive and depressed over the last year. A slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist reveals golden-brown rings encircling the periphery of the corneas bilaterally (Kayser-Fleischer rings). Laboratory testing confirms a low serum ceruloplasmin level.
leadIn: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is most likely to display which of the following characteristic signs?

options.text: "Molar tooth" sign of the cerebellar peduncles
options.rationale: This option is the hallmark of Joubert syndrome (cerebellar vermis hypoplasia).
This option represents midbrain atrophy characteristic of Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP).

options.text: "Face of the giant panda" sign in the midbrain
options.rationale: Progressive extrapyramidal symptoms (dystonia, wing-beating tremor), psychiatric changes, Kayser-Fleischer rings, and low ceruloplasmin in an adolescent confirm the diagnosis of neurologic Wilson disease (ATP7B mutation). The classic MRI finding for Wilson disease involves T2 hyperintensities in the midbrain and thalami with preservation of the red nuclei, producing the "face of the giant panda" sign.

options.text: "Eye of the tiger" sign in the globus pallidus
options.rationale: This option is pathognomonic for Pantothenate Kinase-Associated Neurodegeneration (PKAN).

learningObjective: Identify the defective ion channel in Myotonia Congenita.
leadIn: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for muscle stiffness that makes it difficult for him to stand up from a chair or initiate a run. The stiffness reliably improves after he has been moving for a few minutes (the "warm-up" phenomenon). Physical examination is notable for prominent, generalized muscle hypertrophy, giving him a "bodybuilder" appearance. Electromyography (EMG) demonstrates repetitive, high-frequency discharges with a characteristic "dive bomber" sound. This patient's condition is caused by a mutation affecting which of the following structures?

options.rationale: This option mutations (sodium channels) cause hyperkalemic periodic paralysis and paramyotonia congenita (which worsens, rather than improves, with exercise).
This option mutations (calcium channels) cause hypokalemic periodic paralysis.

The presence of myotonia (delayed muscle relaxation) that improves with repeated muscle contraction (the warm-up phenomenon) combined with diffuse muscle hypertrophy is the classic presentation of Myotonia Congenita (Thomsen or Becker types). This is a primary channelopathy caused by mutations in the voltage-dependent chloride channel gene (CLCN1) on chromosome 7q.
This option are targeted by autoantibodies in Myasthenia Gravis, which presents with fatigable weakness, not myotonia.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical features and anatomic localization of Wallenberg syndrome (Lateral Medullary Syndrome).
leadIn: A patient presents with acute onset of intense vertigo, nausea, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing. Neurologic examination demonstrates loss of pain and temperature sensation on the right side of the face and the left side of the body, as well as a right-sided Horner syndrome and right-sided cerebellar ataxia. This constellation of symptoms (crossed sensory findings) is most commonly caused by an occlusion of which of the following arteries?

options.rationale: This option occlusion typically causes contralateral hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, and aphasia or neglect.

options.text: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery
options.rationale: The classic presentation of crossed sensory deficits (ipsilateral face, contralateral body pain/temp loss), ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ataxia, and bulbar symptoms (hoarseness, dysphagia due to nucleus ambiguus involvement) defines Wallenberg syndrome (Lateral Medullary Syndrome). This is most commonly caused by an infarction in the territory of the vertebral artery or its branch, the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA).
This option occlusion causes severe ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, nausea, and vomiting, but lacks the bulbar symptoms and Horner syndrome seen in PICA lesions.

This option occlusion causes Lateral Pontine Syndrome, which presents similarly but distinctly features ipsilateral facial paralysis and deafness/tinnitus, rather than the prominent hoarseness/dysphagia of a medullary lesion.

learningObjective: Identify the anatomical target of poliovirus leading to flaccid paralysis.
vignette: An unvaccinated 4-year-old child who recently immigrated from a region with endemic infectious diseases presents to the emergency department with a severe, asymmetrical, flaccid paralysis of his right leg. The parents report that three days prior, the child had a high fever, a stiff neck, and complained of a severe headache. On examination, the right leg is completely flaccid with absent deep tendon reflexes, but sensation to light touch and pinprick is fully intact.
leadIn: The pathogen responsible for this child's condition causes neurologic deficits by directly destroying which of the following structures?

options.text: Corticospinal tracts of the lateral funiculus
options.rationale: This option destruction causes upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski), not flaccid areflexia.

options.text: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord
options.rationale: The clinical sequence of a febrile illness with aseptic meningitis followed by acute, asymmetrical, descending flaccid paralysis with absent reflexes and preserved sensation in an unimmunized child is highly characteristic of Poliomyelitis. The poliovirus (an enterovirus) specifically invades and destroys the anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) in the spinal cord.
This option destruction would cause profound sensory loss, whereas polio is purely a motor disease.

This option is the target of the immune-mediated attack in Guillain-Barré syndrome, which typically presents with symmetric, ascending paralysis, not a focal/asymmetric paralysis heralded by acute meningitis.

learningObjective: Diagnose Wernicke encephalopathy based on the clinical triad and target appropriate vitamin replacement.
blueprintTopic: Metabolic Diseases, Nutritional Deficiency States, and Toxins
vignette: A 16-year-old girl with a history of severe anorexia nervosa and recent prolonged fasting is admitted to the hospital and started on total parenteral nutrition (TPN). Three days later, she becomes acutely confused and agitated. Neurologic examination is remarkable for a wide-based, unsteady gait and bilateral abducens nerve (CN VI) palsies resulting in horizontal diplopia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain reveals symmetric T2 hyperintensities and petechial hemorrhages in the mammillary bodies and medial thalami.
leadIn: Immediate intravenous supplementation with which of the following vitamins is required to reverse this patient's acute neurologic decline?

options.rationale: This option deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (sensory ataxia, spasticity, macrocytic anemia), but not the acute Wernicke triad.

The classic clinical triad of acute confusion (encephalopathy), ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia (often CN VI palsies or nystagmus) defines Wernicke encephalopathy. It is caused by severe thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency, which can be acutely precipitated by providing a glucose load (like TPN) to a malnourished patient without prior thiamine supplementation. The hallmark MRI finding is petechial hemorrhages or hyperintensity in the mammillary bodies and medial thalami.
This option deficiency causes Pellagra (diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia).
This option deficiency can cause intractable seizures in neonates or peripheral neuropathy.

learningObjective: Recognize the inheritance pattern, dermatologic stages, and systemic findings of Incontinentia Pigmenti.
leadIn: A 3-week-old female neonate presents with a peculiar rash consisting of linear crops of inflammatory vesicles following the lines of Blaschko on her trunk and extremities. The dermatologist notes that these lesions typically progress to verrucous papules, and eventually to brown/blue-gray hyperpigmented whorls. The infant has also begun experiencing focal seizures. A mutation in the NEMO (IKBKG) gene is confirmed. What is the inheritance pattern of this disorder?

options.rationale: This option describes neurocutaneous syndromes like Tuberous Sclerosis or Neurofibromatosis Type 1.
This option typically affects males severely and spares or mildly affects female carriers (e.g., Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome).

The progression of skin lesions (blaschkoid vesicles -> verrucous papules -> hyperpigmented patches), combined with central nervous system involvement (seizures) in a female infant, is the hallmark of Incontinentia Pigmenti. This condition is caused by an IKBKG (NEMO) mutation and is inherited in an X-linked dominant fashion, which is typically lethal in males in utero (hence presenting almost exclusively in females).
This option describes ataxia-telangiectasia.

learningObjective: Diagnose homocystinuria based on phenotypic similarities to Marfan syndrome, distinct thromboembolic risks, and the underlying enzyme defect.
vignette: A 13-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with acute swelling, pain, and redness in his left calf. Venous ultrasound confirms a deep vein thrombosis (DVT). His physical examination reveals a tall, exceedingly thin habitus with long, spidery fingers (arachnodactyly) and pectus excavatum. His mother notes he has a history of mild intellectual disability and required surgery for downward-dislocated lenses in both eyes.
leadIn: This patient's syndrome is most commonly caused by a deficiency in which of the following enzymes?

options.rationale: This option mutations cause Marfan syndrome, which presents with a similar body habitus but typically features upward lens dislocation, normal intellect, and aortic root dilation rather than massive thromboembolic risk.

A Marfanoid body habitus (tall, arachnodactyly, pectus deformities) combined with intellectual disability, a high risk of thromboembolic events (like DVT or strokes), and downward lens dislocation (ectopia lentis) defines classic Homocystinuria. This is an autosomal recessive disorder most frequently caused by a deficiency in the enzyme cystathionine beta-synthase, leading to toxic elevations of homocysteine.
This option causes classic Galactosemia.
This option causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (self-mutilation, choreoathetosis, hyperuricemia).

learningObjective: Differentiate Sandifer syndrome from epileptic spasms based on symptom triggers and lack of EEG correlates.
vignette: A 4-month-old infant is referred to the pediatric neurology clinic for possible seizures. The parents report that several times a day, the infant will suddenly arch his back, forcefully extend his neck, and stiffen his extremities. Upon careful questioning, the parents confirm that these episodes occur almost exclusively during or immediately following feeding. The infant has no developmental regression, and his neurologic exam is normal. A 24-hour video-EEG captures three of these episodes; none of them are accompanied by epileptiform changes on the EEG.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option present with sudden flexor or extensor spasms that typically occur in clusters upon awakening, are associated with severe developmental regression, and have a highly chaotic EEG pattern (hypsarrhythmia).
This option presents with brief shuddering or shivering spells, not severe tonic back arching associated with feeding.

Sudden episodes of tonic neck extension and severe dystonic arching of the back (opisthotonos) in an infant that occur in strict relation to feeding strongly suggest Sandifer syndrome. This is a non-epileptic paroxysmal disorder associated with severe gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). The posturing is believed to be a pain response to acidic reflux. The lack of EEG correlates and normal neurodevelopment confirm its non-epileptic nature.
This option would show corresponding focal epileptiform activity on the EEG and are not strictly tied to the act of feeding.

learningObjective: Recognize the classic clinical triad and inheritance pattern of Aicardi syndrome.
leadIn: A 3-month-old female infant presents with infantile spasms. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain reveals complete agenesis of the corpus callosum. A subsequent ophthalmologic examination demonstrates multiple, distinct chorioretinal lacunae. What is the inheritance pattern of the genetic disorder that produces this pathognomonic triad?

options.rationale: The triad of infantile spasms, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and pathognomonic chorioretinal lacunae defines Aicardi syndrome. This is a rare genetic disorder inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern. Because it is lethal in utero for males (46, XY), it is seen almost exclusively in females (or males with Klinefelter syndrome, 47, XXY).
This option typically affects males and spares females (e.g., Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy).
This option describes Tuberous Sclerosis Complex, which can cause infantile spasms but features cortical tubers and subependymal nodules rather than callosal agenesis and chorioretinal lacunae.
This option describes Tay-Sachs or Krabbe disease, which have distinct features (e.g., cherry red spot, optic atrophy).

learningObjective: Correlate the clinical presentation and frontal-predominant MRI findings of Alexander disease with its histopathological hallmark.
vignette: An 8-month-old infant is evaluated for rapidly enlarging head circumference (macrocephaly), feeding difficulties, and progressive spastic quadriparesis. Development had initially been normal but has recently arrested. An MRI of the brain reveals diffuse, symmetric white matter signal abnormalities with a strong anterior-to-posterior gradient, indicating severe frontal lobe involvement. Genetic testing confirms a mutation in the GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) gene.
leadIn: If a brain biopsy were performed, which of the following histopathological findings would most likely be observed?

options.rationale: The combination of infantile macrocephaly, rapid developmental regression, spasticity, and a leukodystrophy with strong frontal lobe predominance is classic for Alexander disease. It is caused by a mutation in the GFAP gene. The histopathological hallmark of Alexander disease is the presence of Rosenthal fibers—elongated eosinophilic inclusions composed of GFAP aggregates—clustered in astrocytes throughout the subpial, subependymal, and perivascular areas.

This option are spherical aggregations of tau protein seen in Pick's disease (a variant of frontotemporal dementia). -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- High-Yield Child Neurology Board Review Questions - Set 4 (25) Here is a brand new set of 25 high-yield board-style questions for Child Neurology, crafted strictly according to the Operational Model and six-step development process. These questions explore entirely different diagnoses and concepts from the previous sets, pulling heavily from the ABPN Content Specifications, the Pediatric Board Study Guide, and the Board Review materials provided in your sources.
This option are cytoplasmic viral inclusion bodies found in neurons infected with Rabies.
This option are alpha-synuclein inclusions found in the substantia nigra in Parkinson disease or the cortex in Lewy Body Dementia.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation of stroke in a patient with sickle cell disease.
vignette: A 6-year-old self-identified African American child presents to the emergency department with an acute onset of right-sided weakness and aphasia. The patient has a history of multiple hospitalizations for severe bone and joint pain, as well as one episode of acute chest syndrome.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely underlying etiology for this patient's acute neurologic presentation?

options.rationale: This option is associated with hypercoagulable states (thrombophilias) or severe dehydration, but large-artery ischemic stroke is the classic severe cerebrovascular complication of sickle cell disease.

options.text: Intracranial hemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm
options.rationale: This option is a common cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage, often seen in adults or in patients with specific connective tissue disorders (e.g., Ehlers-Danlos or Marfan syndrome).
This option describes a risk factor associated with Tuberous Sclerosis Complex, not sickle cell disease.

The patient’s history of vaso-occlusive crises and acute chest syndrome indicates sickle cell disease. Sickle cell disease is a major risk factor for large-artery ischemic stroke in children (often involving the internal carotid or middle cerebral arteries) due to chronic intimal damage and stenosis.

learningObjective: Diagnose biotinidase deficiency based on its classic dermatologic and neurologic presentation.
blueprintTopic: Metabolic Diseases, Nutritional Deficiency States, and Toxins
vignette: A 6-month-old infant is evaluated for developmental delay, new-onset seizures, and profound hearing loss. Physical examination is notable for diffuse alopecia and a severe eczematous skin rash resembling acrodermatitis enteropathica. Laboratory studies reveal a high anion gap metabolic acidosis and elevated serum lactate.
leadIn: Which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option typically presents with intellectual disability, fair skin, eczema, and a "musty" odor, but lacks the profound alopecia and acute severe metabolic acidosis.
This option presents acutely in the neonatal period with severe encephalopathy, opsithotonos, and a distinct "sweet" odor to the urine, without alopecia.
This option presents with macrocephaly, acute striatal necrosis, and dystonia, often triggered by an acute illness, but lacks the characteristic rash and alopecia.

The clinical triad of neurologic features (seizures, hearing loss, encephalopathy), distinct dermatologic findings (alopecia, acrodermatitis enteropathica-like skin rash), and metabolic acidosis/lactic acidosis is the classic presentation of biotinidase deficiency, a treatable multiple carboxylase deficiency.

learningObjective: Differentiate congenital toxoplasmosis based on its characteristic neuroimaging findings and clinical triad.
vignette: A neonate is evaluated in the nursery for microcephaly and seizures. Ophthalmologic examination reveals bilateral chorioretinitis. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the head is performed to evaluate for a congenital TORCH infection.
leadIn: Which of the following findings on the CT scan would most strongly support a diagnosis of congenital toxoplasmosis?

options.rationale: This option describes the classic calcification pattern seen in congenital Cytomegalovirus (CMV).
This option is associated with several genetic syndromes (e.g., Aicardi syndrome) but is not the defining infectious imaging hallmark of toxoplasmosis.

options.text: Cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle
options.rationale: This option is the structural hallmark of Dandy-Walker malformation, not a congenital infection.

The classic clinical triad of congenital toxoplasmosis includes chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus/microcephaly, and intracranial calcifications. On neuroimaging, toxoplasmosis classically presents with diffuse intraparenchymal calcifications.

learningObjective: Identify the genetic mechanism underlying Prader-Willi syndrome.
leadIn: A 7-year-old boy is evaluated in the genetics clinic for severe obesity, hyperphagia, and cognitive impairment. The parents report that as an infant, he had profound hypotonia and feeding difficulties. Physical examination reveals small hands and feet, as well as cryptorchidism. This patient's syndrome is most commonly caused by which of the following genetic mechanisms?

options.rationale: Prader-Willi syndrome presents with severe neonatal hypotonia followed by childhood hyperphagia, obesity, intellectual disability, and hypogonadism. It is caused by the absence of expression of imprinted genes in the 15q11-q13 region on the paternal chromosome (most commonly via a microdeletion).

options.text: Expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat on the X chromosome
options.rationale: This option is the genetic mechanism for Fragile X syndrome.
This option causes Patau syndrome, characterized by severe midline defects (cleft lip/palate, holoprosencephaly) and polydactyly.
This option results in Angelman syndrome, which presents with severe intellectual disability, an unsteady wide-based gait, a happy demeanor with frequent laughing, and seizures.

learningObjective: Associate opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome with its most common pediatric occult malignancy.
vignette: A 2-year-old child presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset ataxia and rapid, multi-directional, chaotic eye movements. The parents also report that the child has been experiencing brief, shock-like muscle jerks of the trunk and limbs that worsen when the child is agitated.
leadIn: This paraneoplastic presentation warrants immediate screening for which of the following underlying tumors?

options.rationale: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia (OMA) syndrome, often referred to as "dancing eyes, dancing feet," is a classic pediatric paraneoplastic syndrome. In toddlers, it is most highly associated with an occult neuroblastoma.
This option is a suprasellar tumor presenting with visual field deficits (bitemporal hemianopsia) and endocrine dysfunction, not OMA.
This option are primary posterior fossa brain tumors. While they cause ataxia and increased intracranial pressure, they do not cause the paraneoplastic opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome.
This option are primary posterior fossa brain tumors. While they cause ataxia and increased intracranial pressure, they do not cause the paraneoplastic opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome.

learningObjective: Diagnose juvenile dermatomyositis based on clinical and laboratory findings.
vignette: A 7-year-old girl is evaluated for a progressive inability to climb stairs and comb her hair over the past two months. She frequently complains of joint pain. Physical examination reveals symmetric proximal muscle weakness, a distinct purplish discoloration over her upper eyelids, and erythematous, scaly plaques over her metacarpophalangeal joints. Laboratory testing demonstrates significantly elevated creatine phosphokinase (CPK) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: This option presents with hypotonia, absent reflexes, and tongue fasciculations due to anterior horn cell degeneration, not an inflammatory myopathy.
This option presents with fatigable weakness (ptosis, diplopia) but does not feature markedly elevated CPK, muscle inflammation, or rash.

Symmetric proximal muscle weakness combined with classic dermatologic findings—a heliotrope rash (purplish eyelids) and Gottron papules (scaly plaques on the knuckles)—is diagnostic for juvenile dermatomyositis, an inflammatory myopathy.
This option presents with proximal weakness and high CPK but exclusively affects boys (X-linked recessive) and lacks the classic inflammatory rashes.

learningObjective: Recognize cyclic vomiting syndrome as a migraine equivalent in children.
vignette: A 6-year-old child presents to the clinic with recurrent episodes of severe nausea and vomiting. During an episode, the child vomits multiple times per hour for two days, appears pale, and demonstrates photophobia and lethargy. Between these episodes, the child is completely asymptomatic, active, and growing normally. Comprehensive gastrointestinal evaluations, including endoscopy, have been completely normal.
leadIn: This presentation is most strongly considered an early childhood equivalent or precursor to which of the following disorders?

options.rationale: This option would present with progressive, non-episodic cranial neuropathy, ataxia, and signs of increased intracranial pressure, not completely normal intervals.
This option would likely present with chronic symptoms, weight loss, bloody diarrhea, or abnormal GI scoping, rather than strictly episodic vomiting with symptom-free intervals.
This option features unprovoked seizures, not isolated cyclic vomiting with normal intervening periods.

Cyclic vomiting syndrome (also known as abdominal migraine) is characterized by stereotyped, recurrent bouts of intense nausea and vomiting separated by completely symptom-free intervals. It is widely recognized as a childhood migraine equivalent, and many of these patients go on to develop classic migraine headaches later in life.

learningObjective: Distinguish a simple febrile seizure from a complex febrile seizure.
vignette: A previously healthy 16-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after experiencing a seizure at home. The parents state the child was hot to the touch and suddenly exhibited generalized tonic-clonic movements lasting for approximately 60 seconds. In the emergency department, his temperature is 39.4°C (103°F) due to a confirmed viral upper respiratory infection. He is now awake, alert, and acting at his baseline, with a normal neurologic examination.
leadIn: Which of the following terms best categorizes this patient's event?

options.rationale: This option requires continuous seizure activity or recurrent seizures without returning to baseline for >5 minutes (or 30 minutes by older definitions), far exceeding the 60 seconds seen here.
This option is defined by any of the following features: focal onset, duration greater than 15 minutes, or occurring more than once in 24 hours.

This option presents as clusters of brief, symmetric flexor/extensor spasms typically seen in infants under 1 year of age and is associated with a chaotic EEG (hypsarrhythmia), not an isolated generalized fever-provoked seizure.

A simple febrile seizure occurs in a child aged 6 months to 5 years, is generalized (non-focal), lasts less than 15 minutes, and occurs only once in a 24-hour period. This child meets all criteria for a simple febrile seizure.

learningObjective: Recognize the laboratory profile of Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency.
blueprintTopic: Metabolic Diseases, Nutritional Deficiency States, and Toxins
vignette: A 3-day-old male neonate is admitted to the intensive care unit for poor feeding, worsening lethargy, and tachypnea. Laboratory investigations reveal a markedly elevated serum ammonia level of 1800 µmol/L and a low blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrates a respiratory alkalosis with no significant metabolic ketoacidosis.
leadIn: These findings are most characteristic of a defect in which of the following metabolic processes?

options.rationale: This option involves progressive neurodegeneration and organomegaly, not acute neonatal hyperammonemia.

The presence of massive hyperammonemia, low BUN, and a primary respiratory alkalosis (due to central hyperventilation driven by ammonia) without severe metabolic acidosis/ketosis is the hallmark of a Urea Cycle Defect. In a male neonate, this is most commonly Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency (X-linked recessive).
This option typically presents with hypoketotic hypoglycemia and metabolic acidosis during fasting, rather than primary isolated hyperammonemia with respiratory alkalosis.
This option presents with severe metabolic ketoacidosis and sweet-smelling urine.

learningObjective: Recall the clinical criteria for PHACE syndrome.
leadIn: A large, segmental facial hemangioma in a newborn should prompt investigation for associated systemic and neurologic anomalies. The acronym PHACE syndrome describes a specific association of these facial hemangiomas with posterior fossa malformations, arterial anomalies, cardiac defects, and which of the following other findings?

options.rationale: PHACE syndrome stands for Posterior fossa malformations (e.g., Dandy-Walker), Hemangiomas (large, facial), Arterial anomalies, Cardiac defects (e.g., coarctation of the aorta), and Eye abnormalities. Sternal clefts are also occasionally included (PHACES).
, and D are incorrect elements for the PHACE acronym. (Epidermal nevi are associated with Epidermal Nevus Syndrome).
, and D are incorrect elements for the PHACE acronym. (Epidermal nevi are associated with Epidermal Nevus Syndrome).

Epidermal nevi are the hallmark of Epidermal Nevus Syndrome (Schimmelpenning), not PHACE. The "E" in PHACE stands for Eye abnormalities; sternal/supraumbilical raphe defects extend the acronym to PHACES.

learningObjective: Diagnose an acute dystonic reaction secondary to dopamine-receptor blocking agents.
vignette: A 14-year-old adolescent is brought to the emergency department because of sudden, involuntary, and sustained upward deviation of the eyes (oculogyric crisis) and severe twisting of the neck to the right (torticollis). The patient is fully alert but highly distressed. Medical history is notable for a recent prescription of a phenothiazine antiemetic for severe gastroenteritis.
leadIn: Which of the following medications is the most appropriate acute treatment for this patient's condition?

options.rationale: This option is an anti-seizure medication and is ineffective for dystonia.

The patient is experiencing an acute dystonic reaction caused by a dopamine-receptor blocking agent (a phenothiazine antiemetic). The definitive and rapid treatment is an anticholinergic medication, commonly intravenous diphenhydramine or benztropine.
This option is a typical antipsychotic (a strong dopamine antagonist) and would actively worsen the dystonia.
This option is used for Parkinson disease or Dopa-responsive dystonia, but is not the acute abortive treatment of choice for medication-induced dystonic reactions.

learningObjective: Identify the classic presentation of retinoblastoma.
vignette: A 14-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician by his parents, who noticed an abnormality in recent flash photographs. Instead of the typical "red eye" appearance, the pupil of the child's right eye appears solid white. On physical examination in a darkened room, the pediatrician confirms an absent red reflex and a distinct white pupillary reflex in the right eye.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this ocular finding?

options.rationale: This option presents with acute vision loss, pain with eye movement, and an afferent pupillary defect, but not a white pupillary reflex.
This option presents with tearing, photophobia, and a large, cloudy cornea (buphthalmos), not an isolated white pupillary reflex behind a clear cornea.
Leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex) and an absent red reflex in an infant or toddler is the classic and most common presenting sign of retinoblastoma, a malignant tumor of the retina.
This option presents as sudden, painless vision loss with a "cherry-red spot" on the macula upon fundoscopy, not gross leukocoria.

learningObjective: Diagnose McArdle disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type V) based on clinical presentation.
vignette: A 16-year-old adolescent male presents to the sports medicine clinic complaining of severe muscle cramps and early fatigue during brief, intense exercise. He notes that if he rests briefly when the pain starts, he can often resume the activity with less discomfort (a phenomenon he calls his "second wind"). He recently had an episode of passing dark, tea-colored urine following a vigorous weightlifting session.
leadIn: A deficiency of which of the following enzymes is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

options.rationale: This option presents with recurrent myoglobinuria triggered by prolonged exercise or fasting, but lacks the distinct "second wind" phenomenon seen in McArdle disease.

Exercise intolerance, severe muscle cramping with intense activity, the classic "second wind" phenomenon, and myoglobinuria (dark urine) are the hallmarks of McArdle disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type V). It is caused by a deficiency of muscle phosphorylase (myophosphorylase).
This option is absent in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which presents with progressive proximal weakness and calf pseudohypertrophy, not exercise-induced cramping.
This option is deficient in Pompe disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type II), which presents in infancy with severe hypotonia, massive cardiomegaly, and heart failure.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical triad of classic galactosemia.
vignette: A 10-day-old neonate who is exclusively breastfed presents with poor feeding, vomiting, and worsening lethargy. Physical examination reveals jaundice and hepatomegaly. Ophthalmologic evaluation notes the presence of bilateral cataracts. Laboratory studies are remarkable for profound hypoglycemia and positive urine reducing substances. Blood cultures are drawn and subsequently grow Escherichia coli.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate dietary intervention for this infant?

options.text: Administration of frequent, high-carbohydrate cornstarch meals
options.rationale: This option is the treatment for Glycogen Storage Disease Type 1 (Von Gierke disease) to prevent fasting hypoglycemia.
This option is the treatment for Phenylketonuria (PKU).

options.text: Fortification of breast milk with medium-chain triglycerides
options.rationale: This option is the treatment for long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects, not galactosemia.

options.text: Transition to a soy-based, lactose-free formula
options.rationale: The triad of jaundice/hepatomegaly, cataracts, and E. coli sepsis in a neonate ingesting lactose (breast milk) is the classic presentation of Galactosemia (galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency). The immediate and life-saving intervention is the total elimination of dietary galactose/lactose, transitioning the infant to a soy-based formula.

learningObjective: Diagnose Lyme disease presenting as an isolated cranial neuropathy.
vignette: A 9-year-old boy from New York presents to the clinic with an acute inability to close his right eye or smile on the right side of his face. The physical examination confirms an isolated lower motor neuron facial nerve (CN VII) palsy. He has no rash, fever, or signs of meningeal irritation. The parents report they went on a camping trip in a heavily wooded area three weeks ago.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the diagnostic evaluation of this patient?

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis
options.rationale: This option are generally reserved for signs of more extensive CNS involvement (e.g., meningitis, severe headache, altered mental status) or if the diagnosis remains unclear, but are not the first-line initial diagnostic test for isolated facial palsy suspected of being Lyme.

options.text: Order serologic testing for Borrelia burgdorferi
options.rationale: In an endemic area (such as New York), an isolated facial nerve palsy (especially in a child with a history of outdoor exposure) should prompt immediate serologic testing for Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi). While erythema migrans is the classic rash, it is absent in a significant portion of patients.

options.text: Reassure the parents and observe without testing
options.rationale: This option is appropriate for presumed idiopathic Bell's palsy in a non-endemic region without exposure history, but testing is required here given the high suspicion for a treatable infection.

options.text: Obtain a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain with contrast
options.rationale: This option are generally reserved for signs of more extensive CNS involvement (e.g., meningitis, severe headache, altered mental status) or if the diagnosis remains unclear, but are not the first-line initial diagnostic test for isolated facial palsy suspected of being Lyme.

learningObjective: Recall the cardinal features and serum biomarker for Ataxia-Telangiectasia.
leadIn: A pediatric patient presenting with progressive cerebellar ataxia, recurrent severe sinopulmonary infections, and oculocutaneous vascular anomalies is suspected of having an autosomal recessive DNA repair defect. Which of the following laboratory findings is most classically elevated in patients with this disorder?

options.rationale: This option is deficient in Tay-Sachs disease, not elevated in A-T.

Ataxia-Telangiectasia (A-T) presents with ataxia, telangiectasias, and an immunodeficiency. A highly characteristic laboratory finding in A-T is a persistently elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level.
This option is elevated in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.
This option is highly elevated in muscular dystrophies.

learningObjective: Differentiate an epidural hematoma based on mechanism and neuroimaging appearance.
vignette: A 12-year-old boy is struck in the temporal region of the head by a baseball. He briefly loses consciousness but then quickly recovers and appears lucid and conversational. Two hours later, he rapidly develops a severe headache, vomits, and becomes progressively lethargic. A non-contrast head CT demonstrates a distinct, convex (lens-shaped) hyperdensity over the lateral aspect of the right hemisphere.
leadIn: This hemorrhage is most likely due to the rupture of which of the following vascular structures?

options.rationale: This option is the most common site of a ruptured berry aneurysm causing a subarachnoid hemorrhage.
This option is the source of a subdural hematoma, which appears crescent-shaped on CT.
This option lacerations cause severe venous epidural or subdural bleeds but are typically located at the vertex, not the lateral temporal region.

The classic clinical sequence of a lucid interval followed by rapid neurologic decline after head trauma, combined with a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdensity on CT, is diagnostic of an epidural hematoma. This is almost exclusively caused by a laceration of the middle meningeal artery underneath a temporal bone fracture.

learningObjective: Identify the classic CNS tumor associated with Von Hippel-Lindau disease.
leadIn: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is an autosomal dominant multisystem cancer syndrome characterized by the development of multiple benign and malignant tumors. Which of the following primary central nervous system lesions is a hallmark finding in patients with VHL?

options.rationale: This option is the hallmark lesion defining Neurofibromatosis Type 2.
This option is the hallmark CNS tumor in Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.
This option is the hallmark CNS tumor in Neurofibromatosis Type 1.
Cerebellar and spinal hemangioblastomas are the classic central nervous system tumors associated with Von Hippel-Lindau disease, alongside retinal angiomas and renal cell carcinomas.

learningObjective: Correlate the Chiari II malformation with its classic spinal dysraphism.
leadIn: Anomalies of the craniocervical junction can significantly impact cerebrospinal fluid dynamics and neurological function. A Chiari II malformation, characterized by the downward displacement of the cerebellar vermis and medulla through the foramen magnum, is nearly always associated with which of the following congenital defects?

options.rationale: This option is a defect in the skull with protruding brain tissue, characteristic of Meckel-Gruber syndrome, not directly the primary driver of Chiari II.
This option is a defect in forebrain cleavage associated with Trisomy 13.

The Chiari II malformation involves the downward displacement of the cerebellar vermis, tonsils, and medulla through the foramen magnum and is almost universally associated with a lumbosacral myelomeningocele (spina bifida).
This option occurs in various syndromes (like Aicardi) but is not the defining spinal dysraphism of Chiari II.

learningObjective: Differentiate sleep terrors from nightmares based on clinical features and sleep stage.
vignette: The parents of a 4-year-old boy report that, roughly two hours after falling asleep, he frequently sits up in bed screaming, thrashing, and sweating profusely. He appears terrified and his eyes are wide open, but he does not recognize his parents or respond to their attempts to comfort him. The episode lasts 5 to 10 minutes, after which he returns to sleep. In the morning, he has no memory of the event.
leadIn: Which of the following best classifies this sleep disturbance?

options.rationale: This option refer to obstructive sleep apnea and narcolepsy, respectively, neither of which present with nocturnal screaming and autonomic arousal.

The child is experiencing sleep terrors. These typically occur in the first third of the night during deep slow-wave sleep (Non-REM stage 3). The child cannot be consoled and has amnesia of the event the next day, which categorizes this as a Non-REM arousal disorder.
This option refer to obstructive sleep apnea and narcolepsy, respectively, neither of which present with nocturnal screaming and autonomic arousal.
This option includes nightmares, which occur later in the night (during REM sleep), are fully recalled by the child, and the child can be easily awakened and consoled.

learningObjective: Diagnose Benign Epilepsy with Centrotemporal Spikes (BECTS) from clinical history and presentation.
vignette: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the neurology clinic after his parents witnessed an unusual event during the night. Shortly after falling asleep, the child awoke with unilateral twitching restricted to the right side of his face, accompanied by drooling. He remained fully conscious but was unable to speak during the event. The episode lasted two minutes and resolved spontaneously. He is otherwise developmentally normal and has a normal neurologic examination.
leadIn: An electroencephalogram (EEG) is most likely to demonstrate which of the following interictal abnormalities?

options.rationale: This option is the highly disorganized EEG pattern seen in infantile spasms (West syndrome).
This option is the defining EEG finding for Landau-Kleffner syndrome, which presents with language regression (acquired aphasia).
This option is the classic EEG finding for Childhood Absence Epilepsy, which presents with daytime staring spells, not focal nocturnal motor seizures.

The patient’s clinical presentation of a nocturnal focal motor seizure involving the face (twitching, drooling, speech arrest) in an otherwise healthy school-aged child is classic for Benign Epilepsy with Centrotemporal Spikes (BECTS), also known as Rolandic Epilepsy. The characteristic EEG finding is bilateral (or unilateral) independent centrotemporal spikes.

learningObjective: Diagnose X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy based on combined neurologic and endocrine dysfunction.
vignette: A 7-year-old boy is evaluated for worsening school performance, behavioral outbursts, and a declining attention span over the past year. Recently, he has developed a spastic, unsteady gait. Physical examination reveals generalized hyperpigmentation of the skin, particularly in the palmar creases. Laboratory testing indicates elevated serum very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA).
leadIn: This patient is at the highest risk for developing primary insufficiency of which of the following endocrine organs?

options.rationale: The combination of progressive demyelination (cognitive decline, spasticity), elevated VLCFAs, and skin hyperpigmentation in a male child is diagnostic of X-linked Adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD). Accumulation of VLCFAs in the adrenal cortex causes primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), leading to the classic skin hyperpigmentation.
This option is associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis or congenital anomalies, not specifically targeted by VLCFA accumulation.
This option insufficiency can cause secondary adrenal failure (which would not cause hyperpigmentation, as ACTH is low).
This option insufficiency causes Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, which is an autoimmune process unrelated to X-ALD.

learningObjective: Recognize the classic cardiac, metabolic, and dysmorphic features of Williams syndrome.
vignette: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for developmental delay and a heart murmur. The parents note that he is highly sociable, overly friendly with strangers, and fascinated by music. Physical examination reveals distinct facial features, including a broad forehead, a short nose with a broad tip, and full cheeks. Echocardiography demonstrates supravalvular aortic stenosis.
leadIn: Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities was this patient most likely at risk for during infancy?

options.rationale: , and D are incorrect; hypercalcemia is the hallmark electrolyte derangement associated with this syndrome.

The patient’s clinical presentation of an "elfin" face, hypersociability, and supravalvular aortic stenosis is diagnostic of Williams syndrome (7q11.23 microdeletion). A classic metabolic feature of Williams syndrome, particularly during infancy, is idiopathic hypercalcemia, which can lead to extreme irritability and vomiting.
, and D are incorrect; hypercalcemia is the hallmark electrolyte derangement associated with this syndrome.

Williams syndrome is classically associated with infantile hypercalcemia (not hypophosphatemia), thought to relate to abnormal vitamin D handling and calcium-sensing receptor function in the setting of the 7q11.23 microdeletion.

learningObjective: Identify abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome) based on classic neuroimaging and ophthalmologic findings.
vignette: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department for seizures and altered mental status. The caregiver reports the infant suddenly became limp while feeding. A head CT scan reveals bilateral crescent-shaped hyperdensities along the cerebral convexities crossing the cranial suture lines.
leadIn: A dilated fundoscopic examination is most likely to reveal which of the following findings?

options.rationale: This option can be a late consequence of trauma or Krabbe disease, but acute retinal hemorrhages are the acute diagnostic hallmark of this non-accidental trauma.
This option are iris hamartomas seen in Neurofibromatosis Type 1.

The presence of bilateral subdural hematomas (crescent-shaped hyperdensities crossing suture lines) in an infant without a major traumatic history is highly suspicious for abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome). The classic triad of abusive head trauma includes subdural hematomas, encephalopathy, and widespread retinal hemorrhages.
This option is seen in metabolic storage diseases like Tay-Sachs or Niemann-Pick disease.

learningObjective: Differentiate homocystinuria from Marfan syndrome by specific physical and vascular findings.
vignette: A 10-year-old child presents to the emergency department with acute-onset right leg pain and swelling, which is diagnosed via ultrasound as a deep vein thrombosis. Physical examination reveals a tall, thin habitus, long fingers (arachnodactyly), and pectus excavatum. The patient also has a history of mild intellectual disability. An ophthalmologic consultation identifies bilateral downward subluxation of the lenses.
leadIn: This patient's presentation is most consistent with an inborn error of metabolism affecting which of the following?

options.rationale: This option is the primary defect in Marfan syndrome, which presents with a similar body habitus but typically features upward lens dislocation, normal intellect, and aortic root dilation rather than massive thromboembolic risk. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Child Neurology Board Review Questions Set 3 (25) Here is a set of 25 additional high-yield, board-style questions for Child Neurology, crafted strictly according to your Operational Model. These questions feature clinical vignettes emphasizing clinical reasoning and are mapped to the ABPN Child Neurology Content Specifications and the “Board Review” resources in your materials. None of these duplicate the concepts from the previous sets.

The patient’s marfanoid habitus, downward lens dislocation (ectopia lentis), intellectual disability, and profound risk for thromboembolic events (DVT) describe Homocystinuria. This is an autosomal recessive disorder of sulfur amino acid metabolism (typically cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency).
This option defects result in Menkes disease (kinky hair, regression) or Wilson disease (liver/basal ganglia issues).
This option defects result in Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD), which presents with severe acute encephalopathy in neonates.

learningObjective: Correlate a painful, pupil-involving oculomotor nerve palsy with compression from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
vignette: A 17-year-old adolescent presents to the emergency department with an acute, severe, right-sided headache and double vision that began 6 hours ago. Neurological examination reveals that the right eye is deviated “down and out,” with profound ptosis of the right upper eyelid. The right pupil is 7 mm, fixed, and non-reactive to light, while the left pupil is 3 mm and briskly reactive.
leadIn: An aneurysm of which of the following blood vessels is the most likely cause of this patient's cranial nerve palsy?

options.rationale: This option is associated with Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome), causing ataxia, vertigo, and Horner syndrome.
This option typically presents with bitemporal lower quadrantanopia or optic nerve compression, not an isolated CN III palsy.

The patient has a classic complete right oculomotor (CN III) nerve palsy. Because the parasympathetic fibers responsible for pupillary constriction run on the superficial aspect of the oculomotor nerve (from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus), compression by an external structure—most classically a posterior communicating (PComm) artery aneurysm—results in a dilated, non-reactive pupil alongside the motor deficits.
This option commonly causes contralateral hemiparesis and aphasia if it ruptures or compresses the hemisphere.

learningObjective: Localize a bitemporal hemianopsia to the optic chiasm.
vignette: A 10-year-old boy is evaluated in the neurology clinic for frequent morning headaches and clumsiness, specifically bumping into doorframes on his left and right sides. Growth charts indicate his height velocity has significantly dropped over the past 18 months. Confrontational visual field testing demonstrates a bitemporal hemianopsia.
leadIn: Which of the following anatomical structures is most directly compressed by a mass in this patient?

options.rationale: This option lesions typically cause a homonymous sectoranopia or homonymous hemianopsia.

A bitemporal hemianopsia (loss of the outer visual fields in both eyes) is the hallmark localizing sign of a lesion compressing the optic chiasm, typically a suprasellar tumor such as a craniopharyngioma or a pituitary adenoma. This also explains his growth delay (endocrine dysfunction).
This option lesions produce a contralateral homonymous hemianopsia (e.g., a right optic tract lesion causes a left homonymous hemianopsia).
This option lesions result in monocular vision loss (ipsilateral blindness).

learningObjective: Diagnose carpal tunnel syndrome based on anatomic boundaries and clinical presentation.
vignette: A 17-year-old self-identified female who works part-time as a data entry clerk complains of numbness, tingling, and pain in her right hand that frequently awakens her at night. The symptoms primarily involve her thumb, index, and middle fingers. Physical examination reveals a positive Tinel sign at the wrist.
leadIn: The nerve responsible for this patient's symptoms passes through a space bounded on its palmar aspect by which of the following structures?

options.rationale: This option is located on the dorsal aspect of the wrist, securing the extensor tendons.

The patient has carpal tunnel syndrome, the most common entrapment neuropathy, affecting the median nerve. The carpal tunnel is bounded dorsally and laterally by the carpal bones and on the palmar border by the transverse carpal ligament.
This option is a superficial fascia of the palm, superficial to the transverse carpal ligament, and is implicated in Dupuytren's contracture.
This option is often used interchangeably with transverse carpal ligament in broad terms, but anatomically, the transverse carpal ligament specifically forms the roof of the carpal tunnel itself.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation of Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) Type 1.
vignette: A 3-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department for a weak cry, poor feeding, and severe "floppiness." The parents note the infant has never been able to lift his head. On examination, the infant exhibits severe generalized hypotonia, a bell-shaped chest with paradoxical breathing, absent deep tendon reflexes, and prominent fasciculations of the tongue. Cognitive interaction and eye tracking are normal.
leadIn: This patient's condition is characterized by the progressive degeneration of which of the following anatomical structures?

options.rationale: This option degeneration causes cerebellar ataxia (e.g., spinocerebellar ataxias, paraneoplastic syndromes).

options.text: Posterior columns of the spinal cord
options.rationale: This option degeneration is seen in Vitamin B12 deficiency and neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis), presenting with sensory ataxia.

options.text: Subcortical U-fibers of the cerebral white matter
options.rationale: This option are selectively spared in Krabbe disease and metachromatic leukodystrophy, and affected in Canavan disease.

options.text: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord
options.rationale: Severe hypotonia, absent reflexes, tongue fasciculations, and paradoxical breathing in a cognitively intact infant are classic for Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) Type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann disease). SMA is caused by a mutation in the SMN1 gene leading to progressive degeneration of the anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) in the spinal cord.

learningObjective: Identify the clinical features, genetic mechanism, and systemic complications of Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1.
vignette: A 15-year-old adolescent male presents to the clinic with progressive distal muscle weakness. He complains of difficulty releasing his grip after opening jars or shaking hands. Physical examination is notable for a long, narrow face, bilateral ptosis, wasting of the temporalis and masseter muscles, and frontal balding. Percussion of the thenar eminence elicits a delayed relaxation of the muscle.
leadIn: Which of the following systemic complications is most critical to screen for in this patient?

options.rationale: This option is a complication of Wilson disease or Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

The patient’s clinical presentation (grip myotonia, facial wasting, ptosis, and frontal balding) is classic for Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1, an autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat (CTG) disorder. Cardiac conduction abnormalities (arrhythmias, heart block) are highly prevalent and a leading cause of sudden death in these patients, necessitating routine screening with EKGs.
This option is a classic complication of Von Hippel-Lindau disease.
This option is not a feature of myotonic dystrophy; respiratory issues typically arise from diaphragmatic/intercostal muscle weakness.

learningObjective: Diagnose Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) and identify its associated ophthalmologic finding.
vignette: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated by a pediatrician for developmental delay. During the physical examination, the physician notes nine hyperpigmented macules measuring approximately 10 to 15 mm in diameter across his trunk and extremities, as well as distinct freckling in the bilateral axillary and inguinal regions.
leadIn: A referral to an ophthalmologist is made. Which of the following findings is most strongly associated with this patient's condition?

options.rationale: This option are classic findings in Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC).
This option is seen in metabolic storage disorders such as Tay-Sachs or Niemann-Pick disease.
This option are a diagnostic criterion for Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2).

The patient has Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1), characterized by café-au-lait macules (>6 measuring >5mm before puberty), axillary/inguinal freckling, and neurofibromas. Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas) are a classic ophthalmologic finding required for the clinical criteria of NF1.

learningObjective: Identify the classic EEG finding for infantile spasms (West syndrome).
vignette: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the pediatric neurology clinic due to clusters of abnormal movements. The parents report that just as the infant awakens from sleep, he exhibits sudden, brief, symmetric flexor spasms of his head, trunk, and extremities. These occur in clusters of 10 to 20 over a few minutes. The parents also report that the infant has stopped rolling over and no longer smiles socially.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely finding on an interictal electroencephalogram (EEG) in this patient?

options.rationale: The triad of infantile spasms, developmental regression, and a highly chaotic, high-voltage, disorganized interictal EEG pattern known as hypsarrhythmia defines West Syndrome.
This option is the characteristic EEG finding in Benign Epilepsy with Centrotemporal Spikes (BECTS / Rolandic Epilepsy).
This option is the defining EEG abnormality in Landau-Kleffner syndrome (acquired epileptic aphasia).
This option is the classic EEG finding for Childhood Absence Epilepsy.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation and genetic etiology of Rett syndrome.
vignette: A 24-month-old self-identified female is evaluated for loss of developmental milestones. She achieved normal motor and language milestones until 18 months of age. Since then, her parents report she has lost the ability to speak her previous words and no longer uses her hands to hold toys or feed herself. Instead, she constantly engages in repetitive hand-wringing movements. Her head circumference has dropped from the 50th percentile to the 5th percentile over the last year.
leadIn: A mutation in which of the following genes is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?

options.rationale: This option mutations cause Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), presenting with hypotonia and lower motor neuron signs.

A period of normal development followed by deceleration of head growth, loss of purposeful hand skills, loss of spoken language, and the development of stereotypic hand movements (hand-wringing) in a female toddler is the classic presentation of Rett Syndrome. It is caused by an X-linked dominant mutation in the MECP2 gene.
This option mutations (CGG expansion) cause Fragile X syndrome.
This option mutations cause Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.

learningObjective: Differentiate Tay-Sachs disease from other lysosomal storage diseases based on the absence of organomegaly.
vignette: A 9-month-old infant is evaluated for developmental regression and new-onset seizures. The parents state the child rolls over less frequently and exhibits an exaggerated, symmetric startle response to loud noises (hyperacusis). Physical examination reveals global hypotonia, macrocephaly, and a distinct cherry-red spot on the macula bilaterally. Palpation of the abdomen reveals no hepatomegaly and no splenomegaly.
leadIn: Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is most likely responsible for this patient's clinical presentation?

options.rationale: This option deficiency causes Gaucher disease, which presents with massive hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain/crises, and cytopenias.
This option deficiency causes Metachromatic Leukodystrophy, presenting with demyelinating neuropathy and central leukodystrophy without a cherry-red spot.
This option deficiency causes Niemann-Pick disease (Type A), which also presents with a cherry-red spot and regression, but prominently features hepatosplenomegaly.

The presence of developmental regression, an exaggerated startle response, a cherry-red macula, and the absence of hepatosplenomegaly strongly points to Tay-Sachs disease (GM2 gangliosidosis). Tay-Sachs is caused by a deficiency in Hexosaminidase A.

learningObjective: Identify the clinical presentation and CSF findings of acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP / Guillain-Barré syndrome).
vignette: An 8-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with progressive weakness in his legs over the past 4 days, making it difficult for him to climb stairs or stand from a seated position. He complains of a "tingling" sensation in his toes. Two weeks prior, he recovered from a brief diarrheal illness. On physical examination, he has symmetric, flaccid weakness of the lower extremities with absent deep tendon reflexes.
leadIn: Which of the following findings is most likely to be present on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis?

options.rationale: This option is the classic CSF finding supporting a diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis.
This option describes the classic CSF profile of acute bacterial meningitis.

options.text: Elevated white blood cell count with normal protein
options.rationale: This option describes a viral meningitis or encephalitis pattern.

options.text: Elevated protein with a normal white blood cell count
options.rationale: The patient’s rapidly progressive, symmetric, ascending weakness and areflexia following a GI illness (frequently Campylobacter jejuni) is classic for Guillain-Barré syndrome (AIDP). The hallmark CSF finding is albuminocytologic dissociation—an elevated CSF protein level with a normal white blood cell count.

learningObjective: Differentiate congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) from other TORCH infections based on characteristic neuroimaging.
vignette: A neonate born at 38 weeks of gestation is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit. The infant is small for gestational age and microcephalic. Physical examination is notable for a diffuse petechial rash, hepatosplenomegaly, and jaundice. The infant subsequently fails the newborn auditory brainstem response (ABR) hearing screen bilaterally. A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the head is obtained.
leadIn: Which of the following patterns of intracranial calcifications is most characteristic of this patient's congenital infection?

options.rationale: This option are not the classic localizing patterns for the major TORCH infections.
This option is the classic neuroimaging finding for congenital Toxoplasmosis, which also presents with chorioretinitis and hydrocephalus.

The clinical triad of microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, and a petechial ("blueberry muffin") rash in a neonate strongly suggests congenital Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. The hallmark neuroimaging finding for congenital CMV is periventricular calcifications.
This option are not the classic localizing patterns for the major TORCH infections.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation and focal neuroimaging findings of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) encephalitis.
vignette: A 14-year-old adolescent is brought to the emergency department for a 3-day history of high fever, severe headache, and confusion. Today, the parents witnessed the patient experience a focal motor seizure involving the right face and arm. A lumbar puncture reveals lymphocytic pleocytosis and numerous red blood cells. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain reveals edema and T2 hyperintensity localized to the left medial temporal lobe.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical pharmacologic treatment for this patient?

options.rationale: This option is an antifungal agent used for invasive fungal infections like Cryptococcus or Mucormycosis.
This option covers bacterial meningitis but is not effective against viral encephalitis.
This option is an antiviral for influenza, which rarely causes this specific temporal lobe necrotic encephalitis.

Acute fever, altered mental status, focal seizures, CSF revealing RBCs (due to hemorrhagic necrosis), and MRI showing unilateral temporal lobe edema are the classic hallmarks of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) encephalitis. Intravenous acyclovir is the definitive empirical and targeted treatment and must be started immediately.

learningObjective: Diagnose Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2) based on classic clinical history and neuroimaging findings.
vignette: A 16-year-old self-identified female is evaluated for progressive bilateral hearing loss, ringing in her ears (tinnitus), and mild balance issues over the past two years. Family history is significant for her father, who developed profound deafness in his twenties and subsequently died from complications related to multiple brain tumors.
leadIn: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is most likely to demonstrate which of the following lesions?

options.rationale: This option is highly characteristic of Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1).
This option is a hallmark lesion of Von Hippel-Lindau disease.
This option are characteristic of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.

The patient’s clinical presentation of bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance issues, combined with a strong autosomal dominant family history, points to Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2). The hallmark diagnostic criteria for NF2 is the presence of bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) on MRI.

learningObjective: Diagnose Tourette syndrome based on clinical criteria and symptom duration.
vignette: A 9-year-old boy is evaluated for abnormal movements and sounds. His parents note that he frequently blinks his eyes forcefully, shrugs his shoulders, and occasionally makes loud grunting noises. These behaviors increase when he is anxious about schoolwork and disappear when he is asleep. The parents report these behaviors have waxed and waned but have been consistently present for the past 14 months.
leadIn: Which of the following is an essential diagnostic criterion for this patient's disorder?
