options.text: D) Complete resolution of symptoms during sleep
options.rationale: This option is a true clinical feature of tics (they stop during sleep), but it is not a formal diagnostic criterion for the disorder.
This option is incorrect; while ADHD and OCD are highly prevalent comorbidities in patients with Tourette syndrome, they are not diagnostic criteria.

options.text: Onset of symptoms after the age of 18 years
options.rationale: This option is incorrect as the onset must be before age 18.

options.text: Presence of both multiple motor tics and one or more vocal tics for more than 1 year
options.rationale: The patient meets the DSM-5 criteria for Tourette Syndrome, which requires the presence of multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, waxing and waning but persisting for more than 1 year, with onset before the age of 18.

learningObjective: Identify the phenotypic features and genetic mutation associated with Fragile X syndrome.
vignette: A 5-year-old boy is evaluated in the neurodevelopmental clinic for speech delay and hyperactive behavior. He avoids eye contact, is highly sensitive to loud noises, and frequently engages in hand-flapping. Physical examination is notable for a long, narrow face, prominent ears, and macroorchidism.
leadIn: Expansion of which of the following trinucleotide repeats is the underlying genetic cause of this patient's condition?

options.rationale: This option repeat expansions are the cause of Huntington disease and several spinocerebellar ataxias.
This option repeat expansions are the cause of Friedreich ataxia.

The patient’s clinical presentation of intellectual disability, autism-like behaviors (hand-flapping, poor eye contact), a long face, large ears, and macroorchidism is classic for Fragile X Syndrome. This is caused by a massive expansion of the CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome.
This option repeat expansions are the cause of Myotonic Dystrophy Type 1.

learningObjective: Diagnose idiopathic intracranial hypertension and select the appropriate initial pharmacologic therapy.
vignette: A 14-year-old obese adolescent female is evaluated for daily pulsatile headaches over the past month. She reports transient visual obscurations when standing up and horizontal double vision. Neurological examination is notable for bilateral papilledema and a left sixth cranial nerve palsy. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and MR venography are unremarkable. A diagnostic lumbar puncture demonstrates an opening pressure of 32 cm H2O with normal CSF composition.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic treatment for this patient?

options.rationale: This option are abortive and prophylactic treatments for migraine headaches, respectively, and do not lower intracranial pressure.
This option is used for migraine prophylaxis and has some weak carbonic anhydrase activity (and promotes weight loss), making it a secondary option, but Acetazolamide remains first-line.

The patient’s obesity, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, papilledema, abducens palsy (false localizing sign), normal MRI/MRV, and elevated opening pressure confirm the diagnosis of Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri). Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces CSF production, is the first-line pharmacologic therapy.
This option are abortive and prophylactic treatments for migraine headaches, respectively, and do not lower intracranial pressure.

learningObjective: Correlate the anatomical location and histology of a posterior fossa ependymoma.
vignette: A 6-year-old boy presents with a 3-week history of worsening morning vomiting, occipital headache, and new-onset gait ataxia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain reveals a distinct solid and cystic mass filling the fourth ventricle and extending outward through the foramina of Luschka. The patient undergoes gross total surgical resection of the mass.
leadIn: Histopathological evaluation of the resected tumor tissue is most likely to demonstrate which of the following features?

options.text: Antoni A and Antoni B tissue patterns
options.rationale: This option describes the biphasic architecture of a Schwannoma.
This option are the hallmark of a medulloblastoma, a malignant tumor arising from the cerebellar vermis/roof of the 4th ventricle.

The anatomical location of a mass originating in the floor of the fourth ventricle and exhibiting "plastic" extension through the foramina of Luschka or Magendie is highly characteristic of an ependymoma. The classic histopathologic hallmark of an ependymoma is the presence of perivascular pseudorosettes.
This option are the histologic hallmark of a pilocytic astrocytoma, which typically appears as a cystic mass with a mural nodule in the cerebellar hemisphere.

learningObjective: Identify the classic EEG finding and clinical triad of Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome.
vignette: A 4-year-old boy is evaluated in the epilepsy clinic for medically refractory seizures. His parents report that he experiences multiple different types of seizures daily, including staring spells, generalized stiffening, and sudden drops to the floor resulting in facial injuries. They also report that he has lost significant cognitive and language milestones over the past year.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely finding on this patient's interictal electroencephalogram (EEG)?

options.rationale: The clinical triad of multiple seizure types (especially tonic and atonic "drop" attacks), intellectual disability/cognitive regression, and an EEG demonstrating diffuse slow spike-and-wave complexes (<2.5 Hz) is diagnostic of Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome.
This option is the EEG hallmark of Landau-Kleffner syndrome, presenting with acquired epileptic aphasia.
This option is the classic EEG finding for Childhood Absence Epilepsy, which generally has normal cognition and no "drop" attacks.
This option is the EEG hallmark of West syndrome (infantile spasms), which typically occurs earlier in infancy (4 to 8 months).

learningObjective: Diagnose Phenylketonuria (PKU) based on clinical features and select the deficient enzyme.
blueprintTopic: Metabolic Diseases, Nutritional Deficiency States, and Toxins
vignette: A 12-month-old infant, who immigrated with his family from a region without routine newborn metabolic screening, is evaluated for severe global developmental delay and recent-onset seizures. Physical examination is notable for fair skin, blond hair, blue eyes, and a severe eczematous rash. The parents report a distinct "musty" odor to the infant's urine and sweat.
leadIn: This patient's condition is most likely caused by a deficiency in which of the following enzymes?

options.rationale: This option is deficient in classic Galactosemia, presenting with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and cataracts.
This option is deficient in Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD), which presents with acute neonatal encephalopathy and sweet-smelling urine.

The triad of severe intellectual disability, fair pigmentation (due to lack of tyrosine conversion to melanin), eczema, and a "musty" or "mousy" odor is the classic presentation of untreated Phenylketonuria (PKU). This is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase.
This option is deficient in Alkaptonuria, presenting with dark-pigmented urine and, later in life, severe arthritis (ochronosis).

learningObjective: Recognize Benign Paroxysmal Vertigo of Childhood as a migraine equivalent.
vignette: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician due to episodic attacks of sudden unsteadiness and fear. Her parents report that during an episode, she clings to her mother, refuses to walk, and appears pale and nauseous. There is no loss of consciousness, and she does not exhibit any abnormal posturing or rhythmic jerking. The episodes last 2 to 5 minutes, after which she returns completely to her normal baseline playfulness. Hearing, vision, and comprehensive neurologic examinations are completely normal.
leadIn: This patient's clinical presentation is considered a common childhood precursor to which of the following conditions later in life?

options.rationale: This option can cause vertigo via brainstem demyelination, but presents with other hard focal neurologic signs and does not resolve in 5 minutes.
This option causes episodic vertigo but is accompanied by progressive sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, usually in adults.
This option involve altered awareness and automatisms, and typically have a post-ictal phase, unlike the rapid return to baseline in BPVC.

The patient’s presentation of brief, sudden attacks of vertigo, ataxia, fear, pallor, and nausea in an otherwise healthy toddler is classic for Benign Paroxysmal Vertigo of Childhood (BPVC). BPVC is widely recognized as an early childhood "migraine equivalent" and is a strong predictor of developing classic migraine headaches later in childhood or adolescence.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical triad of Horner syndrome and its underlying anatomical pathway.
vignette: A 2-year-old boy is evaluated for an asymmetry of his eyes noted by his parents. Physical examination reveals mild ptosis of the left upper eyelid, slight elevation of the left lower eyelid (giving the appearance of a sunken eye), and a constricted left pupil (miosis) that reacts normally to light but dilates poorly in the dark. Additionally, the left side of the child's face remains pale and dry compared to the right side when the child cries.
leadIn: This physical examination triad is caused by a disruption of which of the following neural pathways?

options.text: Sensory fibers of the trigeminal nerve
options.rationale: This option disruption causes facial numbness and loss of the corneal reflex.

options.text: Somatic motor fibers of the facial nerve
options.rationale: This option disruption causes weakness of facial expression muscles (e.g., Bell's palsy, inability to close the eye), not miosis or anhidrosis.

options.text: Parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve
options.rationale: This option disruption causes a dilated, non-reactive pupil (mydriasis), not miosis.

The triad of ipsilateral ptosis, miosis (constricted pupil), and anhidrosis (lack of sweating) defines Horner syndrome. This results from a lesion anywhere along the three-neuron oculosympathetic pathway originating in the hypothalamus, traveling down the brainstem/cervical cord, and ascending via the superior cervical ganglion.

learningObjective: Identify the clinical presentation, cardiac association, and genetic repeat of Friedreich Ataxia.
vignette: A 13-year-old boy presents with progressive clumsiness, frequent falls, and difficulty walking over the past year. Physical examination reveals high-arched feet (pes cavus) and kyphoscoliosis. Neurologic examination demonstrates absent deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities, severely impaired vibratory and proprioceptive sense, and bilateral Babinski signs.
leadIn: Which of the following cardiac abnormalities is most highly associated with this patient's neurologic disorder and represents the leading cause of mortality?

options.rationale: The patient has Friedreich Ataxia, an autosomal recessive trinucleotide repeat (GAA) disorder affecting the frataxin gene. It presents with progressive ataxia, sensory neuropathy (absent reflexes, loss of proprioception), upper motor neuron signs (Babinski), and skeletal deformities (pes cavus, scoliosis). Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is present in the vast majority of patients and is the leading cause of death.
This option is common in the general population but strongly associated with Down syndrome.
This option is a classic cardiac defect associated with Turner syndrome.
This option is the most common cardiac tumor in infants and is highly associated with Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.

learningObjective: Recognize the enzyme deficiency in Metachromatic Leukodystrophy.
vignette: A 2-year-old child is brought to the clinic for a progressive gait disturbance. The child had learned to walk independently at 14 months of age but now frequently falls and requires support to stand. Physical examination reveals diffuse hypotonia and absent deep tendon reflexes. Nerve conduction studies demonstrate delayed conduction velocities. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain reveals bilateral, symmetric T2 hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter.
leadIn: A deficiency in which of the following enzymes is the most likely cause of this patient's regression?

options.rationale: This option is deficient in Hurler syndrome (MPS I), which presents with coarse facial features, corneal clouding, and dysostosis multiplex.
This option is deficient in Krabbe disease, which presents earlier (first 6 months) with extreme irritability, hypertonicity, and optic atrophy.
This option is deficient in Canavan disease, which presents with marked macrocephaly and lacks the prominent peripheral neuropathy seen in MLD.

The combination of a central demyelinating process (leukodystrophy on MRI) and a peripheral demyelinating process (peripheral neuropathy resulting in areflexia and delayed nerve conduction) presenting in late infancy/early childhood is the hallmark of Metachromatic Leukodystrophy (MLD). MLD is caused by a deficiency of arylsulfatase A.

learningObjective: Correlate the facial lesion of Sturge-Weber syndrome with the associated intracranial pathology.
vignette: A newborn infant is noted in the nursery to have a large, dark red, flat vascular malformation covering the right forehead, upper eyelid, and right cheek. The pediatrician counsels the parents that the infant will require close neurologic and ophthalmologic follow-up, as this skin lesion is associated with a specific neurocutaneous syndrome.
leadIn: This patient is at the highest risk for developing which of the following intracranial abnormalities?

options.rationale: This option are characteristic of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex.
This option is characteristic of Von Hippel-Lindau disease.

The patient’s facial "port-wine stain" (nevus flammeus) in the distribution of the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) divisions of the trigeminal nerve is the hallmark of Sturge-Weber Syndrome. This sporadic congenital disorder is associated with ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis, which can lead to seizures, intellectual disability, and early-onset glaucoma.
This option are characteristic of Neurofibromatosis Type 2.

learningObjective: Diagnose tick paralysis based on ascending flaccid paralysis and identify the definitive management.
blueprintTopic: Metabolic Diseases, Nutritional Deficiency States, and Toxins
vignette: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department for progressive weakness in her legs that started 24 hours ago. Today, she cannot walk and has developed new weakness in her arms. She recently returned from a family camping trip in a wooded area of the Pacific Northwest. Physical examination reveals an ascending, symmetric flaccid paralysis with completely absent deep tendon reflexes and no sensory deficits. Her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis demonstrates normal protein and zero white blood cells.
leadIn: Which of the following interventions will most rapidly and definitively reverse this patient's symptoms?

options.text: Removal of an attached Dermacentor tick
options.rationale: The patient presents with a rapidly ascending flaccid paralysis following a camping trip, mimicking Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS). However, the complete lack of CSF protein elevation (though early GBS can be normal) and the outdoor exposure history highly suggest Tick Paralysis, caused by a neurotoxin in the tick's saliva. Thorough examination of the scalp and hairline to find and remove the tick is curative, leading to rapid reversal of paralysis within hours.
This option are the mainstays of treatment for Guillain-Barré syndrome, but tick removal is the definitive and immediate treatment for tick paralysis.

This option is the treatment for infant botulism, which classically presents with a descending flaccid paralysis beginning with cranial nerve deficits (ptosis, poor suck/swallow). -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- I hope this additional set hits the exact clinical vignette balance you are looking for! This option are the mainstays of treatment for Guillain-Barré syndrome, but tick removal is the definitive and immediate treatment for tick paralysis.

learningObjective: Diagnose pediatric migraine based on duration, clinical characteristics, and associated symptoms.
vignette: A 10-year-old child is evaluated in the outpatient neurology clinic for a severe headache that began 4 hours ago. The patient reports a throbbing pain localized strictly to the right side of his head. The pain is exacerbated when he attempts to walk up the stairs, prompting him to lie still in a dark room. The parents note he has had four similar episodes in the past year, each lasting between 4 and 12 hours. His neurological examination is unremarkable.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: The diagnosis of a migraine headache requires at least 5 episodes lasting 2 to 72 hours in children. It must have at least two of the following characteristics: unilateral location, pulsating/throbbing quality, moderate to severe intensity, and aggravation by routine physical activity. It must also be accompanied by nausea/vomiting or photophobia/phonophobia.
This option is incorrect as primary stabbing headaches feature very brief, sharp jabs of pain (seconds in duration), not prolonged episodes.
This option is incorrect because cluster headaches present with autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, rhinorrhea, miosis) and extreme restlessness, unlike this patient who prefers to lie still.
This option is incorrect because tension-type headaches are bilateral, pressing or tightening in quality, mild to moderate, and are specifically not aggravated by routine physical activity.

learningObjective: Identify the characteristic neuroimaging finding and defective gene associated with Pantothenate Kinase-Associated Neurodegeneration (PKAN).
blueprintTopic: Metabolic Diseases, Nutritional Deficiency States, and Toxins
leadIn: A mutation in the pantothenate kinase 2 (PANK2) gene is the most common cause of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation. Which of the following magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings is pathognomonic for this disorder?

options.text: Atrophy of the caudate nucleus with ex vacuo ventricular dilatation
options.rationale: This option describes the classic neuroimaging finding in Huntington disease.

options.text: Cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia
options.rationale: This option describes the structural anomaly seen in Dandy-Walker malformation.

options.text: Symmetric periventricular white matter hyperintensities sparing subcortical U-fibers
options.rationale: This option describes the classic MRI finding for Krabbe disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy).

options.text: Hypointensity of the globus pallidus with central hyperintensity
options.rationale: PKAN features a classic MRI finding known as the "eye of the tiger" sign, which consists of hypointensity of the globus pallidus (due to iron accumulation) with a central streak of T2 hyperintensity.

learningObjective: Diagnose Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME) from a clinical history of early morning myoclonus progressing to generalized seizures.
vignette: A 16-year-old self-identified Hispanic female is evaluated in the emergency department following a first-time generalized tonic-clonic seizure. The event occurred this morning shortly after she woke up from a sleepover where she stayed up very late. Upon further questioning, the patient admits that for the past six months, she has experienced frequent, sudden, brief jerking movements of her arms shortly after waking up in the morning, which occasionally cause her to drop her hairbrush or toothbrush.
leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient's presentation?

options.rationale: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) typically presents in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks (often noticed when dropping objects) and generalized tonic-clonic seizures that are heavily provoked by sleep deprivation.
This option presents with staring spells and behavioral arrest rather than prominent morning myoclonic jerks and generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
This option typically presents in early childhood with multiple medically intractable seizure types (tonic, atonic, atypical absence) and cognitive decline.
This option presents with intractable focal seizures (epilepsia partialis continua), hemiparesis, and unilateral hemispheric atrophy.

learningObjective: Identify the histological findings associated with a pilocytic astrocytoma.
vignette: An 8-year-old child presents to the neurology clinic with a two-month history of worsening morning headaches, vomiting, and new-onset gait ataxia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain demonstrates a well-circumscribed, cystic mass with an intensely enhancing mural nodule located in the cerebellar hemisphere. A surgical resection is performed.
leadIn: Microscopic examination of the resected tumor tissue is most likely to reveal which of the following histological features?

options.text: Whorls of meningothelial cells with psammoma bodies
options.rationale: This option describes a meningioma, an extra-axial tumor that is much more common in adults.

options.text: Small round blue cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and frequent mitoses
options.rationale: This option describes medulloblastoma, a malignant, highly cellular tumor of the posterior fossa.

options.text: A biphasic pattern of compact regions with microcystic components and Rosenthal fibers
options.rationale: The patient’s clinical presentation and imaging (cystic cerebellar mass with a mural nodule in a child) are highly characteristic of a pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO Grade I). The classic histological finding is a biphasic tissue pattern featuring Rosenthal fibers (eosinophilic corkscrew-like inclusions).

options.text: Glioneuronal cells packed into fascicles around vessels creating pseudorosettes
options.rationale: This option describes the histology of an ependymoma (perivascular pseudorosettes), which typically arises in the fourth ventricle rather than the cerebellar hemisphere.

learningObjective: Correlate the clinical features of narcolepsy with cataplexy to the underlying cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarker abnormality.
vignette: A 14-year-old adolescent is evaluated in the sleep clinic for severe, excessive daytime sleepiness over the past year. The patient frequently falls asleep during classes despite obtaining nine hours of continuous nighttime sleep. The parents also report distinct episodes where the patient suddenly loses bilateral muscle tone and slumps to the floor when laughing at a joke, without losing consciousness.
leadIn: Analysis of this patient's cerebrospinal fluid is most likely to demonstrate low levels of which of the following substances?

options.rationale: This option is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, and its global alteration is implicated in various epilepsy syndromes, not specifically narcolepsy.
This option depletion in the cortex is a feature of Alzheimer's disease, and its receptors are targeted in Myasthenia Gravis.
This option deficiency is associated with Parkinson disease and Dopa-responsive dystonia.

The patient exhibits excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, like laughter), which are the hallmark features of narcolepsy type 1. The pathophysiology involves the loss of hypocretin (orexin) producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, leading to characteristically low CSF hypocretin levels.

learningObjective: Recognize the anatomical brain malformations that define Dandy-Walker malformation.
leadIn: Developmental malformations of the brain structure can present with variable degrees of neurologic impairment and hydrocephalus. Which of the following combinations of structural brain anomalies is characteristic of Dandy-Walker malformation?

options.text: Absence of the septum pellucidum and hypoplasia of the optic nerves
options.rationale: This option describes Septo-optic dysplasia (De Morsier syndrome).

options.text: Agenesis of the corpus callosum with colpocephaly and parallel lateral ventricles
options.rationale: This option describes isolated agenesis of the corpus callosum.

options.text: Cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, fourth ventricular cystic dilatation, and elevation of the torcula
options.rationale: Dandy-Walker malformation is classically defined by hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, cystic dilatation of the 4th ventricle, and an enlarged posterior fossa with elevation of the torcula and tentorium cerebelli.

options.text: Downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum
options.rationale: This option describes a Chiari I malformation.

learningObjective: Recognize the angiographic appearance and diagnosis of Moyamoya disease in a pediatric stroke patient.
vignette: A 7-year-old child is brought to the emergency department after experiencing a sudden onset of right-sided hemiparesis and expressive aphasia that resolved completely after thirty minutes. The child has no history of trauma, fever, or prior medical conditions. A magnetic resonance angiogram (MRA) of the brain is performed to evaluate the cerebral vasculature. The imaging reveals progressive stenosis of the bilateral supraclinoid internal carotid arteries with a prominent collateral vascular network at the base of the brain.
leadIn: How is this collateral network classically described on neurovascular imaging?

options.rationale: This option describes fibromuscular dysplasia, which primarily affects the renal and mid-cervical internal carotid arteries.

The patient presents with a transient ischemic attack secondary to Moyamoya disease. This condition is characterized by progressive occlusion of the distal internal carotid arteries and the compensatory development of a fragile network of collateral vessels, which is classically described as a "puff of smoke" on angiography.
This option describes the spoke-wheel appearance of a developmental venous anomaly (DVA).
This option describes the classic MRI appearance of a cavernous malformation due to blood products in various stages of evolution.

learningObjective: Diagnose juvenile myasthenia gravis based on the clinical presentation of fatigable weakness and identify the primary autoantibody.
vignette: A 15-year-old adolescent presents to the neurology clinic complaining of double vision and drooping eyelids. The symptoms are generally absent in the morning upon awakening but become progressively worse by the late afternoon or after reading for prolonged periods. Neurological examination confirms bilateral ptosis that worsens significantly with one minute of sustained upward gaze.
leadIn: The pathogenesis of this patient's condition is most commonly driven by autoantibodies directed against which of the following targets?

options.rationale: This option describes the target in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, which typically presents with proximal muscle weakness that improves with repeated use, often associated with malignancy.
This option antibodies are present in a smaller subset (approx. 5-10%) of generalized Myasthenia Gravis cases, making option A the most common target.

The patient presents with classic features of Juvenile Myasthenia Gravis, including fatigable weakness (worsening by the end of the day) and extraocular muscle involvement (ptosis, diplopia). In 80-85% of cases, the condition is mediated by autoantibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic neuromuscular junction.
This option is the defective protein in Spinal Muscular Atrophy, a genetic anterior horn cell disorder, not an autoimmune condition.

learningObjective: Identify the teratogenic/metabolic risks of specific anti-seizure medications during pregnancy.
leadIn: An 18-year-old female patient with epilepsy who is currently pregnant is maintained on phenobarbital monotherapy. Phenobarbital is known to interfere with the metabolism of a specific vitamin, which poses a significant risk of bleeding in the newborn. Supplementation with which of the following is most appropriate for the mother prior to delivery to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn?

options.rationale: This option deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration, but is not specifically depleted by phenobarbital.
This option supplementation is crucial for preventing neural tube defects (particularly high risk with valproic acid and carbamazepine), but it does not prevent hemorrhagic disease.
This option is supplemented in patients taking isoniazid or with pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy.

Enzyme-inducing anti-seizure medications, particularly phenobarbital (as well as phenytoin and carbamazepine), interfere with Vitamin K metabolism. Supplementation with Vitamin K in the final month of pregnancy is necessary to prevent severe hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

learningObjective: Differentiate cyanotic breath-holding spells from seizures based on triggering events and clinical sequence.
vignette: A 15-month-old toddler is evaluated in the pediatric clinic for episodes of loss of consciousness. The parents report that when the child becomes frustrated or angry because a toy is taken away, he cries vigorously, forcefully exhales, and then turns blue around the lips. He then loses muscle tone, goes limp, and briefly loses consciousness before spontaneously recovering and returning to baseline. An interictal electroencephalogram (EEG) is completely normal.
leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient's episodes?

options.rationale: This option features sustained rhythmic jerking and a post-ictal state of confusion, and is not strictly provoked by anger/crying.
This option is typically triggered by a sudden painful event or startle, resulting in marked paleness (pallor) rather than cyanosis.

This option typically occurs in older children and adolescents in response to prolonged standing, heat, or emotional distress, accompanied by prodromal lightheadedness and diaphoresis. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Board Review Questions Set 1 Here is a set of 10 high-yield board-style questions for Child Neurology, crafted using the Operational Model and six-step development process you provided. These questions emphasize the "Board Review.pdf" and the comprehensive ABPN curricular analysis (acting as the Deep Research Report) from your sources, balancing clinical application vignettes with essential recall items.

The sequence of anger/frustration, vigorous crying, forced exhalation, cyanosis, loss of tone, and brief loss of consciousness is the classic presentation of a cyanotic breath-holding spell. They most commonly occur between 6 and 18 months of age and are benign.

learningObjective: Identify the clinical presentation and characteristic electroencephalographic (EEG) findings of Landau-Kleffner syndrome.
vignette: A 5-year-old child is brought to the pediatric neurology clinic by their parents due to a sudden loss of language skills over the past three months. The child had normal language development until recently but now no longer responds to verbal commands and has stopped speaking entirely. The parents note no obvious clinical seizures or motor deficits. An overnight electroencephalogram (EEG) is ordered.
leadIn: What is the most likely electroencephalographic finding in this patient?

options.text: Continuous spike-and-wave discharges during slow-wave sleep
options.rationale: Landau-Kleffner syndrome, also known as acquired epileptic aphasia, presents in early childhood (ages 3 to 7) with auditory agnosia and language regression. The characteristic EEG finding is continuous spike-and-wave during sleep (CSWS).

options.text: High voltage occipital spikes in 1-3 Hz bursts that disappear with eye opening
options.rationale: This option is incorrect because occipital spikes that attenuate with eye opening are seen in childhood occipital epilepsy (Panayiotopoulos or Gastaut types).

options.text: Bilateral independent centrotemporal spikes with a normal background
options.rationale: This option is incorrect as bilateral independent centrotemporal spikes are characteristic of Benign Epilepsy with Centrotemporal Spikes (BECTS).

options.text: 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges provoked by hyperventilation
options.rationale: This option is incorrect as 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave discharges are classic for Childhood Absence Epilepsy.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical and imaging presentation of Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) and identify its underlying enzyme defect.
blueprintTopic: Metabolic Diseases, Nutritional Deficiency States, and Toxins
vignette: A 6-day-old neonate is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit for poor feeding, worsening lethargy, and vomiting. Physical examination reveals irregular respirations, loss of the Moro reflex, and profound opisthotonos rigidity. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain demonstrates marked edema and restricted diffusion involving the posterior limbs of the internal capsule, brainstem, and cerebellar white matter.
leadIn: A deficiency in which of the following enzymes is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

options.rationale: This option causes Galactosemia, presenting with jaundice, cataracts, and hepatomegaly, rather than acute early encephalopathy with brainstem edema.
This option causes Glutaric aciduria type 1, which typically presents with macrocephaly and dystonia, with MRI showing bilateral basal ganglia hyperintensities and frontotemporal atrophy.

The presentation of severe encephalopathy, opisthotonos in the first week of life, and characteristic MRI findings (edema in actively myelinating areas like the brainstem and internal capsule, known as the "four dots" sign) points to Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD). This condition is caused by a deficiency in branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase.
This option causes Propionic acidemia, presenting with hyperammonemia, severe ketoacidosis, and bone marrow suppression.

learningObjective: Identify the inheritance pattern and defective protein in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.
leadIn: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy is characterized by progressive proximal muscle weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy, and a highly elevated creatine kinase (CK) level. What is the inheritance pattern and the primary defective protein associated with this disorder?

options.rationale: This option has the correct protein but incorrect inheritance; muscular dystrophies like myotonic dystrophy are autosomal dominant, but Duchenne is strictly X-linked recessive.
This option describes the inheritance and defective gene involved in Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA).

options.text: X-linked dominant, Methyl CpG binding protein 2 (MECP2)
options.rationale: This option describes the inheritance and defective gene responsible for Rett Syndrome.
Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy is an X-linked recessive disorder that results from a mutation or deletion in the gene encoding the dystrophin protein.

learningObjective: Diagnose Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) based on clinical and dermatologic manifestations, and identify associated organ involvement.
vignette: A 7-month-old infant is brought to the pediatric emergency department after experiencing several episodes of rapid truncal flexion and arm extension over the last two days. Wood's lamp examination of the skin reveals multiple hypomelanotic macules on the infant's trunk and extremities.
leadIn: Which of the following cardiac findings is most likely to be present in this infant?

options.rationale: This option is a common congenital heart defect but is particularly associated with Down syndrome, not TSC.
This option is classic for Turner syndrome, not TSC.
This option is characteristically associated with DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome).

The infant presents with infantile spasms and hypomelanotic "ash-leaf spots," which are pathognomonic clinical features of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC). Cardiac rhabdomyomas are the most frequent cardiac finding in infants with TSC and may spontaneously regress over time.

learningObjective: Diagnose infant botulism and identify its definitive clinical treatment.
vignette: A 4-month-old infant is evaluated in the pediatric intensive care unit for progressive, generalized weakness over the past three days. The parents report the infant has had significant constipation for one week, a feeble cry, and difficulty suckling. On physical examination, the infant exhibits severe hypotonia, an absent gag reflex, sluggish pupils, and poor head control.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line targeted management for this patient?

options.rationale: This option is contraindicated, as raw honey is a known source of Clostridium botulinum spores that cause the disorder.
This option is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used in the treatment of Myasthenia Gravis.

The infant's descending paralysis, sluggish pupils, hypotonia, and preceding constipation are classic for infant botulism, frequently caused by ingestion of spores from soil or honey. The definitive and specific treatment is botulism immune globulin (BIG).
This option is the standard treatment for Guillain-Barré syndrome, which causes ascending, not descending, paralysis.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation, MRI findings, and specific enzyme deficiency in Krabbe disease.
vignette: A 5-month-old infant is evaluated for extreme irritability, hypersensitivity to sensory stimuli, and developmental regression. On physical examination, the infant is highly hypertonic with opisthotonic posturing, hyperreflexia, and optic atrophy. A lumbar puncture reveals elevated cerebrospinal fluid protein. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain shows symmetric periventricular white matter T2 hyperintensities with notable sparing of the subcortical U-fibers.
leadIn: This patient's condition is caused by a deficiency in which of the following enzymes?

options.rationale: This option is deficient in Tay-Sachs disease, which involves a cherry-red macula and extreme startle response, but is a gray matter disease rather than a leukodystrophy.
This option is deficient in Canavan disease, which features megalencephaly and prominent involvement of the subcortical U-fibers on MRI.

This option is deficient in Metachromatic Leukodystrophy, which generally presents later in infancy or childhood with ataxia and demyelination that also spares U-fibers but does not typically present with the extreme early irritability and hypersensitivity of Krabbe.

Irritability, hypertonicity, optic atrophy, elevated CSF protein, and white matter demyelination sparing the U-fibers are hallmark features of Krabbe disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy). Krabbe disease is caused by a deficiency of galactocerebrosidase.

learningObjective: Identify standard physiologic targets in the management of elevated intracranial pressure.
leadIn: In the management of severe traumatic brain injury and increased intracranial pressure (ICP), maintaining adequate cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is crucial to prevent secondary ischemic injury. What is the ideal target range for cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) in this clinical setting?

options.rationale: This option represent pressures that are too low and would result in cerebral ischemia.
This option represent pressures that are too low and would result in cerebral ischemia.
The ideal cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) in the setting of increased ICP is >70 mm Hg, with the lower acceptable limit being 50 mm Hg, to maintain adequate cerebral blood flow and oxygenation.
This option represents a severely elevated pressure that exceeds normal vascular autoregulation mechanisms (effective MAP is 60-150 mm Hg) and risks hemorrhagic conversion or worsening edema.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical presentation and primary antecedent pathogen responsible for Sydenham chorea.
vignette: A 9-year-old girl is evaluated in the neurology clinic for abnormal, involuntary movements that began two weeks ago. The parents report the child exhibits sudden, purposeless, nonrhythmic movements of her arms and face that resolve when she sleeps. Additionally, she has become uncharacteristically emotional and impulsive. Medical history is notable for a severe sore throat treated with antibiotics three months ago.
leadIn: This patient's movement disorder is most strongly associated with a prior infection by which of the following organisms?

options.rationale: This option causes Lyme disease, which can cause facial nerve palsy or meningitis, not isolated delayed chorea.

Sydenham chorea is characterized by chaotic, purposeless movements, hypotonia, and emotional lability, typically emerging weeks to months after a Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcal infection. It is a major criterion for acute rheumatic fever.
This option causes Herpes simplex encephalitis, typically presenting acutely with fever, altered mental status, and focal neurologic deficits, rather than delayed chorea.
This option causes infectious mononucleosis and rarely acute cerebellar ataxia, but is not the causative agent of Sydenham chorea.

learningObjective: Identify the clinical trigger and first-line treatment for Childhood Absence Epilepsy.
vignette: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because his teacher noted frequent episodes of staring and unresponsiveness in class. Each episode lasts approximately 5 to 10 seconds, during which he sometimes flutters his eyelids. He returns to his baseline immediately afterward and has no postictal confusion. In the clinic, the physician asks the child to hyperventilate for 3 minutes, which successfully provokes an episode.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic treatment for this patient?

options.rationale: The patient's clinical presentation (brief staring spells, automatisms, no postictal state, and provocation by hyperventilation) is classic for Childhood Absence Epilepsy. Ethosuximide is the most effective and best-tolerated first-line treatment for isolated absence seizures.
This option are generally reserved for focal or generalized tonic-clonic seizures and are not first-line for absence epilepsy.
This option are generally reserved for focal or generalized tonic-clonic seizures and are not first-line for absence epilepsy.
This option is used for focal seizures and can actively worsen absence seizures.

learningObjective: Recall the epidemiology and localization of common pediatric brain tumors.
leadIn: Primary central nervous system tumors are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in pediatric patients. Which of the following represents the most common malignant posterior fossa tumor in the pediatric population?

options.rationale: This option is a benign, calcified tumor that arises in the supratentorial region (suprasellar/pituitary area), not the posterior fossa.
Medulloblastoma is a "small round blue" cell tumor that is the most common malignant CNS tumor overall in children, typically arising in the posterior fossa (cerebellum).
This option occurs in the posterior fossa (4th ventricle) but is far less common than medulloblastoma.
This option is the most common overall brain tumor in children and arises in the posterior fossa, but it is benign (Grade I), not malignant.

learningObjective: Select first-line and contraindicated anti-seizure medications for Dravet syndrome.
vignette: A 14-month-old with a history of prolonged hemiclonic febrile seizures since 5 months of age now has multiple daily afebrile myoclonic and focal seizures. SCN1A sequencing identifies a heterozygous loss-of-function variant.
leadIn: Which of the following anti-seizure medications should be avoided in this patient?

options.rationale: Valproate is one of the recommended first-line agents in Dravet syndrome and is broadly effective across seizure types.

Sodium-channel blockers (lamotrigine, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin) worsen seizures in Dravet syndrome because the SCN1A loss-of-function disproportionately affects inhibitory interneurons; further sodium-channel blockade unmasks excitation.
Clobazam is a standard adjunct in Dravet and is frequently used with stiripentol.
Fenfluramine is FDA-approved for Dravet seizures and substantially reduces convulsive seizure frequency.

learningObjective: Identify first-line treatment for infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis complex.
vignette: A 7-month-old with several hypopigmented macules and a history of cardiac rhabdomyoma develops clusters of brief flexor spasms upon awakening. EEG shows hypsarrhythmia and brain MRI demonstrates multiple cortical tubers.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this patient’s seizures?

options.rationale: In infantile spasms due to tuberous sclerosis complex, vigabatrin is preferred first-line because of higher response rates than hormonal therapy in this specific etiology, despite the risk of irreversible peripheral visual field constriction.
ACTH is first-line for infantile spasms of non-TSC etiology, but vigabatrin has superior response rates when TSC is the cause.
Levetiracetam has limited efficacy in infantile spasms and is not first-line.
Topiramate is occasionally used as add-on for refractory spasms but is not first-line.

learningObjective: Sequence the stepwise pharmacologic treatment of pediatric convulsive status epilepticus.
leadIn: A 4-year-old has been actively convulsing for 8 minutes despite two doses of intramuscular midazolam in the field. On arrival to the emergency department, she remains in generalized convulsive status epilepticus. Which of the following is the most appropriate next medication?

options.rationale: After two adequate benzodiazepine doses without seizure cessation, additional benzodiazepines provide diminishing benefit and increase the risk of respiratory depression. Move to a second-line agent.
Phenobarbital is an acceptable second-line agent but is generally reserved for neonates or when fosphenytoin/levetiracetam/valproate fail; it carries higher sedation and respiratory risk.

After two doses of a benzodiazepine, the next step in pediatric convulsive status epilepticus is a second-line agent: fosphenytoin (20 mg PE/kg), levetiracetam (60 mg/kg), or valproate (40 mg/kg). The ESETT trial showed comparable efficacy among these three.
Continuous anesthetic infusions (midazolam, pentobarbital, propofol) are reserved for refractory status epilepticus after second-line agents fail.

learningObjective: Identify the gene responsible for self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy.
leadIn: A term newborn develops brief, multifocal clonic seizures on day of life 3. Examination, glucose, electrolytes, and brain imaging are normal. The mother reports that her father had a similar self-limited seizure disorder in the newborn period that resolved by 6 months of age. A pathogenic variant in which of the following genes is most likely responsible?

options.rationale: SCN1A loss-of-function causes Dravet syndrome, which presents with prolonged febrile hemiclonic seizures around 6 months of age, not self-limited neonatal seizures.

Self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy is most commonly caused by autosomal-dominant variants in KCNQ2 (and less often KCNQ3), which encode voltage-gated potassium channel subunits. Severe de novo KCNQ2 variants cause a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy; familial loss-of-function variants tend to produce the benign phenotype.
CDKL5 encephalopathy presents with refractory infantile-onset epilepsy with hypsarrhythmia and severe developmental impairment, not self-limited neonatal seizures.
STXBP1 variants cause early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (Ohtahara phenotype), not self-limited seizures.

learningObjective: Recognize the EEG and clinical features of Ohtahara syndrome.
vignette: A 3-week-old former term neonate is admitted for frequent tonic spasms occurring up to 100 times per day in clusters during both wakefulness and sleep. Examination reveals profound encephalopathy. Brain MRI shows a structural malformation of cortical development.
leadIn: Which of the following EEG patterns is most likely to be present in this patient?

options.rationale: Ohtahara syndrome (early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy) presents in the first months of life with tonic spasms and a burst-suppression EEG pattern present in both wakefulness and sleep. Common etiologies include structural brain malformations and STXBP1, KCNQ2, or ARX variants.
Hypsarrhythmia is the EEG signature of West syndrome (infantile spasms), which typically appears at 4–8 months of age.
3-Hz spike-and-wave is the hallmark of childhood absence epilepsy.
CSWS is the EEG hallmark of Landau-Kleffner syndrome / ESES, which presents in school-age children with language regression.

learningObjective: Diagnose and treat pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy.
vignette: A term neonate develops refractory tonic-clonic seizures within hours of birth. The seizures fail to respond to phenobarbital, fosphenytoin, and levetiracetam. There is no perinatal asphyxia, infection, hypoglycemia, or electrolyte derangement. Brain MRI is normal.
leadIn: Administration of which of the following is most appropriate next?

options.rationale: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (caused by ALDH7A1 variants) presents in the neonatal period with seizures refractory to standard anti-seizure medications. A trial of intravenous pyridoxine produces dramatic seizure cessation within minutes and is both diagnostic and therapeutic; lifelong supplementation is required.
Folinic acid–responsive seizures are a related disorder also due to ALDH7A1 variants and warrant a trial when pyridoxine fails, but pyridoxine is the standard first empiric therapy.
Biotinidase deficiency presents with seizures, alopecia, hearing loss, and metabolic acidosis later in infancy, not within hours of birth.
Therapeutic hypothermia is indicated for hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy of moderate to severe degree within the first 6 hours of life; this neonate has no perinatal asphyxia.

learningObjective: Select pharmacologic treatment for electrical status epilepticus during slow-wave sleep (ESES / CSWS).
vignette: A 6-year-old with previously normal development has a 6-month history of language regression, behavioral changes, and academic decline. Overnight EEG demonstrates near-continuous bilateral spike-and-wave activity occupying more than 85% of non-REM sleep.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.rationale: Carbamazepine and other sodium-channel blockers can paradoxically worsen ESES and are generally avoided.
Vigabatrin is first-line for infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis complex; it is not a standard treatment for ESES.

ESES (Landau-Kleffner / continuous spike-and-wave during sleep) is treated with high-dose benzodiazepines (e.g., overnight diazepam pulses) or corticosteroids (oral prednisone or ACTH); both can dramatically reduce sleep-activated spike burden and may improve cognitive trajectory.
Levetiracetam has only modest efficacy for ESES and is rarely sufficient as monotherapy.

learningObjective: Identify appropriate candidates for vagus nerve stimulator placement.
leadIn: Vagus nerve stimulation is most appropriately considered in which of the following patients?

options.text: A 12-year-old with drug-resistant focal epilepsy who is not a candidate for resective surgery
options.rationale: Vagus nerve stimulation is FDA-approved as adjunctive therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy in patients ≥4 years old who are not candidates for resective surgery; it typically achieves about 50% reduction in seizure frequency in roughly half of patients.

options.text: A newly diagnosed 7-year-old with childhood absence epilepsy who has not yet started medication
options.rationale: Childhood absence epilepsy responds well to ethosuximide; VNS is not indicated as first-line treatment.
Functional (non-epileptic) seizures are not treated with neuromodulation; the management is psychiatric and rehabilitative.

options.text: A 9-year-old with a single resectable mesial temporal lesion causing focal seizures
options.rationale: A single resectable epileptogenic lesion is best treated with resective surgery, which offers the highest chance of seizure freedom; VNS is reserved for patients who are not surgical candidates.

learningObjective: Differentiate psychogenic non-epileptic seizures from epileptic seizures by clinical features.
vignette: A 15-year-old presents with episodes of bilateral rhythmic limb shaking lasting 20–30 minutes. The episodes have a gradual buildup, occur exclusively when others are present, include eye closure with active resistance to passive eye opening, and are followed by immediate return to baseline conversation. Multiple captured events on inpatient video-EEG show no ictal or post-ictal EEG changes.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Long duration (>2 minutes), waxing-and-waning motor activity, forced eye closure with resistance, ictal awareness, lack of post-ictal confusion, and an absence of EEG correlate during typical events strongly support psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (functional seizures). Treatment is psychiatric, with cognitive-behavioral therapy as first-line.
Frontal lobe seizures are typically brief (<1 minute), stereotyped, often occur from sleep, and are accompanied by ictal EEG changes in most cases.
Focal seizures with impaired awareness produce reduced responsiveness, automatisms, and post-ictal confusion, with ictal EEG changes in most cases.
Convulsive syncope produces brief (<30 seconds) myoclonic jerks following a clear vasovagal trigger and rapid pallor, not 20–30 minutes of rhythmic shaking.

learningObjective: Identify the genetic cause of PCDH19 epilepsy.
leadIn: A 14-month-old girl has clusters of brief focal seizures triggered by fever, lasting 1–5 days at a time, separated by months of seizure freedom. A heterozygous loss-of-function variant in PCDH19 is identified. Which of the following statements about this disorder is most accurate?

options.text: It is X-linked and only affects hemizygous males
options.rationale: PCDH19 epilepsy is X-linked but, paradoxically, affects heterozygous females and rare mosaic males. Hemizygous transmitting males are typically unaffected, presumably because uniform PCDH19 loss does not produce the cellular interference effect.

options.text: It causes a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with hypsarrhythmia from age 4 months
options.rationale: PCDH19 epilepsy presents with seizure clusters and variable cognitive impact, not the hypsarrhythmia of West syndrome.

options.text: It is X-linked and produces seizures predominantly in heterozygous females and mosaic males
options.rationale: PCDH19-related epilepsy is the second most common monogenic epilepsy after Dravet. The mechanism is cellular interference: a mosaic pattern of PCDH19-expressing and PCDH19-null neurons disrupts cell-cell adhesion and is more pathogenic than uniform loss. Affected patients are therefore heterozygous females and rare somatically mosaic males.

options.text: It responds robustly to lamotrigine monotherapy
options.rationale: No single ASM is reliably effective in PCDH19 epilepsy; treatment is empiric and often unsatisfying. Lamotrigine in particular is not preferred.

learningObjective: Identify the typical age at which a child sits independently.
blueprintTopic: Normal Structure and Life Cycle Development
leadIn: At what median age does a typically developing child first sit independently without support?

options.rationale: At 4 months an infant typically holds the head steady when seated and rolls from front to back, but does not yet sit independently.
Independent sitting (sitting alone for at least a few seconds without hand support) is typically achieved around 6 months. By 9 months most infants sit steadily and can manipulate objects in sitting.
By 9 months most infants are pulling to stand and cruising along furniture. Sitting alone has typically been present for 2–3 months by this point.
12 months is the typical age for first independent steps; sitting is well-established months earlier.

learningObjective: Identify the typical age range for independent walking.
blueprintTopic: Normal Structure and Life Cycle Development
leadIn: A child who is not walking independently by which of the following ages should prompt formal developmental evaluation?

options.rationale: Although the median age for first independent steps is approximately 12 months, the normal range extends to 18 months. Failure to walk by 12 months alone is not a red flag.
Some typically developing children take their first steps as late as 15–18 months, particularly if there is a strong family history of late walking.

A child not walking independently by 18 months has crossed the upper limit of the typical range and warrants formal developmental and neuromuscular evaluation, including consideration of cerebral palsy, hip dysplasia, neuromuscular disorders, and global delay.
Waiting until 24 months delays diagnosis of conditions such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy or spinal muscular atrophy, where earlier identification meaningfully changes management.

learningObjective: Identify the typical age at which the pincer grasp emerges.
blueprintTopic: Normal Structure and Life Cycle Development
leadIn: A neat pincer grasp (picking up a small object with the tip of the thumb and the tip of the index finger) is typically present by which of the following ages?

options.rationale: At 6 months an infant typically uses a raking grasp (gross use of the whole hand) rather than isolated finger movements.
At 9 months an immature ("inferior") pincer using the pad of the thumb and index finger emerges, but not yet the fingertip-to-fingertip neat pincer.
A neat pincer grasp using the fingertips is typically established by 12 months and is one of the prerequisites for self-feeding small objects.
By 18 months pincer grasp is well-established and the child is using utensils with some skill.

learningObjective: Identify the typical ages at which children copy specific geometric shapes.
blueprintTopic: Normal Structure and Life Cycle Development
leadIn: A typically developing child can usually first copy a square at approximately what age?

options.rationale: At 2 years children can imitate a vertical line; copying geometric shapes from a model is not yet expected.
At 3 years children can copy a circle; the square is not yet within reach.

The classic visuomotor sequence is: vertical line by 2, circle by 3, cross by 4, square by 4–5, triangle by 5–6, and diamond by 7. Failure to meet these milestones suggests visuomotor or fine-motor delay.
A diamond is the figure typically copied around age 7. The square is achieved earlier.

learningObjective: Identify the typical age at which a child speaks two-word phrases.
blueprintTopic: Normal Structure and Life Cycle Development
leadIn: A typically developing child first combines two words into meaningful phrases (e.g., "more milk") at approximately what age?

options.rationale: At 12 months children typically speak their first true word; two-word combinations come about a year later.
At 18 months a typical vocabulary is 10–25 single words; two-word phrases are emerging but not yet consistent.

Two-word phrases are typically spoken by 24 months. A useful rule of thumb is that vocabulary should be ≥50 words and the child should be combining two words by age 2; failure to meet this milestone warrants speech and hearing evaluation.
By 36 months children typically speak in 3–4 word sentences and are intelligible to strangers about 75% of the time.

learningObjective: Identify the typical age at which the social smile emerges.
blueprintTopic: Normal Structure and Life Cycle Development
leadIn: The social smile (smiling responsively to a caregiver’s face) is typically present by what age?

options.rationale: A reliable, responsive social smile is typically present by 2 months. Absence of the social smile by this age is an early red flag for autism spectrum disorder, visual impairment, or global delay.
By 4 months social smiling is well-established and the infant laughs aloud. 4 months is too late as a milestone for first emergence.
By 6 months the infant has stranger awareness and engages in reciprocal social interactions; the social smile is many months old.
By 9 months stranger anxiety and joint attention emerge; social smiling has been present since 2 months.

learningObjective: Identify the typical age range for disappearance of the Moro reflex.
blueprintTopic: Normal Structure and Life Cycle Development
leadIn: Persistence of which of the following primitive reflexes beyond 6 months of age is most concerning for an underlying upper motor neuron disorder?

options.rationale: The Moro reflex is normally present at birth and disappears by 4–6 months. Persistence beyond 6 months suggests an upper motor neuron lesion, most commonly cerebral palsy.
The plantar grasp normally persists until 9–12 months, so its presence at 6 months is age-appropriate.
The parachute reflex normally appears at 6–9 months and persists for life; its presence is expected, and its absence at 12 months is pathologic.
An upgoing toe (Babinski) is a normal finding in infants until approximately 12–24 months because of incomplete corticospinal tract myelination.

learningObjective: Identify the typical age at which the parachute (protective extension) reflex appears.
blueprintTopic: Normal Structure and Life Cycle Development
leadIn: The parachute (protective extension) reflex — forward extension of the arms when the suspended infant is plunged head-first toward a surface — typically emerges at what age?

options.rationale: At 2 months postural reflexes are immature; the parachute is not present.
At 4 months the head-righting and lateral propping responses begin to appear, but the parachute reflex emerges later.
The parachute reflex normally emerges between 6 and 9 months and persists throughout life. Its absence by 12 months is abnormal and may indicate cerebral palsy or other CNS dysfunction.
By 12–15 months the parachute reflex should be well-established; its first appearance this late is delayed.

learningObjective: Describe the typical pattern of CNS myelination on MRI.
blueprintTopic: Normal Structure and Life Cycle Development
leadIn: On a brain MRI of a typically developing child, the white matter myelination pattern matures in which general direction?

options.text: Anterior to posterior, superior to inferior, and central to peripheral
options.rationale: Myelination proceeds in the opposite direction in each axis: posterior to anterior, inferior to superior, and central to peripheral.

options.text: Posterior to anterior, inferior to superior, central to peripheral, and proximal to distal
options.rationale: CNS myelination proceeds in a stereotyped pattern: caudal to rostral (brainstem and posterior limb of internal capsule first, then frontal lobes and subcortical U-fibers last), central to peripheral, and proximal to distal. Adult myelination pattern is essentially complete by 24 months on T1 and 36 months on T2.

options.text: Frontal lobe first, then occipital, parietal, and temporal in sequence
options.rationale: The frontal lobes are among the last to myelinate, not the first. Occipital and posterior structures myelinate before frontal.

options.text: Cortex first, then deep white matter, then brainstem
options.rationale: Brainstem myelinates first (largely complete at term), with cortical projections and subcortical U-fibers last to mature.

learningObjective: Identify the typical age at which hand preference develops.
blueprintTopic: Normal Structure and Life Cycle Development
leadIn: A 14-month-old has consistently used the right hand for all reaching and manipulation since 9 months of age, while the left hand remains fisted with limited spontaneous use. This finding is most concerning for which of the following?

options.rationale: Established hand preference before 18–24 months is abnormal. Most typically developing children do not show consistent hand dominance until age 2–4 years.

options.text: A contralateral upper motor neuron lesion (e.g., perinatal stroke or hemiplegic cerebral palsy)
options.rationale: Hand preference established before 18 months is a red flag for contralateral hemiparesis. The "preferred" hand is typically the unaffected one because the affected side cannot be used effectively. Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke and hemiplegic cerebral palsy are the most common causes.
Familial handedness does not produce its phenotype until well after 2 years, and the contralateral hand is normally used capably even before dominance emerges.

options.text: Mild fine-motor delay of no clinical significance
options.rationale: Asymmetric hand use this early should never be dismissed as benign delay; it warrants neuroimaging and a focused neurologic exam.

learningObjective: Select first-line immunotherapy for anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
vignette: A 16-year-old previously healthy adolescent presents with two weeks of bizarre behavior, paranoia, choreoathetoid orofacial movements, and new focal seizures. CSF shows mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and is positive for anti-NMDA receptor IgG antibodies. Pelvic ultrasound is unrevealing.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial immunotherapy?

options.text: High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone plus IVIG (or plasma exchange)
options.rationale: First-line treatment for anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is high-dose IV methylprednisolone with IVIG or plasma exchange. Patients failing first-line therapy escalate to rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide. Tumor screening (especially ovarian teratoma in adolescent girls) is essential because tumor removal is itself therapeutic.
Acyclovir is appropriate empirically while HSV encephalitis is being ruled out, but is not the disease-specific therapy for autoimmune encephalitis.
Rituximab is escalation (second-line) therapy when first-line agents fail. It is not standard first-line.

options.text: Watchful waiting until tumor is identified
options.rationale: Treatment delays worsen long-term outcomes; immunotherapy should not be deferred while tumor work-up is in progress.

learningObjective: Select disease-modifying therapy for spinal muscular atrophy.
vignette: A 6-week-old infant is identified through state newborn screening as having a homozygous deletion of SMN1 with two copies of SMN2. He is asymptomatic on examination.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-modifying therapy?

options.text: Onasemnogene abeparvovec (one-time intravenous AAV9 gene replacement)
options.rationale: Pre-symptomatic infants under 2 years with SMA identified on newborn screening are candidates for one-time AAV9-based SMN1 gene replacement (onasemnogene abeparvovec). Two other SMN-augmenting agents — nusinersen (intrathecal antisense) and risdiplam (oral SMN2 splicing modifier) — are also approved across ages and SMN2 copy numbers; choice depends on age, weight, and access.
IVIG is used in immune-mediated neuromuscular diseases such as Guillain-Barré syndrome and CIDP, not in SMA.
Glucocorticoids are first-line in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, not SMA.

options.text: Watchful waiting until the infant becomes symptomatic
options.rationale: Pre-symptomatic treatment dramatically improves motor outcomes versus initiating therapy after symptom onset, when motor neuron loss has already occurred.

learningObjective: Identify glucocorticoid therapy as standard of care for Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
vignette: A 5-year-old boy with confirmed Duchenne muscular dystrophy is being seen for routine follow-up. He is ambulatory but has begun using the Gowers maneuver to stand from the floor.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-modifying treatment to initiate now?

options.rationale: Daily glucocorticoid therapy is standard of care for ambulatory boys with DMD aged ≥4 years. It prolongs ambulation by approximately 2 years, slows decline of pulmonary and cardiac function, and reduces scoliosis. Vamorolone is an alternative dissociative steroid with comparable efficacy and a more favorable side-effect profile.
Cyclophosphamide is not used in DMD.
Plasmapheresis is used in immune-mediated neuropathies and antibody-mediated CNS disorders, not in genetic muscular dystrophies.

options.text: Watchful waiting until the patient loses ambulation
options.rationale: Delaying glucocorticoids forfeits the window when they can prolong ambulation and protect cardiopulmonary function.

learningObjective: Select maintenance therapy for Wilson disease.
vignette: A 14-year-old with newly diagnosed neurologic Wilson disease has been initiated on chelation therapy with trientine. Six months later her neurologic symptoms have stabilized and 24-hour urinary copper has decreased.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term maintenance therapy?

options.text: Lifelong zinc therapy (often after a course of chelation)
options.rationale: After initial decoppering with a chelator (penicillamine or trientine), maintenance therapy is typically zinc, which induces intestinal metallothionein and blocks dietary copper absorption. Some practitioners maintain trientine indefinitely; either approach must continue lifelong because the underlying ATP7B defect is permanent.

options.text: Discontinue all therapy once urinary copper normalizes
options.rationale: Treatment must continue lifelong; cessation reliably leads to relapse and progressive liver and CNS injury.

options.text: Switch to a low-protein diet alone
options.rationale: Dietary modification (avoiding high-copper foods like shellfish, liver, nuts, chocolate) is supportive but cannot replace pharmacologic copper management.

options.text: Initiate a high-dose oral iron supplement
options.rationale: Iron supplementation has no role in Wilson disease and can compete with copper handling unfavorably.

learningObjective: Identify the criteria and time window for therapeutic hypothermia in neonatal HIE.
vignette: A term newborn with cord arterial pH of 6.9 and a 10-minute Apgar of 4 is admitted to the NICU. At 4 hours of life, examination demonstrates lethargy, hypotonia, weak suck, and seizures. Background EEG is moderately abnormal.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Initiate therapeutic hypothermia (33.5°C core temperature for 72 hours)
options.rationale: Therapeutic hypothermia is indicated for moderate-to-severe HIE in infants ≥36 weeks gestation when initiated within the first 6 hours of life. Cooling to 33.5°C for 72 hours followed by slow rewarming reduces death and major neurodevelopmental disability at 18 months. Eligibility requires evidence of acute peripartum event (cord pH ≤7.0 or BD ≥16, or 10-minute Apgar ≤5) plus moderate-to-severe encephalopathy.

options.text: Initiate prophylactic phenobarbital before seizures recur
options.rationale: Routine prophylactic phenobarbital in HIE has not been shown to improve neurodevelopmental outcome and is not standard. Treat clinical or electrographic seizures as they arise.

options.text: Defer cooling because the infant is already 4 hours old
options.rationale: The 6-hour window is the upper limit, not the start. Initiating cooling at 4 hours is well within the recommended time frame.
Magnesium has been studied as a potential neuroprotectant but is not standard of care for term HIE in current guidelines.

learningObjective: Select first-line pharmacologic treatment for Tourette syndrome.
vignette: An 11-year-old with a 2-year history of motor and vocal tics is now being teased at school and finds his neck-jerking tic painful. The family asks about pharmacologic treatment.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic agent?

options.rationale: Alpha-2 agonists (guanfacine, clonidine) are typically first-line pharmacologic therapy for tics in children, particularly given the high comorbidity with ADHD that they can also help. Comprehensive Behavioral Intervention for Tics (CBIT) is the recommended first-line treatment overall and should be offered when available.

Typical antipsychotics have proven efficacy but carry significant risk of weight gain, sedation, extrapyramidal effects, and tardive dyskinesia. They are reserved for refractory cases, with newer VMAT2 inhibitors and atypicals often preferred when needed.
Levetiracetam has limited evidence in tic disorders and is not standard.
Chronic benzodiazepine therapy is not appropriate for Tourette syndrome given dependence and cognitive risk.

learningObjective: Select disease-modifying therapy for pediatric multiple sclerosis.
vignette: A 14-year-old girl is diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis after two clinically distinct demyelinating events with new T2 lesions on interval MRI. She has had two relapses in the past 12 months and shows enhancing lesions on her current scan.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-modifying therapy?

options.text: A high-efficacy agent such as fingolimod, natalizumab, or anti-CD20 (ocrelizumab/rituximab)
options.rationale: Pediatric MS tends to be highly inflammatory with frequent relapses. The PARADIGMS trial demonstrated superiority of fingolimod over interferon beta-1a in pediatric MS, and current consensus increasingly favors initial high-efficacy therapy in children with active disease over the older "escalation" approach.

options.text: Interferon beta-1a as initial therapy in all pediatric patients
options.rationale: Although interferons were historically first-line, they are now considered modest-efficacy therapy and are typically chosen only for milder disease courses or where higher-efficacy agents are not feasible.
Cyclophosphamide is reserved for refractory cases or fulminant presentations and is not standard first-line therapy due to toxicity.

options.text: No treatment until a third relapse occurs
options.rationale: Withholding therapy after a confirmed second clinical event allows accumulation of irreversible disability and brain volume loss; treatment should not be deferred.

learningObjective: Apply current evidence-based guidance to migraine prophylaxis in children.
vignette: A 12-year-old with episodic migraine without aura has 6–8 disabling headaches per month despite reliable acute treatment with ibuprofen and triptans, adequate hydration, and sleep hygiene. The family asks about preventive medication.
leadIn: Which of the following best reflects current evidence on pharmacologic migraine prevention in children?

options.text: The CHAMP trial showed that placebo was equivalent to amitriptyline and topiramate, so non-pharmacologic strategies (CBT, lifestyle, biobehavioral therapy) should be optimized first
options.rationale: The CHAMP trial (NEJM 2017) demonstrated that placebo, amitriptyline, and topiramate produced statistically indistinguishable reductions in pediatric migraine frequency, with adverse events more common in the active arms. Current practice prioritizes lifestyle counseling, CBT/biobehavioral therapy, and adequate acute treatment before resorting to daily prophylaxis.

options.text: Topiramate is the universally agreed first-line prophylactic agent and should be started immediately
options.rationale: Topiramate has FDA approval for migraine prevention in adolescents and may have a role in selected patients, but CHAMP showed it was not superior to placebo in children, and side effects (cognitive slowing, paresthesias, weight loss) frequently limit use.

options.text: Daily ibuprofen prophylaxis is preferred to neuromodulators
options.rationale: Daily NSAID use risks medication-overuse headache, gastritis, and renal toxicity; it is not appropriate as prophylactic therapy.

options.text: Onabotulinumtoxin-A injections are FDA-approved as first-line in children
options.rationale: OnabotulinumtoxinA is FDA-approved for chronic migraine in adults but not in children under 18; pediatric data are limited.

learningObjective: Select acute and preventive treatment for stroke in sickle cell disease.
vignette: An 8-year-old girl with hemoglobin SS disease presents within 90 minutes of acute right hemiparesis and aphasia. MRI confirms an acute left middle cerebral artery territory infarct. Her hemoglobin S percentage is 78%.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate acute treatment?

options.text: Emergent exchange transfusion to reduce hemoglobin S to under 30%
options.rationale: Acute ischemic stroke in sickle cell disease is treated with emergent exchange transfusion to lower hemoglobin S to under 30% (some recommend under 20%) and total hemoglobin to about 10 g/dL. Chronic transfusion therapy is then continued for secondary prevention. Hydroxyurea and bone marrow transplantation are also disease-modifying.

IV thrombolysis has not been studied prospectively in pediatric stroke and is generally not recommended in children with sickle cell disease, where the underlying mechanism is large-artery vasculopathy rather than thromboembolism.
Antiplatelet therapy alone is inadequate; the priority is to reduce hemoglobin S burden urgently to limit further infarction.
Anticoagulation is not standard for arterial ischemic stroke in sickle cell disease and increases hemorrhagic risk.

learningObjective: Identify standard treatment for Sydenham chorea.
leadIn: A 9-year-old with confirmed Sydenham chorea following streptococcal pharyngitis is being treated. In addition to symptomatic management of the involuntary movements, which of the following is most important to initiate?

options.text: Lifelong (or extended) prophylactic penicillin to prevent rheumatic fever recurrence
options.rationale: Sydenham chorea is a major manifestation of acute rheumatic fever. Long-term secondary prophylaxis with penicillin is recommended to prevent recurrent streptococcal infection and progression of rheumatic heart disease, with duration determined by carditis status (often through age 21 or longer if carditis is present).

Symptomatic treatment of chorea (when needed) is typically with valproate or low-dose dopamine antagonists, but most patients improve spontaneously over weeks to months and do not require chronic therapy.
Aspirin is used for arthritis or carditis in acute rheumatic fever but not as long-term therapy specifically for chorea.
IVIG, plasmapheresis, and corticosteroids have been used in severe or refractory cases but are not standard initial therapy.

learningObjective: Diagnose dopa-responsive dystonia (Segawa syndrome) and identify its definitive treatment.
vignette: A 7-year-old girl is referred for progressive abnormal gait. Her parents note that she walks normally in the morning but develops a "stiff" foot posture and toe-walking by late afternoon.
