Examination at 5 PM shows lower-limb dystonia, brisk reflexes, and equinovarus posturing of the right foot.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.rationale: Diurnal variation (worsening through the day, improvement with sleep) in childhood-onset dystonia is the hallmark of dopa-responsive dystonia (Segawa syndrome), most often due to GCH1 (GTP cyclohydrolase 1) mutations. A small dose of levodopa produces dramatic and sustained improvement and is both diagnostic and definitive treatment. Failing to consider DRD risks misdiagnosis as cerebral palsy.

options.text: Initiate baclofen and refer for selective dorsal rhizotomy
options.rationale: These are management options for spasticity in cerebral palsy, but DRD is exquisitely responsive to levodopa, which should always be tried first.
Benzodiazepines are not first-line in childhood dystonia and do not address the underlying dopaminergic deficit in DRD.

options.text: Order serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urinary copper
options.rationale: Wilson disease is reasonable to consider in childhood movement disorders but typically presents in adolescence with mixed extrapyramidal-psychiatric features and Kayser-Fleischer rings, not isolated diurnal lower-limb dystonia.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical features of Niemann-Pick disease type C.
vignette: An 11-year-old boy presents with a 2-year history of progressive clumsiness, dysarthria, learning difficulties, and recent cataplexy-like episodes triggered by laughter. Examination reveals vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (with preserved oculocephalic reflexes), mild dystonia, ataxia, and splenomegaly.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: The combination of vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (especially downgaze), gelastic cataplexy, splenomegaly, ataxia, dystonia, and progressive cognitive decline in a school-aged child is highly characteristic of Niemann-Pick disease type C, due to NPC1 or NPC2 mutations causing impaired intracellular cholesterol trafficking. Miglustat is approved for the neurologic manifestations.

Wilson disease may present with movement disorders and psychiatric symptoms but does not typically cause vertical supranuclear gaze palsy or cataplexy, and characteristically features Kayser-Fleischer rings and hepatic involvement.
Juvenile Huntington (Westphal variant) presents with rigidity, dystonia, and seizures rather than chorea, but does not feature vertical supranuclear gaze palsy or splenomegaly.

X-ALD presents in school-aged boys with behavioral/cognitive decline, hyperpigmentation, and adrenal insufficiency, with white-matter changes on MRI rather than vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and splenomegaly.

learningObjective: Differentiate stereotypies from tics by clinical features.
leadIn: Which of the following clinical features most reliably distinguishes complex motor stereotypies from motor tics in children?

options.text: Stereotypies are rhythmic, prolonged, fixed in pattern, and non-suppressible by distraction; tics are brief, variable, and suppressible with effort
options.rationale: Stereotypies (e.g., complex hand-flapping during excitement) are rhythmic, repetitive, prolonged, fixed in pattern, often start before age 3, are typically triggered by excitement or concentration, and are not preceded by an urge or suppressible. Tics are brief, jerky, variable, often migrate, are preceded by a premonitory urge, and are at least partially suppressible.

options.text: Stereotypies always involve vocalizations; tics never do
options.rationale: Vocalizations are characteristic of tics (Tourette syndrome). Stereotypies are typically purely motor.

options.text: Stereotypies always indicate autism spectrum disorder; tics never do
options.rationale: Complex motor stereotypies occur in many typically developing children without autism (primary stereotypies). They are common in autism but are not pathognomonic.

options.text: Tics typically begin in infancy; stereotypies typically begin in adolescence
options.rationale: The opposite is true: stereotypies typically begin before age 3, whereas tics typically begin between ages 4 and 8.

learningObjective: Recognize PANDAS and its proposed clinical criteria.
vignette: A 9-year-old previously well boy develops abrupt-onset severe obsessive-compulsive symptoms and motor tics within one week of a confirmed group A streptococcal pharyngitis. His symptoms wax and wane, with each exacerbation temporally linked to documented streptococcal infections.
leadIn: This presentation is most consistent with which of the following diagnoses?

options.text: PANDAS (Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal infections)
options.rationale: PANDAS criteria include prepubertal onset, abrupt-onset OCD or tic disorder, episodic course with relapses temporally linked to group A streptococcal infections, and associated neurologic abnormalities (choreiform movements, motor hyperactivity). PANS is a broader umbrella that does not require streptococcal trigger. Treatment typically combines management of OCD/tics, antimicrobials for active infection, and in some cases immunomodulation.
Sydenham chorea presents with chorea and emotional lability rather than abrupt-onset OCD as the dominant feature, although the conditions overlap conceptually.
Tourette syndrome is characterized by waxing-and-waning tics over more than a year without an abrupt-onset, infection-linked relapsing course or prominent OCD.
Conversion (functional) disorders may include movements but lack the streptococcal temporal linkage and waxing-waning relapsing course.

learningObjective: Recognize ATP1A3-related rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism and alternating hemiplegia of childhood.
vignette: A 6-month-old infant has stereotyped episodes of unilateral hemiplegia lasting hours to days, alternating between sides, occasionally bilateral, with abnormal eye movements and dystonic posturing. Episodes begin and end abruptly, do not correlate with EEG seizure activity, and resolve with sleep. Genetic testing reveals a heterozygous de novo ATP1A3 variant.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: Alternating hemiplegia of childhood is caused by ATP1A3 mutations and presents before 18 months with recurrent episodes of hemiplegia (alternating sides), abnormal ocular movements, dystonia, and developmental delay. Episodes resolve with sleep. Flunarizine reduces severity in some patients. Other ATP1A3-related disorders include rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism and CAPOS syndrome.
Familial hemiplegic migraine produces hemiplegia in association with migraine headache, typically beginning in adolescence or adulthood, not infantile-onset alternating hemiplegia.
Focal epilepsy would be accompanied by ictal EEG correlates and would not selectively alternate sides over hours to days.
Sandifer syndrome features tonic posturing in association with feeding due to GERD, not multi-day hemiplegia.

learningObjective: Recognize tardive dyskinesia from chronic dopamine receptor antagonism.
vignette: A 17-year-old has been on risperidone for 3 years for irritability associated with autism. Over the past 6 months, the family has noticed persistent involuntary chewing and lip-smacking movements as well as choreiform finger movements. The movements are present at rest and persist when the patient is distracted.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Gradual taper of risperidone with consideration of a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine) if symptoms persist
options.rationale: The clinical picture is tardive dyskinesia from chronic dopamine receptor blockade. Management is to attempt cautious withdrawal of the offending agent (paradoxically, abrupt withdrawal can transiently worsen the movements) and to consider VMAT2 inhibitors such as valbenazine or deutetrabenazine, which are FDA-approved for tardive dyskinesia.

options.text: Increase the risperidone dose to suppress the movements
options.rationale: Higher doses of dopamine antagonists may transiently mask tardive dyskinesia but worsen the underlying problem and accelerate progression.
IV diphenhydramine is treatment for acute dystonic reactions to dopamine antagonists, not for chronic tardive dyskinesia.
Levodopa would worsen tardive dyskinesia by adding to the dopaminergic mismatch; it is not appropriate.

learningObjective: Identify iron deficiency as a treatable contributor to pediatric restless legs syndrome.
vignette: A 10-year-old with chronic insomnia describes uncomfortable "creepy-crawly" sensations in his legs that worsen at bedtime, are relieved by walking, and prevent him from falling asleep. Family history is significant for similar symptoms in his mother. Serum ferritin is 18 ng/mL.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.rationale: In children and adolescents with restless legs syndrome and serum ferritin under 50 ng/mL, oral iron supplementation often produces substantial symptom improvement. Dopaminergic agents are generally avoided in pediatric RLS as first-line because of the risk of augmentation; gabapentinoids are used in selected refractory cases.
Dopamine agonists are second- or third-line in pediatric RLS due to augmentation risk and limited safety data in children.
Melatonin can shorten sleep latency but does not address the underlying dopamine-iron pathophysiology of RLS.
Sleep hygiene alone is insufficient when an identified, treatable cause (low iron) is present.

learningObjective: Differentiate chorea from athetosis, dystonia, and myoclonus by clinical features.
leadIn: Which of the following statements most accurately describes chorea?

options.text: Sustained co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles producing patterned twisting postures
options.rationale: This describes dystonia, which is sustained, often patterned, and may build up over time.

options.text: Brief, sudden, shock-like contractions that are typically focal or generalized
options.rationale: This describes myoclonus.

options.text: Brief, irregular, non-stereotyped movements that flow from one body part to another and cannot be predicted
options.rationale: Chorea is brief, irregular, non-stereotyped, and unpredictable, typically involving the limbs and face. Patients often appear restless and may incorporate the movements into purposeful motion (parakinesia). Athetosis describes slower, writhing distal movements and is often considered part of the chorea-athetosis spectrum.

options.text: Coarse rhythmic oscillations of an extremity, present at rest and improved with movement
options.rationale: This describes a resting tremor, classically seen in Parkinson disease.

learningObjective: Recognize focal cerebral arteriopathy as a leading cause of pediatric arterial ischemic stroke.
vignette: A previously healthy 5-year-old presents with acute right hemiparesis. He had primary varicella infection 4 months earlier. MRI shows an acute infarct in the left basal ganglia and MRA demonstrates focal stenosis and irregularity of the supraclinoid left internal carotid artery and proximal middle cerebral artery, without involvement of more distal vessels or the contralateral side.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

options.text: Focal cerebral arteriopathy of childhood (post-varicella arteriopathy)
options.rationale: Focal cerebral arteriopathy of childhood is the single most common cause of arterial ischemic stroke in previously healthy school-aged children. It is unilateral, typically affects the supraclinoid ICA and proximal MCA/ACA, and is often post-infectious (classically following varicella by weeks to months). Most cases are monophasic, and short-course corticosteroids plus antiplatelet therapy are commonly used.

Moyamoya disease is bilateral and progressive, with characteristic "puff of smoke" collateral vasculature on angiography. The unilateral, monophasic post-varicella pattern here is more consistent with FCA.

options.text: Cardiac embolism from a patent foramen ovale
options.rationale: Cardiac embolism produces small, often multiple cortical infarcts in different vascular territories, not focal arteriopathy on imaging.

Dissection typically follows trauma or neck manipulation and on imaging shows long-segment irregularity, intramural hematoma, or a flame-shaped occlusion of the cervical (not intracranial) carotid or vertebral artery.

learningObjective: Recognize the typical presentation of perinatal arterial ischemic stroke.
vignette: A term newborn delivered after an uncomplicated pregnancy develops focal clonic seizures of the right arm and face on day of life 2. The infant is otherwise alert and feeding well between events. Brain MRI on day 3 demonstrates restricted diffusion in the left middle cerebral artery territory.
leadIn: Which of the following best characterizes this presentation?

options.text: Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke, most often presenting with focal seizures in the first days of life
options.rationale: Perinatal arterial ischemic stroke (PAIS) most often presents in term newborns within the first 72 hours of life with focal seizures, typically in the left MCA territory. Risk factors include cardiac disease, hypercoagulable states, infection, and chorioamnionitis. Acute treatment is supportive; anticoagulation is generally not indicated for PAIS.
HIE produces global encephalopathy with seizures and hypotonia and a watershed/deep-grey injury pattern, not a single arterial territory infarct in an otherwise well infant.
Neonatal CSVT typically produces multifocal venous infarcts (often hemorrhagic) along venous drainage rather than a discrete arterial-territory infarct on MRI.
Benign familial neonatal seizures present with brief, multifocal clonic seizures in the setting of normal imaging and a positive family history, not with an MCA territory infarct on MRI.

learningObjective: Recognize the enzyme deficiency and peripheral nerve involvement in Metachromatic Leukodystrophy.
vignette: A 2-year-old child is brought to the clinic for a progressive gait disturbance. The child had learned to walk independently at 14 months of age but now frequently falls and requires support to stand. Physical examination reveals diffuse hypotonia and completely absent deep tendon reflexes. Nerve conduction studies demonstrate markedly delayed conduction velocities. MRI of the brain reveals bilateral, symmetric T2 hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter with a "tigroid" pattern of perivenular sparing.
leadIn: A deficiency in which of the following enzymes is the most likely cause of this patient's regression?

options.rationale: This option is deficient in Hurler syndrome (MPS I).
This option is deficient in Krabbe disease, which presents earlier with extreme irritability, hypertonicity, and optic atrophy.

The combination of a central demyelinating process (tigroid leukodystrophy on MRI) and a peripheral demyelinating process (peripheral neuropathy resulting in areflexia and delayed nerve conduction) presenting in late infancy/early childhood is the hallmark of Metachromatic Leukodystrophy (MLD). MLD is caused by an autosomal recessive deficiency of arylsulfatase A.
This option is deficient in Canavan disease, which presents with marked macrocephaly and lacks the prominent peripheral neuropathy.

learningObjective: Recognize the typical cerebrospinal fluid profile supporting a diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis in an adolescent.
vignette: A 15-year-old female presents with subacute onset of right eye pain with movement and blurred vision. Examination reveals an afferent pupillary defect and central scotoma in the right eye. She had an episode of transient right leg weakness and numbness one year ago that resolved spontaneously. A lumbar puncture is performed as part of a demyelinating workup.
leadIn: Which of the following cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings is highly characteristic of this patient's most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Markedly decreased glucose with elevated neutrophils
options.rationale: This option describes acute bacterial meningitis.

options.text: Presence of oligoclonal bands (OCBs) with a normal white blood cell count
options.rationale: The patient's history of optic neuritis and a prior episode of focal neurologic deficit separated in time and space strongly suggests Relapsing-Remitting Multiple Sclerosis (RRMS). The classic CSF finding supporting MS is the presence of oligoclonal bands (OCBs) representing intrathecal IgG synthesis, typically accompanied by a normal or only slightly elevated white blood cell count.

options.text: Elevated opening pressure greater than 25 cm H2O with normal CSF composition
options.rationale: This option describes idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri). -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- SLEEP DISORDERS (9 Questions)

options.text: Albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, normal white blood cell count)
options.rationale: This option is the hallmark of Guillain-Barré syndrome (AIDP).

learningObjective: Diagnose Kleine-Levin syndrome based on the classic triad.
vignette: A 16-year-old adolescent male is brought to the neurologist because of recurrent episodes of extreme hypersomnolence. During an episode, he sleeps for 18 to 20 hours a day for two weeks. When he is awake during these periods, his parents note that he eats ravenously (hyperphagia) and exhibits hypersexual behaviors and inappropriate comments. Between these distinct episodes, his sleep, behavior, and cognition return completely to normal.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: The triad of episodic hypersomnolence, hyperphagia, and hypersexuality in an adolescent male, punctuated by periods of completely normal behavior and sleep, is the classic, pathognomonic presentation of Kleine-Levin syndrome.
This option typically presents with a decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, and flight of ideas.
This option causes chronic daily fatigue and poor school performance due to airway obstruction, not episodic hyperphagia/hypersexuality.
This option presents with chronic, daily excessive daytime sleepiness, not multi-week episodic hypersomnolence with severe behavioral changes.

learningObjective: Identify Delayed Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder in an adolescent.
vignette: A 15-year-old girl is referred to the sleep clinic for insomnia and morning fatigue. Her parents report she cannot fall asleep until 2:00 AM or 3:00 AM every night, despite going to bed at 10:00 PM. She struggles immensely to wake up for school at 6:30 AM and frequently falls asleep in her morning classes. However, during the summer and on weekends, she falls asleep at 3:00 AM, wakes up naturally at 11:30 AM, and feels completely refreshed and energetic all day.
leadIn: This patient's sleep difficulty is best explained by an abnormality involving which of the following?

options.rationale: This option causes an urge to move the legs at night, relieving discomfort.
This option causes narcolepsy (chronic daytime sleepiness regardless of nighttime sleep duration, plus REM intrusion).
This option causes obstructive sleep apnea (snoring, fragmented sleep).

The patient has a classic Delayed Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder, which is very common in adolescents. It is a circadian rhythm sleep disorder characterized by a significant delay in the phase of the major sleep period relative to desired sleep/wake times. When allowed to sleep on her own schedule (weekends/summer), her sleep architecture and duration are completely normal, distinguishing it from true insomnia or primary hypersomnolence.

learningObjective: Differentiate benign neonatal sleep myoclonus from epileptic seizures.
vignette: A 2-week-old neonate is evaluated for repetitive jerking movements. The mother reports that the infant exhibits symmetric, synchronous myoclonic jerks of the arms and legs that occur only when the infant is fast asleep. The jerking stops immediately and completely when the mother gently shakes the infant awake. An electroencephalogram (EEG) performed during a sleep cycle, capturing these jerking events, is completely normal.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassurance that this is a benign, self-limiting condition
options.rationale: The occurrence of myoclonic jerks exclusively during sleep that cease immediately upon awakening, coupled with a normal EEG, is the classic presentation of benign neonatal sleep myoclonus. It is a non-epileptic paroxysmal disorder that is entirely self-limiting, requiring only parental reassurance.
This option are treatments for neonatal seizures, which are inappropriate for a non-epileptic condition.
This option are treatments for neonatal seizures, which are inappropriate for a non-epileptic condition.

options.text: Lumbar puncture and initiation of empiric acyclovir
options.rationale: This option is the workup for suspected neonatal encephalitis/meningitis, which presents with encephalopathy, fever, and true seizures.

learningObjective: Correlate Restless Legs Syndrome with iron deficiency.
vignette: An 8-year-old boy has difficulty initiating sleep. Every night, as he lies in bed trying to fall asleep, he complains of an uncomfortable "creepy-crawly" sensation deep in his calves. He states the only way to make the feeling go away is to get out of bed and walk around the room or stretch his legs. The sensation returns when he gets back into bed.
leadIn: In addition to a comprehensive history, the initial laboratory evaluation for this patient should specifically include which of the following tests?

options.rationale: This option evaluates for narcolepsy.

The patient describes the classic symptoms of Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS): an urge to move the legs, accompanied by uncomfortable sensations that occur predominantly at rest/evening and are relieved by movement. RLS in children and adults is highly associated with central iron deficiency. Checking a serum ferritin level is standard practice, and iron supplementation is often curative if levels are low.
This option evaluates for diabetes mellitus (which can cause painful diabetic neuropathy, but RLS is driven by dopamine/iron pathways).
This option evaluates for muscular dystrophies/myopathies.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical features of Nightmare Disorder.
vignette: A 6-year-old girl frequently wakes up crying between 4:00 AM and 5:00 AM. When her parents enter her room, she is fully awake, easily consoled, and vividly describes a frightening dream about a monster chasing her. She often resists going back to sleep because she is afraid the dream will return. She does not thrash or sweat profusely during the sleep period prior to waking.
leadIn: These events are most likely occurring during which of the following stages of sleep?

options.rationale: N2 (light sleep) is when most non-REM time is spent, but it is not the stage associated with vivid dream imagery; nightmares are a REM phenomenon.
N1 is the brief transition between wake and sleep; nightmares are not characteristic of this stage.

This option is the stage during which Sleep Terrors (a non-REM arousal disorder) occur, typically in the first third of the night, characterized by thrashing, inconsolability, and complete amnesia for the event. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- AUTONOMIC DISORDERS (4 Questions)

Nightmares are a REM-related parasomnia. Because REM sleep is concentrated in the latter half of the night, nightmares typically occur in the early morning hours. Children awake fully alert, remember the dream vividly, and can be consoled.

learningObjective: Diagnose Familial Dysautonomia (Riley-Day Syndrome).
vignette: An 18-month-old infant of Ashkenazi Jewish descent is evaluated for failure to thrive, recurrent aspiration pneumonias, and episodic extreme blood pressure fluctuations. The parents note that the child never produces tears when crying. On physical examination, the child has an absent corneal reflex, decreased response to painful stimuli, and inspection of the tongue reveals a completely smooth surface with an absence of fungiform papillae.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.rationale: The constellation of absent tears (alacrima), insensitivity to pain, temperature dysregulation, BP instability, and a smooth tongue (absence of fungiform papillae) in an Ashkenazi Jewish child is pathognomonic for Familial Dysautonomia (Riley-Day syndrome, HSAN III).
This option is a lysosomal storage disease presenting with acroparesthesias and angiokeratomas.
This option is an acute post-infectious polyneuropathy causing ascending flaccid paralysis.

options.text: Congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis (CIPA)
options.rationale: This option presents with profound insensitivity to pain and anhidrosis leading to hyperthermia and self-mutilation, but tear production is typically normal and fungiform papillae are present.

learningObjective: Recognize the clinical triad of Horner syndrome and its association with neuroblastoma in infants.
vignette: A 1-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician because his parents noticed his left eye looks "droopy" and his left pupil is smaller than the right (anisocoria). They also note that when the child plays and gets hot, only the right side of his face sweats and becomes flushed; the left side remains pale and dry. A firm, palpable mass is discovered in the left cervical/apical thoracic region.
leadIn: This autonomic physical examination triad (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) is caused by a disruption of which of the following neural pathways?

options.rationale: The clinical triad of ptosis, miosis (constricted pupil), and anhidrosis defines Horner syndrome. It results from a disruption of the oculosympathetic pathway. In an infant with an associated cervical or apical thoracic mass, this is highly suspicious for a neuroblastoma compressing the sympathetic chain.

options.text: Somatic motor fibers of the facial nerve
options.rationale: This option disruption causes facial weakness (Bell's palsy), not pupillary/sweating autonomic signs.

options.text: Parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve
options.rationale: This option disruption causes a dilated, poorly reactive pupil (mydriasis), not miosis.

options.text: Sensory fibers of the trigeminal nerve
options.rationale: This option carries sensory information from the face.

learningObjective: Recognize the neurovascular and autonomic neuropathic manifestations of Fabry disease.
blueprintTopic: Autonomic Nervous System Disorders / Metabolic Diseases
vignette: A 16-year-old adolescent male presents to the clinic with severe, episodic burning pain in his hands and feet (acroparesthesias) that is prominently induced by exposure to cold temperatures. He also complains that he is unable to sweat normally (hypohidrosis) when playing sports, causing him to overheat. Physical examination reveals punctate, non-blanching blue-black lesions (angiokeratomas) on his lower abdomen and groin.
leadIn: The underlying enzymatic deficiency in this disorder results in the toxic accumulation of which of the following substances in epithelial, mesenchymal, and neural cells?

options.rationale: This option accumulates in Adrenoleukodystrophy.

The clinical triad of acroparesthesias (small fiber neuropathy), profound autonomic dysfunction (anhidrosis/hypohidrosis causing heat intolerance), and angiokeratomas is diagnostic of Fabry disease. It is an X-linked recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by an alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, which results in the toxic accumulation of ceramide trihexoside.
This option accumulates in Krabbe disease.
This option accumulates in Molybdenum cofactor deficiency.

learningObjective: Differentiate pallid breath-holding spells from seizures based on autonomic triggers and clinical sequence.
blueprintTopic: Autonomic Nervous System Disorders / Episodic Disorders
vignette: A 14-month-old toddler is running through the house and trips, lightly bumping his head on the carpet. The injury is minor, but he is startled. He lets out a brief gasp, immediately turns stark white (pallor), loses muscle tone, and falls unconscious to the floor. He remains limp for 20 seconds, exhibits a few brief myoclonic jerks, and then spontaneously awakens. Within minutes, he is playing normally again.
leadIn: The loss of consciousness in this event is driven by an exaggerated autonomic reflex predominantly mediated by which of the following?

options.text: Intense Valsalva maneuver preventing venous return to the right heart
options.rationale: This option describes the mechanism of a cyanotic breath-holding spell, which is triggered by anger/frustration and vigorous crying/holding breath in expiration.

options.text: Vagal nerve hypertonia causing profound bradycardia or asystole
options.rationale: The sequence of a sudden, unexpected pain or startle followed immediately by extreme pallor, loss of tone, and brief syncope (sometimes with brief convulsive myoclonus) is the classic presentation of a pallid breath-holding spell. It is driven by an exaggerated, centrally mediated vagal (parasympathetic) reflex leading to profound bradycardia or transient asystole, dropping cerebral perfusion.

options.text: Hypocretin deficiency leading to sudden muscle atonia
options.rationale: This option describes cataplexy seen in narcolepsy. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- VASCULAR NEUROLOGY (3 Questions)

options.text: Sudden failure of the sympathetic nervous system to maintain vascular tone
options.rationale: This option describes orthostatic hypotension or classic vasovagal syncope in older patients.

learningObjective: Recognize the angiographic appearance and clinical presentation of Moyamoya disease.
vignette: A 6-year-old girl of East Asian descent is brought to the emergency department after experiencing sudden, transient weakness of her right arm and difficulty speaking. Her parents note that the episode began immediately after she was crying vigorously and hyperventilating because she dropped her ice cream cone. She had a similar transient episode of left-sided weakness two months ago.
leadIn: A cerebral angiogram is performed. Which of the following classic descriptions best matches the expected findings at the base of the brain in this disorder?

options.rationale: This option describes fibromuscular dysplasia or reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS).

The child has Moyamoya disease, characterized by non-inflammatory progressive occlusion of the intracranial internal carotid arteries and the compensatory formation of a fragile collateral vascular network at the base of the brain. In children, it classically presents with recurrent alternating TIAs or ischemic strokes that are uniquely provoked by hyperventilation (like intense crying), which causes cerebral vasoconstriction and transiently drops perfusion past the stenosis. The collateral network is classically described as a "puff of smoke" on angiography.
This option describes a developmental venous anomaly (DVA).
This option describes the classic MRI appearance of a cavernous malformation.

learningObjective: Localize Horner syndrome using pharmacologic testing.
vignette: A 45-year-old woman presents with right-sided ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis. To definitively localize the lesion within the oculosympathetic pathway, the neurologist instills 1% hydroxyamphetamine drops into both eyes. Following administration, the left pupil dilates widely, but the right pupil does not change in size.
leadIn: This pharmacologic response confirms that the lesion is located in which of the following?

options.rationale: This option would result in dilation of the pupil after hydroxyamphetamine.
This option would result in dilation of the pupil after hydroxyamphetamine.

Hydroxyamphetamine stimulates the release of stored norepinephrine from the third-order (postganglionic) neuron. If the affected pupil fails to dilate, it indicates that the third-order neuron is damaged and depleted of norepinephrine. If it does dilate, the lesion involves the 1st or 2nd order neurons (which leave the 3rd order neuron intact).

options.text: Parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve
options.rationale: This option is the pathway for pupillary constriction, not sympathetic dilation.

learningObjective: Localize visual field defects to the temporal radiations (Meyer's loop).
vignette: A 35-year-old man undergoes a right anterior temporal lobectomy for medically refractory complex partial seizures. Post-operatively, his seizures are well-controlled, but he reports a new visual disturbance.
leadIn: Formal perimetry testing is most likely to reveal which of the following visual field defects?

options.rationale: This option is caused by an optic chiasm lesion.

The inferior optic radiations travel through the temporal lobe, forming Meyer's loop. They carry visual information from the contralateral superior visual field. Thus, a right temporal lobe lesion causes a left homonymous superior quadrantanopia (a "pie in the sky" defect).
This option is caused by a lesion in the parietal lobe (superior optic radiations).
This option is caused by a complete left optic tract or left occipital lobe lesion.

learningObjective: Identify the relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil).
vignette: A 25-year-old woman presents with acute, painful vision loss in her right eye. During the physical examination, the physician performs the swinging flashlight test. When light is shined into the left eye, both pupils constrict briskly. When the light is rapidly swung to the right eye, both pupils paradoxically dilate.
leadIn: This abnormal pupillary response specifically localizes a lesion to which of the following structures?

options.rationale: The swinging flashlight test detects a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD, or Marcus Gunn pupil). When light shines in the affected eye (right optic nerve lesion), the reduced afferent signal causes both pupils to dilate relative to their constricted state from the normal eye's illumination.
This option carries efferent pupillary fibers. A lesion here causes a fixed, dilated pupil that does not constrict when light shines in either eye.
This option handles efferent parasympathetic outflow.
This option lesions cause bitemporal hemianopsia, not an isolated RAPD.

learningObjective: Identify the cranial nerves traversing the cavernous sinus.
leadIn: A 35-year-old woman develops a rapid-onset complete ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, facial numbness, and proptosis secondary to a cavernous sinus thrombosis. Which of the following cranial nerves travels directly through the center of the cavernous sinus adjacent to the internal carotid artery, rather than within its lateral dural wall?

options.rationale: , and D are located in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus.
, and D are located in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus.
CN V1 (ophthalmic division of the trigeminal) runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus alongside CN III, CN IV, and CN V2 — not centrally with the internal carotid and CN VI.
Within the cavernous sinus itself, the internal carotid artery and the Abducens nerve (CN VI) run centrally. The lateral wall contains CN III, CN IV, CN V1, and CN V2.

learningObjective: Localize Millard-Gubler syndrome to the ventral pons.
vignette: A 62-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents with acute neurologic deficits. On examination, he has a left-sided lower motor neuron facial weakness (Bell's palsy pattern) and an inability to abduct his left eye (left CN VI palsy). However, he also exhibits a dense right-sided spastic hemiparesis.
leadIn: This specific constellation of crossed deficits is known as Millard-Gubler syndrome and is caused by an infarction in which of the following regions?

options.rationale: This option causes Wallenberg syndrome (loss of pain/temp, ataxia, Horner's).
This option causes a pure sensory stroke. HIGH-YIELD ABPN TOPICS (CHILD & GENERAL NEUROLOGY)
This option causes Weber syndrome (ipsilateral CN III palsy, contralateral hemiplegia).

Millard-Gubler syndrome is characterized by ipsilateral facial nerve (CN VII) and abducens nerve (CN VI) palsies combined with contralateral hemiplegia (due to corticospinal tract involvement). It localizes to the basis pontis (ventral pons).

learningObjective: Identify the classic histopathological findings of Alzheimer disease.
leadIn: Alzheimer disease is the most common cause of neurodegenerative dementia, typically presenting with prominent loss of anterograde memory. A definitive diagnosis of Alzheimer disease at autopsy requires the identification of two hallmark histopathological features in the cerebral cortex. Which of the following pairs represents these classic findings?

options.text: Pick bodies containing tau and diffuse severe atrophy of the frontal and temporal lobes
options.rationale: This option describes Pick's disease (a subtype of frontotemporal dementia).

options.text: Intracellular Lewy bodies containing alpha-synuclein and loss of pigmented neurons in the substantia nigra
options.rationale: This option describes the pathology of Parkinson's disease and Dementia with Lewy Bodies.

options.text: Spongiform vacuolization of the gray matter and florid plaques containing prion protein
options.rationale: This option describes Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

options.text: Neuritic plaques containing beta-amyloid and neurofibrillary tangles containing hyperphosphorylated tau
options.rationale: The hallmark pathology of Alzheimer's disease includes extracellular neuritic (amyloid) plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (composed of abnormally hyperphosphorylated tau).
